# IOStreams

> IOStreams is a Ruby gem for streaming I/O that makes file formats, compression, encryption,
> and storage mechanisms (local file, S3, Google Cloud Storage, SFTP, HTTP) transparent to the application. Files of
> any size are processed one block at a time without loading them into memory.

The public entry points are `IOStreams.path(...)`, `IOStreams.join(...)` and `IOStreams.stream(io)`,
which return a path or stream. Its settings describe the file: `#stream`/`#option` for compression and
encryption, `#encoding` for its text, `#format` and `#schema` for its rows and records, and `#raw` to
read and write it as stored. It is read and written with `#each`, `#reader`, `#writer`, `#read`,
`#write`, `#copy_from`, `#copy_to` and `#move_to`, in the `:stream`, `:line`, `:array`, `:hash` or `:slice` mode.

# What is IOStreams?

IOStreams is a streaming library for Ruby that makes the format, compression, encryption and storage location of a
file transparent to your code. Read and write files of any size, one block at a time, whether they are CSV, JSON,
Excel or Parquet, compressed with gzip, zip, bzip2 or Zstandard, encrypted with PGP, and whether they are stored on
local disk, AWS S3, Google Cloud Storage, an SFTP server, or a web server.

## Why IOStreams?

Processing files in Ruby usually means writing different code for every variation. One customer sends a gzip
compressed CSV file, another a PGP encrypted file, a third uploads an Excel spreadsheet. The files are on local disk in
development, but in AWS S3 in production. Each combination needs its own handling, and reading a large file into
memory all at once risks exhausting it.

Consider reading a gzip compressed CSV file from S3, one record at a time, _without_ IOStreams:

~~~ruby
require "aws-sdk-s3"
require "zlib"
require "csv"

response = Aws::S3::Client.new.get_object(bucket: "my-bucket", key: "data.csv.gz")
gz       = Zlib::GzipReader.new(response.body)
headers  = nil
gz.each_line do |line|
  row = CSV.parse_line(line)
  if headers.nil?
    headers = row
  else
    record = headers.zip(row).to_h
    # ... process record ...
  end
end
~~~

Change that file to plain CSV, to a PGP encrypted file, or move it back to local disk, and this code has to change
every time. It also downloads the whole object before the first record is processed. With IOStreams the same code
handles all of them, while it streams the file:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("s3://my-bucket/data.csv.gz").each(:hash) do |record|
  # ... process record ...
end
~~~

IOStreams reads the file name, `data.csv.gz`, infers that it is a gzip compressed CSV file, and builds the
[pipeline of streams](#how-it-works) that reads it from S3, decompresses it, and parses it. Point the same code at
`data.csv`, `data.xlsx`, a local file, or `data.csv.pgp` with its passphrase set on the path, and nothing else
changes.

### One API, whatever the format, compression or encryption

IOStreams detects the streams of a file from the extensions of its name and applies them in order, so
`sample.csv.gz.pgp` is decrypted, then decompressed, then parsed as CSV, without a line of special handling. The same
code that reads a plain CSV file also reads an Excel spreadsheet, a PGP encrypted JSON file, or a Parquet file. A
single background job can process files from many senders, in many formats, with no code for each format.

### One API, wherever the file is stored

Local disk, AWS S3, S3 compatible stores, Google Cloud Storage, SFTP and HTTP(S) share the same `IOStreams.path` interface, and the
same operations, such as `#each_child`, `#exist?`, `#delete` and `#move_to`, behave the same way on each of them.

### Constant memory, even for huge files

Everything is read and written a block at a time, so a 10 GB compressed file uses about as much memory as a 10 KB
one, and the code that processes ten rows processes ten million without changes. Files on S3 and HTTP are read as
your code reads them, and S3 objects are uploaded as they are written, without a copy on local disk.

### Paths are configuration, not code

A path or url can come from an environment variable or a configuration system, so the exact same application code
runs against local files in development and S3 or SFTP in production. With [roots](config#add_root), the storage
location is set once, at startup. See [Paths are configuration](config#paths-are-configuration).

## A quick tour

Write a CSV file, compressed with gzip, a record at a time:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("people.csv.gz").writer(:hash) do |io|
  io << {"name" => "Jack", "born" => "1990-02-01"}
  io << {"name" => "Jill", "born" => "1992-07-14"}
end
~~~

Read it back a record at a time, as a Hash, while it is decompressed:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("people.csv.gz").each(:hash) do |person|
  p person
end
# {"name" => "Jack", "born" => "1990-02-01"}
# {"name" => "Jill", "born" => "1992-07-14"}
~~~

The same code reads `s3://my-bucket/people.csv.gz` or `sftp://sftp.example.org/people.csv.gz` instead: only the name
changes. See [Paths](path) for the gems and credentials of each store.

Describe the columns of the file with a [schema](formats#schema), so that each value is read as its type:

~~~ruby
people = IOStreams.path("people.csv.gz").schema(
  fields: [
    {name: "name", type: "string"},
    {name: "born", type: "date"}
  ]
)
people.each(:hash) do |person|
  p person
end
# {"name" => "Jack", "born" => #<Date: 1990-02-01 ((2447924j,0s,0n),+0s,2299161j)>}
# {"name" => "Jill", "born" => #<Date: 1992-07-14 ((2448818j,0s,0n),+0s,2299161j)>}
~~~

Convert it to another format by copying it to a path whose name says so:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("people.json").copy_from(people, mode: :hash)

IOStreams.path("people.json").read
# => "{\"name\":\"Jack\",\"born\":\"1990-02-01\"}\n{\"name\":\"Jill\",\"born\":\"1992-07-14\"}\n"
~~~

The target can be anywhere, compressed and encrypted, such as JSON on S3, encrypted with PGP for a partner whose public
key is in your keyring, see [PGP](pgp):

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("s3://my-bucket/exports/people.json.gz.pgp").
  option(:pgp, recipient: "partner@example.org").
  copy_from(people, mode: :hash)
~~~

Write an Excel spreadsheet from records. A Parquet file is written the same way, with a schema that gives the type of
each column, see [Parquet files](formats#parquet-files):

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("report.xlsx").writer(:hash) do |io|
  io << {"name" => "Jack", "total" => 12}
  io << {"name" => "Jill", "total" => 20}
end
~~~

Rescue a missing file the same way wherever it is stored, so that the path can come from configuration:

~~~ruby
begin
  IOStreams.path("missing.csv").each(:hash) do |record|
    p record
  end
rescue IOStreams::Errors::NotFound => e
  puts "Nothing to process: #{e.message}"
end
# Nothing to process: No such file or directory @ rb_sysopen - missing.csv
~~~

## How it works

* A **path** names a file and the store that holds it, such as `IOStreams.path("s3://my-bucket/people.csv.gz")`.
  `IOStreams.stream(io)` reads or writes an IO that you already have, such as a `StringIO`, the same way. See
  [Paths](path).
* Each extension at the end of the file name, such as `.gz` or `.pgp`, names a **stream** that the data passes
  through, a block at a time. In order, they are the **pipeline** of the path: reading `people.csv.gz.pgp` decrypts the
  data and then decompresses it, and writing it compresses the data and then encrypts it. See
  [Streams from the file name](streams#streams-from-the-file-name).
* The **tabular format** of the file, such as `.csv`, `.json` or `.xlsx`, says how its rows and records are stored.
  See [Tabular formats](formats).
* The **mode** says what your code reads or writes: blocks of bytes (`:stream`), lines of text (`:line`), **rows**,
  each an Array of the values of a line (`:array`), or **records**, each a Hash of those values by column name
  (`:hash`). For a CSV file, the names of the columns come from its **header row**, its first line. See
  [Reading and writing](streams).
* A **schema** names the columns of a file, gives the type of each one, such as a `Date`, and says which columns a
  file can have. See [Schema](formats#schema).

## Common tasks

**Read a CSV, JSON or Excel file a record at a time**, see [Reading](streams#reading):

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("people.csv").each(:hash) do |record|
  p record
end
~~~

**Write a file compressed with gzip**, see [gzip](extensions#gzip):

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("people.csv.gz").writer(:hash) do |io|
  io << {name: "Jack", born: "1990-02-14"}
end
~~~

**Convert CSV to JSON**, see [Converting rows and records](copy_files#converting-rows-and-records):

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("people.json").copy_from("people.csv", mode: :hash)
~~~

**Export a database query to CSV, keeping the types of its columns**, see [Exporting queries](queries):

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("orders.csv").copy_from(Order.where(paid: true), mode: :hash)
~~~

**Upload a file to S3**, see [Copying and moving](copy_files):

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("s3://my-bucket/people.csv").copy_from("people.csv")
~~~

**Encrypt a file with PGP**, see [PGP](pgp):

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("people.csv.pgp").
  option(:pgp, recipient: "partner@example.org").
  copy_from("people.csv")
~~~

**Decrypt a PGP file**, see [PGP](pgp):

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("people.csv.pgp").
  option(:pgp, passphrase: ENV.fetch("PGP_PASSPHRASE")).
  read
~~~

**Read numbers and dates as their types, and skip the other columns**, see [Schema](formats#schema):

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("people.csv").
  schema(fieldsMatch: "partial", fields: [{name: "born", type: "date"}]).
  each(:hash) do |record|
    p record
  end
~~~

**Read a Windows-1252 file as UTF-8**, see [Character encoding](streams#character-encoding):

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("people.csv").encoding("Windows-1252:UTF-8").each(:hash) do |record|
  p record
end
~~~

**Process a large file in background jobs**, a slice of 500 rows in each job, see [Background jobs](background_jobs):

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("s3://my-bucket/people.csv.gz").each(:slice, size: 500) do |slice|
  ImportPeopleSliceJob.perform_later(slice.to_h)
end
~~~

**List the CSV files in a directory or bucket**, see [Listing files](path#listing-files):

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("s3://my-bucket/inbound").each_child("*.csv") do |path|
  p path
end
~~~

**Keep the location of the files in configuration**, see [Configuration](config#add_root):

~~~ruby
# At startup
IOStreams.add_root(:default, ENV.fetch("FILES_ROOT"))

# Then anywhere in the application
IOStreams.join("people.csv").each(:hash) do |record|
  p record
end
~~~

**Handle a missing file wherever it is stored**, see [Errors](errors):

~~~ruby
begin
  IOStreams.path("s3://my-bucket/people.csv").read
rescue IOStreams::Errors::NotFound
  puts "people.csv has not arrived yet"
end
~~~

**Keep untrusted file names within a directory**, see [Security](security#allowed-paths):

~~~ruby
IOStreams.add_allowed_path("/var/my_app/uploads")
~~~

## What IOStreams supports

| Storage | Url |
|---------|-----|
| [Local files](path#file) | `/data/file.csv`, `~/data/file.csv`, `file:///data/file.csv` |
| [AWS S3](path#aws-s3-s3), and S3 compatible stores | `s3://bucket/key` |
| [Google Cloud Storage](path#google-cloud-storage-gs) (experimental) | `gs://bucket/name` |
| [SFTP](path#sftp-sftp) | `sftp://host/path`, `sftp://host/~/path` within the login directory |
| [HTTP and HTTPS](path#http-http-https) | `https://host/path`, read with GET and written with PUT |

| Tabular format | Extension | Read | Write |
|----------------|-----------|------|-------|
| [CSV](formats#csv-and-psv-files) | `.csv` | yes | yes |
| [Pipe separated values](formats#csv-and-psv-files) | `.psv` | yes | yes |
| [JSON Lines](formats#json-files), one JSON object on each line | `.json` | yes | yes |
| [Fixed width](formats#fixed-width-files) | `.fixed`, or `format(:fixed)` | yes | yes |
| [Excel spreadsheet](formats#excel-spreadsheets) | `.xlsx`, `.xlsm` | yes | yes |
| [Apache Parquet](formats#parquet-files) | `.parquet` | yes | yes |
| [Text](formats#text), such as one email address on each line | `.text`, or `format(:text)` | yes | yes |

| Compression and encryption | Extension |
|----------------------------|-----------|
| [gzip](extensions#gzip) | `.gz`, `.gzip` |
| [bzip2](extensions#bzip2) | `.bz2` |
| [Zip](extensions#zip) | `.zip` |
| [Zstandard](extensions#zstandard) | `.zst` |
| [PGP](pgp), with GnuPG | `.pgp`, `.gpg` |
| [Symmetric Encryption](extensions#symmetric-encryption) | `.enc` |

## Installation

Add the gem to your Gemfile, for Ruby 3.3 or later:

~~~ruby
gem "iostreams"
~~~

IOStreams itself needs no other gems. Each feature that needs one loads it when it is first used, so add only the
gems of the features that your application uses:

| Feature | Gems and programs |
|---------|-------------------|
| AWS S3, Google Cloud Storage | `aws-sdk-s3` |
| SFTP | The `sftp` program of OpenSSH, and `sshpass` to log in with a password. `net-sftp` to list, check and delete files, with `ed25519` and `bcrypt_pbkdf` for ed25519 keys |
| bzip2 | `bzip2-ffi` |
| Zip | `rubyzip` to read, `zip_kit` to write |
| Zstandard | `zstd-ruby`, or on JRuby the zstd-jni jar, see [Compression and encryption](extensions#zstandard) |
| Excel spreadsheets | `creek` to read, `xlsxtream` to write |
| PGP | The `gpg` program of GnuPG 2.1 or later, see [PGP](pgp#installation) |
| Symmetric Encryption | `symmetric-encryption` |
| Parquet | `parquet`, which is not available on JRuby |
| [Active Record queries](queries) | `activerecord` 7.2 or later, and the driver of the database: `pg`, `mysql2` or `sqlite3` |
| The `number` fields of a schema | `bigdecimal`, a bundled gem from Ruby 3.4 |

When a gem is missing, the feature that needs it raises `LoadError`, naming the gem to install.

## Next steps

* The [tutorial](tutorial) walks through reading and writing files, step by step.
* [Reading and writing](streams): lines, rows, records and text encodings.
* [Tabular formats](formats): CSV, JSON, Excel, fixed width and Parquet files, and schemas.
* [Compression and encryption](extensions): gzip, zip, bzip2, Zstandard, PGP and Symmetric Encryption.
* [Paths](path): local files, S3, Google Cloud Storage (experimental), SFTP and HTTP, and the operations on a path.
* [Copying and moving](copy_files): copying files between stores, and converting them on the way.
* [Exporting queries](queries): exporting the rows of an Active Record query to any format and store.
* [Background jobs](background_jobs): processing a large file or query in background jobs, in parallel, or in one job that
  resumes where it stopped.
* [Errors](errors): rescuing a missing file the same way wherever it is stored.
* [PGP](pgp): encrypting, decrypting, signing and verifying files, and managing keys.
* [Configuration](config): roots, temp files and logging.
* [Security](security): allowed paths, untrusted urls and credentials.
* [Upgrading](upgrading): what changed in v3.0, for applications that use an earlier version.

---

# File / Data Streaming with Ruby

When a file is small it can simply be read into memory. A file of many gigabytes cannot. On Linux, pipes stream the
data between programs instead, a block at a time:

~~~
# Count the lines in a file that was compressed with gzip
cat abc.gz | gunzip -c | wc -l
~~~

Ruby reads and writes files as streams, but has no built-in way to pass one stream through another, for example to
compress data, encrypt it, and then write the result to a file. IOStreams chains streams together like that, so that
only the current block of the file is in memory, whatever its size, and so that your code does not change when the
format, compression, encryption or location of the file does.

## Install

Install the gem:

~~~
gem install iostreams
~~~

In an application, add `gem "iostreams"` to its Gemfile instead, with the gems of the features that it uses, see
[Installation](index.html#installation).

To follow the S3 steps below, also install the AWS SDK, and configure its credentials as described in
[Configuring the AWS SDK for Ruby](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sdk-for-ruby/v3/developer-guide/setup-config.html):

~~~
gem install aws-sdk-s3
~~~

Open an interactive Ruby console, and load IOStreams:

~~~ruby
require "iostreams"
~~~

## Write and read a file

A path names a file. Writing creates the file, and any directories that it is in:

~~~ruby
path = IOStreams.path("sample/hello.txt")
path.write("Hello World\n")

path.read
# => "Hello World\n"
~~~

To write a large file, write it a block at a time in a block, which closes the file when it returns:

~~~ruby
path.writer do |io|
  io << "Hello World\n"
  io << "Goodbye World\n"
end
~~~

## Compression by name

The extensions of the file name say how the file is stored. Name the file `.gz`, and it is compressed with gzip:

~~~ruby
path = IOStreams.path("sample/example.csv.gz")
# => #<IOStreams::Paths::File:sample/example.csv.gz pipeline={gz: {}}>

path.writer do |io|
  io << "name,login\n"
  io << "Jack Jones,jjones\n"
  io << "Jill Smith,jsmith\n"
end
~~~

Reading the file decompresses it, as it is read:

~~~ruby
path.read
# => "name,login\nJack Jones,jjones\nJill Smith,jsmith\n"
~~~

The `pipeline` above lists the streams that the file name implies. A file name can imply several, which are applied
in order, so `example.csv.gz.pgp` is encrypted with PGP after it is compressed with gzip, and decrypted before it is
decompressed:

| File name | Streams |
|-----------|---------|
| `hello.zip` | Compressed with Zip |
| `hello.gz.enc` | Compressed with gzip, then encrypted with Symmetric Encryption |
| `hello.csv.zst.pgp` | Compressed with Zstandard, then encrypted with PGP |

## Lines, rows and records

Rather than parse the file yourself, read it a line, a row or a record at a time:

~~~ruby
path.each do |line|
  puts line
end
~~~

Output:

~~~
name,login
Jack Jones,jjones
Jill Smith,jsmith
~~~

Pass `:array` to `each` to have IOStreams parse each line as CSV:

~~~ruby
path.each(:array) do |row|
  p row
end
~~~

Output:

~~~ruby
["name", "login"]
["Jack Jones", "jjones"]
["Jill Smith", "jsmith"]
~~~

And pass `:hash` to read each record as a Hash, keyed by the header row:

~~~ruby
path.each(:hash) do |record|
  p record
end
~~~

Output:

~~~ruby
{"name" => "Jack Jones", "login" => "jjones"}
{"name" => "Jill Smith", "login" => "jsmith"}
~~~

`:line`, `:array` and `:hash` are the **modes** of `#each`, which say what your code reads: a line is a String, a
**row** an Array of the values of a line, and a **record** a Hash of those values, keyed by the names in the header
row. `#writer` takes the same modes. See [Reading and writing](streams).

As the file grows to millions of rows, this code does not change, and its memory use stays about the same, since the
file is read, decompressed and parsed one block at a time.

## Writing records

Write records the same way, and IOStreams writes the header row and the CSV for you, quoting values as needed:

~~~ruby
path.writer(:hash) do |io|
  io << {name: "Jack Jones", login: "jjones"}
  io << {name: "Jill Smith", login: "jsmith"}
end

path.read
# => "name,login\nJack Jones,jjones\nJill Smith,jsmith\n"
~~~

The keys of the first record become the header row. Change the file name to `example.json`, and the same code writes
one JSON object on each line instead:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("sample/example.json").writer(:hash) do |io|
  io << {name: "Jack Jones", login: "jjones"}
  io << {name: "Jill Smith", login: "jsmith"}
end

IOStreams.path("sample/example.json").read
# => "{\"name\":\"Jack Jones\",\"login\":\"jjones\"}\n{\"name\":\"Jill Smith\",\"login\":\"jsmith\"}\n"
~~~

Name it `example.xlsx` to write an Excel spreadsheet, or `example.psv` for pipe separated values. Reading any of them
with `each(:hash)` returns the same records.

## Describe the file with a schema

Every value of a CSV file is text. A [schema](formats#schema) gives each column a name and a type, so that reading
returns each value as its type, and writing writes each value in the text form of its type. A `number` field, such
as `salary` below, needs the `bigdecimal` gem: with Bundler on Ruby 3.4 or later, add `gem "bigdecimal"` to the
Gemfile, since it is a bundled gem.

~~~ruby
path = IOStreams.path("sample/people.csv").schema(
  fields: [
    {name: "name",   type: "string"},
    {name: "born",   type: "date"},
    {name: "salary", type: "number", decimals: 2}
  ]
)

path.writer(:hash) do |io|
  io << {"name" => "Jack Jones", "born" => Date.new(1990, 2, 1), "salary" => BigDecimal("1234.5")}
end

path.read
# => "name,born,salary\nJack Jones,1990-02-01,1234.50\n"

path.each(:hash) do |person|
  p person
end
# => {"name" => "Jack Jones", "born" => #<Date: 1990-02-01 ((2447924j,0s,0n),+0s,2299161j)>, "salary" => 0.12345e4}
~~~

The schema also checks the columns of the file, so that a file with other columns raises
`IOStreams::Errors::InvalidHeader`, rather than being read wrongly. A schema can accept extra columns, match columns
named another way, such as `First Name` for the field `first_name`, describe a file without a header row, and give
the position of each field of a fixed width file. See [Schema](formats#schema).

## Same code, any file type

Here is a method that writes a few lines to a file:

~~~ruby
def write_lines(path)
  IOStreams.path(path).writer do |io|
    io << "name,login\n"
    io << "Jack Jones,jjones\n"
    io << "Jill Smith,jsmith\n"
  end
end
~~~

And one that displays a file a line at a time, with the number of each line:

~~~ruby
def show_lines(path)
  line_number = 0
  IOStreams.path(path).each(:line) do |line|
    line_number += 1
    puts "[#{line_number}] #{line}"
  end
end
~~~

Use them with a plain file, a compressed file, and a file encrypted with PGP. A PGP file needs the recipient that can
decrypt it, so set its option on the path, and pass the path to the method. The PGP lines need GnuPG and a key for
`receiver@example.org`, which [Create the keys](pgp#create-the-keys) in the PGP tutorial creates. Without them, skip
the PGP lines.

~~~ruby
write_lines("sample/example.csv")
write_lines("sample/example.csv.gz")

encrypted = IOStreams.path("sample/example.csv.pgp").option(:pgp, recipient: "receiver@example.org")
write_lines(encrypted)

show_lines("sample/example.csv")
show_lines("sample/example.csv.gz")
show_lines(encrypted.option(:pgp, passphrase: "receiver_passphrase"))
~~~

`IOStreams.path` accepts a path as well as a name, and returns a copy of it with its streams and options, so the
methods do not need to know about PGP at all. Each file displays the same lines:

~~~
[1] name,login
[2] Jack Jones,jjones
[3] Jill Smith,jsmith
~~~

## Same code, any storage

The same unchanged methods read and write files on S3, by prefixing the names with the bucket:

~~~ruby
write_lines("s3://my-iostreams-bucket/sample/example.csv")
write_lines("s3://my-iostreams-bucket/sample/example.csv.gz")

show_lines("s3://my-iostreams-bucket/sample/example.csv")
show_lines("s3://my-iostreams-bucket/sample/example.csv.gz")
~~~

They also work with SFTP, `sftp://host/path`, and HTTP, `https://host/path`. S3 objects and HTTP files are read as
the code reads them, and S3 objects are uploaded as they are written, so a large file never has to fit in memory or on
local disk. A zip file or a spreadsheet is the exception: one stored elsewhere is copied into a temp file first, since
it is read from a local file, so prefer gzip or Zstandard for large files, see
[When temp files are used](config#when-temp-files-are-used).

### Configure storage once, not in every call

The `s3://my-iostreams-bucket/` prefix in each call still makes the code decide where the files are stored. Instead,
keep the location in configuration, so that the same code runs against local files in development and S3 in
production. Roots make that possible. Set the location once, at startup:

~~~ruby
# config/initializers/iostreams.rb (development)
IOStreams.add_root(:default, "tmp/files")

# config/initializers/iostreams.rb (production)
IOStreams.add_root(:default, "s3://my-iostreams-bucket/files")
~~~

Then use `IOStreams.join` instead of `IOStreams.path`, and never mention the location again:

~~~ruby
write_lines(IOStreams.join("sample/example.csv"))
show_lines(IOStreams.join("sample/example.csv"))
~~~

A whole path can also come from configuration, such as `IOStreams.path(ENV.fetch("EXPORT_PATH"))`. See
[Configuration](config) for several roots, for example separate locations for uploads, downloads and reports.

## Files in another encoding

Lines, rows and records are read as UTF-8, and a file that is not valid UTF-8 raises
`IOStreams::Errors::InvalidEncoding`, which names the invalid byte, its offset, and its line. To read a file exported
in another encoding, such as Windows-1252, set its encoding on the path, here converting it to UTF-8:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("sample/legacy.csv").encoding("Windows-1252:UTF-8").each(:hash) do |record|
  p record
end
~~~

See [Text and binary data](streams#text-and-binary-data).

## When a file is missing

Each store raises its own error for a missing file, such as `Errno::ENOENT` for a local file. IOStreams also tags it
with `IOStreams::Errors::NotFound`, so that the same rescue works wherever the file is stored:

~~~ruby
begin
  show_lines(IOStreams.join("sample/missing.csv"))
rescue IOStreams::Errors::NotFound => e
  puts "Not found: #{e.message}"
end
~~~

See [Errors](errors) for the other kinds of failure.

## Copy and convert

`copy_from` copies a file, applying the streams of both names, so this copy decompresses the source and encrypts the
target:

~~~ruby
target = IOStreams.path("sample/example.csv.pgp").option(:pgp, recipient: "receiver@example.org")
target.copy_from("sample/example.csv.gz")
~~~

With a mode, it converts the format of each record too, here from CSV to JSON:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("sample/people.json").copy_from("sample/example.csv.gz", mode: :hash)
~~~

See [Copying and moving](copy_files).

## Next steps

* [Reading and writing](streams): every way to read and write a path, and text encodings.
* [Tabular formats](formats): CSV, JSON, fixed width, Excel and Parquet, and schemas.
* [Compression and encryption](extensions): the options of each stream.
* [Paths](path): local files, S3, SFTP and HTTP, and the operations on a path.
* [Copying and moving](copy_files): copying files between stores, and converting them on the way.
* [Errors](errors): rescuing failures the same way wherever a file is stored.
* [PGP](pgp): encrypting, decrypting and signing files with PGP, and managing keys.
* [Configuration](config) and [Security](security): roots, temp files, logging and allowed paths.

---

# Reading and Writing

Once you have a [path](path), read it and write it with a small set of methods, a block, a line, a row or a record at
a time, so that memory use stays low however large the file is. Each method takes a mode, which says what your code
reads or writes:

| Mode | Reads or writes | Read with | Write with |
|------|-----------------|-----------|------------|
| `:stream`, the default for `#reader` and `#writer` | Bytes, a block at a time | `reader { \|io\| io.read(1024) }` | `writer { \|io\| io << data }` |
| `:line`, the default for `#each` | Lines of text | `each(:line) { \|line\| }` | `writer(:line) { \|io\| io << line }` |
| `:array` | Rows: an Array of the values of each line | `each(:array) { \|row\| }` | `writer(:array) { \|io\| io << row }` |
| `:hash` | Records: a Hash of the values of each line, by column | `each(:hash) { \|record\| }` | `writer(:hash) { \|io\| io << record }` |
| `:slice` | Slices: up to `size` rows as they are in the file, with its header row | `each(:slice, size: 100) { \|slice\| }` | `writer(:slice) { \|io\| io << slice }` |

The tabular format of the file, such as CSV or JSON, says how rows and records are read from lines and written as
lines, see [Tabular formats](formats). The extensions of the file name also say how the file is compressed or
encrypted, which IOStreams applies as the data is read or written, see
[Streams from the file name](#streams-from-the-file-name).

## Reading

`#each` yields each line, row or record:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("example.csv").each do |line|
  puts line
end

IOStreams.path("example.csv").each(:hash) do |record|
  p record
end
~~~

`#each` requires a block, so that the file is closed once it has been read, rather than returning an Enumerator,
which could leave the file open if it was not read to its end. To collect the records, add each one to an Array within
the block.

`#reader` yields the stream itself, for the code that reads it: in the `:stream` mode, an IO that responds to
`#read(length = nil, outbuf = nil)`, `#readpartial` and `#eof?`. This reads 128 bytes at a time:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("example.csv").reader do |io|
  while (data = io.read(128))
    p data
  end
end
~~~

`#reader` and `#writer` return the result of the block.

In the `:line`, `:array`, `:hash` and `:slice` modes, the reader that `#reader` yields is `Enumerable`, and its
`#each` returns an Enumerator without a block, so methods such as `io.first(10)` and `io.each.with_index` read it.
Use them within the block, since the file is closed once the block returns:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("example.csv").reader(:hash) do |io|
  io.each.with_index do |record, index|
    puts "#{index}: #{record}"
  end
end
~~~

`#read` returns the whole file, which is only suitable for a small one, since all of it is held in memory:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("example.csv.gz").read
# => "name,login\nJack Jones,jjones\n"
~~~

Within a `#reader` block, an S3 object or an HTTP response is read as the block reads it, so the IO is not a `File`.
Like the IO of every stream, such as of a `.gz` file, it has the methods of an IO that read, such as `#read`, `#gets`
and `#each_line`, so a library that reads an IO, such as `CSV.new(io)`, reads it, but not `#rewind`, `#pos`, `#size`
or `#path`. Where the code needs a `File`, copy the file to a local file first, see [Copying and moving](copy_files).

### Blank rows

A blank row holds no data. It is the same in every format, so that a file holds the same rows whichever format it is
in:

* a line that is empty, or only whitespace, including Unicode whitespace such as a no-break space, as Rails'
  `String#blank?` matches it;
* a row or record whose every value is `nil` or such text, such as a line of CSV of only commas, a row of empty
  spreadsheet cells, a fixed width line whose every field is spaces, a JSON line of `null` or `{}`, or a JSON or
  Parquet record whose every value is null.

A value such as `false` or `0` is data, so a row that holds one is not blank. `each(:array)` and `each(:hash)` yield
`nil` for each blank row, so that the rows yielded count the lines of the file, for example to report the line of a
row that is not valid. Supply `skip_blanks: true` to skip them instead:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("people.csv").each(:hash, skip_blanks: true) do |person|
  p person
end
~~~

* The header row is the first row that is not blank, with or without `skip_blanks`.
* A blank row is not checked against a [schema](formats#schema), so it does not raise for a field that is required, as
  a row with other values does.
* Only the values that are read count: the fields of a fixed width line, not its filler, and of a Parquet file read
  with a schema that skips columns, only the columns of its fields.
* A copy always skips blank rows, so `#copy_from` and `#writer` raise `ArgumentError` for `skip_blanks:`, which only
  applies when reading.
* `each(:line)` and `each(:slice)` hand on every row as it is in the file, so they do not take `skip_blanks:`. Supply it
  where the rows of a slice are read, such as `IOStreams.stream(slice).each(:hash, skip_blanks: true)`.
* A `skip_blanks` that is not true or false raises `ArgumentError` before the file is opened.

### Resuming at a record

`resume_at:` starts reading at the record of the number supplied, so that a job that stopped part way through a file,
such as one that a deploy interrupted, carries on where it left off, rather than processing the file again from its
start. Records are numbered as the slices of a file number their rows: from 1, without the header row, nor the blank
lines before it, so that a blank row after it counts:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("people.csv.gz").each(:hash, resume_at: 1_001) do |person|
  # Starts with the 1,001st person.
  p person
end

IOStreams.path("people.csv.gz").each(:slice, size: 500, resume_at: 1_001) do |slice|
  # 1001, then 1501, and so on.
  p slice.record_number
end
~~~

* The `:array`, `:hash` and `:slice` modes take it, for a file, a query or a slice. `nil` reads every record, so the
  cursor of a job that has not started yet, which is usually `nil`, can be supplied as it is. A job that keeps the
  number of the last record that it processed resumes at the record after it.
* The file is still read up to that record, since it cannot be read from the middle, such as when it is compressed, but
  the rows before it are not parsed, so a value that is not valid in one of them does not raise. The one exception is
  the first record of JSON without a schema in the `:array` mode, whose keys are the columns of every row, so it is
  read for them, and raises when it is not valid JSON, as reading every row would: give the file a schema, or read it
  in the `:hash` or `:slice` mode.
* The header row is still read, and matched to the [schema](formats#schema), and `each(:array)` yields it first.
* A query is read again from its start, so give the relation an order, such as `order(:id)`, so that its rows come back
  in the same order each time. Without one, a database may return them in another order, so that the rows skipped are
  not those that were processed. `in_batches` reads each batch in the order of its primary key.
* `each(:hash)` yields one record, or `nil` for a blank one, for each record, unless `skip_blanks: true`, so counting
  the records yielded from `resume_at` gives the number of each one. Each slice holds the line and record number of
  each of its rows in the file, see [Find a row in the file](background_jobs#find-a-row-in-the-file).
* A slice resumes at a record number that it holds, as `slice.each` gives them, such as
  `IOStreams.stream(slice).each(:hash, resume_at: 502)` for a slice of records 501 to 600, or at the record after its
  last, which reads no rows. A record between its first and last that it no longer holds, such as one removed with
  `slice.delete_at`, resumes at the row after it, and a slice without rows reads none. A record before its first row,
  such as the position of a row within it, or after the record after its last, raises `ArgumentError`, so that a cursor
  of another slice cannot skip its rows, also once its first or last rows were removed, since a slice holds only the
  numbers of its rows. The slices read from it keep the line and record number of each row.
* A copy reads every record, so `#copy_from` and `#writer` raise `ArgumentError` for `resume_at:`, which only applies
  when reading, and a `resume_at` that is neither `nil` nor a positive Integer raises `ArgumentError` before the file
  is opened.

### Slices

`each(:slice)` yields the rows of the file a slice at a time, as they are in the file, without parsing them, so that
other threads, processes or jobs can parse them in parallel. Each slice, an `IOStreams::Slice`, holds up to `size`
rows, with the line and record number of each one, and carries the header row of its file and the format of its rows,
and the header row is matched to the schema before the first slice is yielded:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("people.csv.gz").schema("people.json").each(:slice, size: 500) do |slice|
  queue << slice
end
~~~

Where a slice is processed, `IOStreams.stream(slice)` reads its rows as the rows of its file:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.stream(slice).schema(schema).each(:hash) do |person|
  p person
end
~~~

See [Background jobs](background_jobs) for handing slices to background jobs or threads, resuming a job, sending them as plain data with
`slice.to_h` and `IOStreams.slice`, validating a file before the work starts, and writing the results back to one file.

## Writing

`#writer` yields the stream to write to:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("example.txt").writer do |io|
  io << "This is "
  io << "one line\n"
end
~~~

In the `:line` mode, each value written is followed by a newline:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("example.txt").writer(:line) do |io|
  io << "these"
  io << "are separate"
  io << "lines"
end
~~~

`#write` writes a whole String:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("example.txt").write("Hello World\n")
~~~

The streams that the file name implies are applied as the data is written, so writing `example.csv.gz` compresses it,
and writing a path on S3 uploads it, see [Paths](path). The block decides what is kept:

* When the block returns, or leaves early, such as with `break` or `return`, everything written is kept, and the file is
  complete, whichever streams and store it uses.
* When the block raises, or its thread is killed, nothing is kept: a local file is removed, an S3 upload is aborted,
  and a file is not uploaded to SFTP or HTTP. An IO supplied to `IOStreams.stream` keeps what was written to it, but a
  compressed or encrypted stream does not end its data, so that it cannot be mistaken for a complete file.
* A write that cannot succeed raises before the file is opened, so that an existing file is kept: an option that a
  stream cannot write with, such as a compression level that is out of range, an encoding that Ruby does not know, or
  cannot convert text to, such as UTF-7, see [Character encoding](#character-encoding), or a gem that a stream needs
  and that is not installed.

### Writing slices to a file

`writer(:slice)` writes slices to a file, after their header row, which it writes once. A slice in the format of the
file is written line for line without parsing its rows, and a slice in another format is read by its header row and
written in the format of the file:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("people.csv.gz").schema("people.json").writer(:slice) do |io|
  slices.each do |slice|
    io << slice
  end
end
~~~

See [Writing the results](background_jobs#writing-the-results).

### A store of slices

To write the lines, rows or records that your code writes, or copies from a file or a query, in slices, write them to
a store of your own: include `IOStreams::Slice::Target` in its class and implement `#write_slice(slice)`.
`IOStreams.stream(store)` then writes to it in slices, as `each(:slice)` reads them from a file:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.stream(store).schema("people.json").copy_from("people.csv.gz", mode: :line)
~~~

See [A store of slices](background_jobs#a-store-of-slices).

## Lines

Lines are split at the line ending of the file, which is the first `\r\n`, `\n` or `\r` that it holds, and the line
ending is removed from each line. When it is `\r\n`, as in a file written on Windows, or `\n`, every line ends at a
`\n`, and a `\r` before it is removed, so a file whose lines end in both ways, such as a Windows file to which a program
on Linux added lines, is read line by line, whichever way its first line ends. A `\r` alone within a line of such a
file is a character of the line. When the first line ends with a `\r` alone, as an old Mac wrote it, every line ends at
a `\r` instead, and a `\n` is a character of its line.

`delimiter:` splits the file at the String supplied instead, such as `delimiter: "|"`, and then only at it, so
`delimiter: "\r\n"` keeps a `\n` alone within its line, and `delimiter: "\n"` keeps the `\r` before a `\n`. When
writing, it is written after each line, `"\n"` by default.

A quoted value of a CSV file can contain a line break, which must not end the line. Lines are split where the format
of the file expects, so `each(:array)` and `each(:hash)` keep a quoted line break within its row. So does `each(:line)`,
for a format that quotes its values, such as CSV, whether it is set with `#format` or comes from a `.csv` file name.
Supply `embedded_within:` to the `:line` mode to choose: `nil` for the physical lines of the file, or the quote
character, such as `'"'`, for the lines of a file whose format is not set:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("example.csv").each(:line, embedded_within: nil) do |line|
  puts line
end
~~~

To read each line as a row in the `:array`, `:hash` or `:slice` mode, without a header row or quoting, such as a file of
email addresses, set the `:text` format, see [Text](formats#text).

The reader that `reader(:line)` yields also passes each line to `each_with_line_number` with the number of the line of
the file that it starts on, as a text editor numbers it, so that a line that holds a quoted line break is named by its
first line:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("example.csv").reader(:line) do |io|
  io.each_with_line_number do |line, line_number|
    puts "#{line_number}: #{line}"
  end
end
~~~

For an Excel spreadsheet, `.xlsx`, the lines are those of the CSV text that its rows are read as, so their numbers are
not the rows of the sheet, since a cell that holds line breaks takes a line for each. That is why the slices of a
spreadsheet hold no line numbers, see [Find a row in the file](background_jobs#find-a-row-in-the-file).

Other notes:

* A blank line is yielded as an empty String by `each(:line)`, and as `nil` by `each(:array)` and `each(:hash)`, see
  [Blank rows](#blank-rows).
* Lines are read 64KB at a time, which `buffer_size:` changes, such as `each(:hash, buffer_size: 1_048_576)`.
* A line without a delimiter within 100 blocks, 6.4MB by default, raises `IOStreams::Errors::DelimiterNotFound`, rather
  than reading the whole of a file that has no line endings into memory.
* A quoted value that is not closed raises `IOStreams::Errors::MalformedDataError`, with the number of the line that it
  starts on, once the line that holds it reaches 10 blocks, 640KB by default, or at the end of the file, rather than
  reading the rest of the file into one line.

## Text and binary data

Lines, rows and records are read as UTF-8 text, whichever streams the file is read through, such as gzip or PGP,
apart from [fixed width files](formats#fixed-width-files), which are read as ASCII. Data that is not valid UTF-8 raises
`IOStreams::Errors::InvalidEncoding`, an `Encoding::UndefinedConversionError`, whose message gives the invalid bytes,
their byte offset, and the line that they are on, once the lines before them have been read:

~~~
IOStreams::Errors::InvalidEncoding: "\xE9" is not valid UTF-8 at byte offset 1043 on line 12
~~~

The byte order mark (U+FEFF) that programs such as Excel write at the start of a UTF-8 file is removed, so that the
first column name of a CSV file is read as it appears. So is the one at the start of UTF-16 or UTF-32 text, such as
the "Unicode Text" that Windows programs export, read with `encoding("UTF-16LE:UTF-8")`.

`"UTF-16"` and `"UTF-32"`, which name no byte order, read the text in the byte order that the byte order mark at its
start tells, such as the little-endian "Unicode Text" of Windows programs read with `encoding("UTF-16:UTF-8")`, and
write it big-endian, after one byte order mark, as Ruby does. The byte order mark is removed, as it is from UTF-16LE
text, so the text read without an internal encoding is in the encoding of its byte order, such as UTF-16LE, as Ruby
reads `"BOM|UTF-16"`. To copy such a file as it is, copy it without an encoding, since setting one on the target too
writes the text big-endian, after a byte order mark. Binary data that is written, such as a copy of a file, keeps the
byte order that its own byte order mark tells. Text in either one that does not start with a byte order mark raises
`IOStreams::Errors::InvalidEncoding`, since only the mark tells its byte order, so name the byte order instead, such
as `"UTF-16LE"`, or supply `replace:`, which reads it big-endian, as Unicode reads such text.

`#read` returns the whole file as UTF-8 without checking it, like `File.read`, so that it can also read a binary
file, such as an image, whose bytes are unchanged. The `:stream` mode of `#reader` reads bytes, so `io.read(128)`
returns up to 128 bytes of binary data, whether the file is plain, compressed or encrypted.

Writing writes the bytes of each String as they are, unless an encoding is set. Fixed width files and JSON are the
exceptions: fixed width files are written as ASCII, and JSON, which holds only UTF-8 text, writes a binary String,
such as one read with `encoding("BINARY")`, as the UTF-8 text of its bytes, also as a key, and within the JSON of a
Hash or an Array value in another format, such as CSV, and converts text in another encoding, while text that is not
valid UTF-8, or a character that UTF-8 does not have, raises `IOStreams::Errors::InvalidEncoding`.

### Character encoding

To read or write text in another encoding, set it on the path with `#encoding`, which describes the file, whichever
streams it has. Name the encoding of the file, and the encoding that your code reads, in Ruby's `"external:internal"`
form, as `File.read` does:

~~~ruby
# Read a Windows-1252 file as UTF-8 strings.
IOStreams.path("export.csv").encoding("Windows-1252:UTF-8").each(:hash) do |record|
  p record
end

# Write UTF-8 strings as a Windows-1252 file, with the same setting.
IOStreams.path("export.csv").encoding("Windows-1252:UTF-8").writer(:hash) do |io|
  io << {"name" => "José"}
end
~~~

With just one encoding, such as `encoding("Windows-1252")`, the strings read are in that encoding, rather than
converted to UTF-8, and cannot be combined with UTF-8 text. `encoding("BINARY")` reads lines, rows and records as
binary strings.

`#encoding` also takes these options, which change how the text is converted:

* `replace:` replaces each character that is not valid, or that the target encoding does not have, rather than raising,
  such as `encoding("UTF-8", replace: "?")`. With `replace: ""` such characters are removed.
* `cleaner:` cleans the text as it is read or written: `:printable` removes the characters that are not printable,
  apart from line endings, `:replace_non_printable` replaces them with `replace:`, and a Proc is called with the text
  and the `replace:` value, and returns the cleaned text.

~~~ruby
# Remove the characters that are not printable, and replace those that are not valid UTF-8 with a space.
IOStreams.path("upload.csv").encoding("UTF-8", cleaner: :printable, replace: " ").each(:hash) do |record|
  p record
end
~~~

Each call to `#encoding` merges its options with those already set, and `#encoding` without arguments returns the
encoding that was set. An encoding that Ruby does not know, a conversion that Ruby has no converter for, such as
`"Windows-1258:UTF-8"`, an encoding that is not ASCII compatible and that Ruby cannot convert text to or from, such
as UTF-7, or a cleaner that is neither a built-in rule nor a Proc, raises `ArgumentError` when it is set. The text of
an ASCII compatible encoding that Ruby cannot convert, such as `"Windows-1258"`, is read and written as it is, while
writing text in another encoding to it, such as UTF-8 text that is not ASCII, raises
`Encoding::ConverterNotFoundError`.

The encoding of the text is converted closest to your code, after the file is decompressed or decrypted, so
`IOStreams.path("data.csv.gz").encoding("BINARY")` still decompresses the file, and reads its text as bytes.

With an encoding, the stream that `#reader` supplies reads like an IO that converts text, such as
`File.open(name, "r:Windows-1252:UTF-8")`, so a library that reads an IO, such as `CSV`, reads the text in the encoding
that your code reads:

~~~ruby
require "csv"

IOStreams.path("export.csv").encoding("Windows-1252:UTF-8").reader do |io|
  CSV.new(io, headers: true).map(&:to_h)
end
# => [{"name" => "José", "city" => "Málaga"}]
~~~

Its `read(length)` and `#readpartial` read text too, rather than bytes: whole characters, up to `length` bytes of them,
or the first character when it is longer.

### Data as it is stored

`#raw` reads and writes the data as it is stored, without the streams that the file name implies, and without any
encoding, so that text is read and written as bytes. For example, to checksum a compressed file as it is stored, or to
write data that is already compressed:

~~~ruby
require "digest"

Digest::SHA256.hexdigest(IOStreams.path("data.csv.gz").raw.read)

IOStreams.path("data.csv.gz").raw.write(gzipped_data)
~~~

`#raw` changes the path that it is called on, so that reading it afterwards also reads the stored bytes. To keep the
path as it is, call it on a copy, such as `IOStreams.path(path).raw.read`. Setting a stream, option or encoding after
`#raw` raises `ArgumentError`, and `#raw?` returns whether it was called.

To copy a file as it is stored, such as to download a zip file without unzipping it, use
`copy_to(target, convert: false)`, since `#raw` on the source would still apply the streams of the target, see
[Copying and moving](copy_files).

## Settings on the path, options for each call

A setting that describes the file is set on the path, and an option that says what your code wants from the file is
supplied to each call. A path is configuration: it can be held in a configuration system and handed to code that only
calls `each(:hash)`, so the settings of the path are all that it takes to read or write the file the right way, by
any code, including `#copy_from` and `#copy_to`.

| Setting | Where | Because it says |
|---------|-------|-----------------|
| The path or url, and `#file_name` | The path | Where the file is, and the extensions that name its streams and format |
| `#stream` and `#option` | The path | How the file is compressed or encrypted |
| `#encoding` | The path | The encoding of the text of the file |
| `#format` | The path | The tabular format of the file, such as `:json` |
| `#schema` | The path | The fields of the file and their types, which columns it can have and must have, the position of each fixed width field, and whether it has a header row |
| The mode, such as `:hash` | Each call | Whether the code reads or writes blocks, lines, rows or records |
| `delimiter:` and `buffer_size:` | Each call | How lines are split or ended, and how much is read at a time |
| `embedded_within:` | Each call, in the `:line` mode | Whether the code reads the physical lines, or the logical lines of a quoted format |

IOStreams checks where each setting is supplied:

* A setting of the path supplied to a call, such as `each(:hash, format: :json)`, raises `ArgumentError`, as do
  `file_name:` and `schema:`.
* An option that only applies when reading, such as `buffer_size:`, raises `ArgumentError` when it is supplied to
  `#writer`, rather than being ignored.
* Any other option that the mode does not take, such as a misspelled `delimitr:`, raises `ArgumentError` before the
  file is opened, naming the mode and listing the options that it takes:

  ~~~
  ArgumentError: Unknown option :delimitr for the :hash mode. Valid options: :delimiter, :buffer_size, :skip_blanks.
  ~~~
* `#copy_from` and `#copy_to` use their options to write the target, so an option that only applies when reading
  raises `ArgumentError` for them too. The copy reads the source with the settings of the source path, so set what
  describes the source, such as its schema, on its path.

~~~ruby
# The configuration describes the file.
people = IOStreams.path(ENV["PEOPLE_PATH"]).format(:csv).schema(ENV["PEOPLE_SCHEMA"])

# The code says what it wants from it: records, whose columns the schema checks.
people.each(:hash) do |person|
  p person
end

# A copy reads the source with the settings of its path, and writes the target with the settings of its own.
target = IOStreams.path("people.json").schema(
  fieldsMatch: "subset",
  fields:      [
    {name: "name"},
    {name: "age"}
  ]
)
target.copy_from(people, mode: :hash)
~~~

## Streams from the file name

The extensions at the end of the file name name its streams, and IOStreams applies them in order: `example.csv.gz.pgp`
is decrypted with PGP, then decompressed with gzip. Only the registered extensions at the end of the name count, so
`data.gz.csv` and `report.csv.bak` have no streams. `#pipeline` lists them, from the one closest to your code to the
one closest to the stored data:

~~~ruby
path = IOStreams.path("somewhere/example.csv.gz.pgp")
# => #<IOStreams::Paths::File:somewhere/example.csv.gz.pgp pipeline={gz: {}, pgp: {}}>

path.pipeline
# => {gz: {}, pgp: {}}
~~~

`#compressed?` and `#encrypted?` say whether a stream in the pipeline compresses or encrypts the data, whether it comes
from the file name or is set with `#stream`:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("example.csv.gz.pgp").compressed?
# => true

IOStreams.path("example.csv.gz.pgp").encrypted?
# => true
~~~

Compression within an encrypted file, such as PGP or Symmetric Encryption, is not reported, since only the encrypted
data records whether it was compressed.

### Option

`#option` sets the options of a stream, for when the file name includes it:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("example.csv.pgp").option(:pgp, passphrase: "receiver_passphrase").read
~~~

An option for a stream that the file name does not include has no effect, so the same code can supply the options of
every stream that a file might use, and read a PGP file, a Symmetric Encryption file, or a plain file, whichever the
configured path names:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path(ENV.fetch("IMPORT_PATH")).option(:pgp, passphrase: "receiver_passphrase").read
~~~

An option for a stream applies to each of its extensions, so `option(:pgp, ...)` also applies to a `.gpg` file,
`option(:gz, ...)` to a `.gzip` file, and `option(:xlsx, ...)` to a `.xlsm` file. So a file name held in configuration
can change from one extension to the other without changing the code. When options are set for more than one
extension of a stream, those for the extension in the file name take precedence.

`#setting` returns the options set for a stream:

~~~ruby
path = IOStreams.path("example.pgp").option(:pgp, passphrase: "receiver_passphrase")
path.setting(:pgp)
# => {passphrase: "receiver_passphrase"}
~~~

### Options for reading and writing

The options of a stream are passed to its reader when reading, and to its writer when writing, and the two directions
usually take different options: the PGP writer needs the `recipient` to encrypt for, while the PGP reader needs the
`passphrase` of the private key. So that a path can be written and then read with the same options, each direction
ignores the options of the other that it does not need:

~~~ruby
path = IOStreams.path("example.csv.pgp").
  option(:pgp, recipient: "receiver@example.org", passphrase: "receiver_passphrase")

path.write("name,login\nJack Jones,jjones\n")
path.read
~~~

Reading ignores the options that only say how to write the file, such as the gzip compression `level`, or `compress`
for `.enc`, whose header records whether the file was compressed. Writing ignores the options that only say how to
read the file, such as the PGP `passphrase`.

Some options apply to both: `entry_file_name` names the file within a zip file when writing, and chooses the file to
read. The PGP `signer` signs the file when writing, and when reading requires that the file was signed by that key. An
option of one direction that the other could seem to use, but does not, such as the `sheet_name` of a spreadsheet,
which names the worksheet that is written, while reading always reads the first, raises `ArgumentError` in that
direction.

An option that neither direction accepts, such as a misspelled one, raises an `ArgumentError` that lists the valid
options as soon as it is set, even when the file name does not include that stream. So the same code reports it
wherever it runs, rather than only where the path, for example from configuration, includes that extension:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("example.csv").option(:enc, compres: false)
# ArgumentError: Unknown option :compres for a :enc stream.
#   Valid options: :buffer_size, :version, :compress, :cipher_name, :header, :random_key, :random_iv.
~~~

### Stream

`#stream` replaces the streams that the file name implies, for example for a file whose name has none:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("tempfile2527").stream(:zip).stream(:pgp, passphrase: "receiver_passphrase").read
~~~

The first stream set is the one closest to your code, so the file above is decrypted, and then unzipped:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("tempfile2527").stream(:zip).stream(:pgp, passphrase: "receiver_passphrase").pipeline
# => {zip: {}, pgp: {passphrase: "receiver_passphrase"}}
~~~

`#stream` and `#option` cannot both be used on the same path. When the original file name is known, set it with
`#file_name` instead, so that IOStreams takes the streams and the format from it:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("tempfile2527").file_name("file.json.zip").each(:hash) do |record|
  p record
end
~~~

## Streams of an IO

`IOStreams.stream(io)` reads or writes an IO that you supply, such as a `StringIO` or a socket, with the same methods
as a path. Set its file name, or its streams, since an IO has no name to take them from:

~~~ruby
io = StringIO.new
IOStreams.stream(io).file_name("example.csv.gz").writer(:hash) do |stream|
  stream << {name: "Jack", address: "There", zip_code: 1234}
  stream << {name: "Joe", zip_code: 1234, address: "Over There somewhere"}
end
~~~

IOStreams never closes an IO that you supply, so close it yourself when you are done with it.

The streams write their data to your IO as it is, the bytes of a compressed or encrypted stream, or of text in the
encoding set with `#encoding`, even when your IO converts the text written to it to its external encoding, as a
`StringIO` does, a file opened with an encoding, such as `File.open(name, "w:UTF-8")`, and any file opened in text
mode, such as a `Tempfile`, in a Rails process. Without any streams, or with `#encoding` options that set no
encoding, such as `encoding(cleaner: :printable)`, what you write goes to your IO as text, which it converts. An IO
whose encoding is not ASCII compatible, such as `File.open(name, "w:UTF-16LE")`, converts what is written to it by
way of UTF-8, so it can only store text, and one that changes the bytes written to it otherwise, such as
`File.open(name, "w:UTF-8", newline: :crlf)`, raises `ArgumentError` for the bytes of a compressed or encrypted
stream, so open it in binary mode, such as `File.open(name, "wb")`.

A line, row or record writer that is already open, such as the one that `writer(:hash)` yields, can be handed to code
that calls `IOStreams.stream(io).writer(:hash)` itself, or `IOStreams.stream(io).copy_from(source, mode: :hash)`, which
then writes into it. Since the open writer writes with its own settings, options, streams or an encoding supplied to
that call raise `ArgumentError`, and a copy into a row or record writer does not give it the schema of the rows of an
Active Record query. A row, record or slice writer is only written in its own mode, such as `:hash` for the one that
`writer(:hash)` yields, so any other mode raises `ArgumentError`. A line writer takes text, as an IO does, so it is
written in any mode.

---

# Paths

A path names a file, and the store that holds it: the local file system, AWS S3, Google Cloud Storage, an SFTP server,
or a web server.
Every path has the same methods, so the code that reads, writes, lists or deletes a file does not change when the file
moves to another store.

This page describes how to create a path, what is particular to each store, and the operations on a path. Reading and
writing a path is described in [Reading and writing](streams), copying and moving it in
[Copying and moving](copy_files), rescuing its failures in [Errors](errors), and allowed paths, untrusted urls and
credentials in [Security](security).

## Creating a path

`IOStreams.path` returns the path of a file name or url:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("example.csv")
# => #<IOStreams::Paths::File:example.csv pipeline={}>

IOStreams.path("s3://my-bucket/exports/daily.csv")
# => #<IOStreams::Paths::S3:s3://my-bucket/exports/daily.csv pipeline={}>
~~~

The scheme of a url chooses the store, and the class of the path:

| Name or url | Store |
|-------------|-------|
| `example.csv`, `/var/data/example.csv`, `~/data/example.csv`, `file:///var/data/example.csv` | [Local files](#file) |
| `s3://my-bucket/exports/daily.csv` | [AWS S3](#aws-s3-s3), or another store that implements the S3 API |
| `gs://my-bucket/exports/daily.csv` | [Google Cloud Storage](#google-cloud-storage-gs), experimental |
| `sftp://sftp.example.org/inbound/data.csv` | [SFTP](#sftp-sftp) |
| `http://example.com/files/data.csv`, `https://example.com/files/data.csv` | [HTTP and HTTPS](#http-http-https) |

The scheme is compared without case. Any other scheme raises `ArgumentError`, such as `Unknown Scheme type: "ftp"`,
unless a path class is registered for it, see [Registering a storage scheme](extending#registering-a-storage-scheme).

Several elements are joined with `/`. Each element can be a String, a `Pathname`, which names a file, or anything
else whose `to_s` is a name:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("/var/data", "exports", "daily.csv")
# => #<IOStreams::Paths::File:/var/data/exports/daily.csv pipeline={}>

IOStreams.path(Pathname.new("/var/data/daily.csv.gz"))
# => #<IOStreams::Paths::File:/var/data/daily.csv.gz pipeline={gz: {}}>
~~~

The arguments of the store follow the name, such as the credentials of an SFTP server. Each store describes its own
below, and an argument that the store does not take raises `ArgumentError`:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("sftp://sftp.example.org/inbound/data.csv", username: "jack", password: "secret")
~~~

`#inspect` shows the class of the path, its full name without any credentials, and the `pipeline` of streams that
its file name implies, see [Streams from the file name](streams#streams-from-the-file-name).

There are other ways to create a path or a stream:

* `IOStreams.join("exports", "daily.csv")` joins the names to a root path, a location that is configured once, at
  startup, see [Using root paths](#using-root-paths).
* `IOStreams.stream(io)` reads or writes an IO that you supply, such as a `StringIO` or a socket, with the same methods
  for reading and writing, but without the [operations on the store](#operations-on-the-store), since an IO is not
  stored anywhere. See [Streams of an IO](streams#streams-of-an-io). It raises `ArgumentError` for a String or a
  `Pathname`, which name a file.
* `IOStreams.stream(relation)` reads the rows of an Active Record query, such as to copy them to a path, see
  [Exporting queries](queries).
* `IOStreams.new(name_or_io)` returns the path of a name, or the stream of an IO, for code that accepts either.

### Paths are configuration

A path or url is configuration, rather than code. Keep it in an environment variable or a configuration system, so
that the same code reads and writes local files in development, and S3 or an SFTP server in production. Where a store
can, it gives a name the meaning that it has in the others: `~/exports` is within the home directory, and
`sftp://sftp.example.org/~/exports` is within the login directory on the SFTP server. To keep code independent of the
store, use the methods of the path, rather than passing `#to_s` to `File` or `Dir`, which only work with local files,
and rescue the kind of failure, such as `IOStreams::Errors::NotFound`, rather than the exception of one store, see
[Errors](errors). See [Paths are configuration](config#paths-are-configuration).

## Local files {#file}

A name without a scheme is a local file, relative to the current directory unless it starts with `/`:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("exports/daily.csv")
IOStreams.path("/var/data/exports/daily.csv")
~~~

A `file://` url is absolute, so its host is empty, or `localhost`, and any other host raises `ArgumentError`. A `%`,
`?` or `#` in the name must be percent-encoded, as `%25`, `%3F` or `%23`, and any other character can be, such as a
space as `%20`. A relative name has no `file://` form, so supply it without `file://`.

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("file:///home/user/my%20file.csv").to_s
# => "/home/user/my file.csv"
~~~

### The home directory

A name of `~`, or one that starts with `~/`, is within the home directory of the current user, as an SFTP url that
starts with `~` is within the login directory. So the location of a file can be configured as a local file in one
environment, and on an SFTP server in another, without changing the code. A `file://` url can also start with `~`,
although that is not part of the `file://` standard:

~~~ruby
# When the home directory is /home/user
IOStreams.path("~/data/example.csv").to_s
# => "/home/user/data/example.csv"

IOStreams.path("file://~/data/example.csv").to_s
# => "/home/user/data/example.csv"

# The file data/example.csv within the login directory on the SFTP server
IOStreams.path("sftp://sftp.example.org/~/data/example.csv")
~~~

Only a leading `~` on its own is the home directory, so `~user/a.csv`, `~$Book1.xlsx` and `a/~/b.csv` are unchanged.
Use `./~/example.csv` for a directory called `~` within the current directory. When the current directory has one, a
name within the home directory, such as `~/example.csv`, logs a warning via `IOStreams.logger`.

`IOStreams.home` returns the home directory of the current user as a path, `IOStreams.home("username")` that of
another user, and `IOStreams.working_path` the current directory:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.home.join("my file.csv").to_s
# => "/home/user/my file.csv"
~~~

### Arguments {#optional-arguments}

| Argument | Meaning | Default |
|----------|---------|---------|
| `create_path:` | Whether writing the file creates the directories that it is in. With `false`, writing to a directory that does not exist raises `Errno::ENOENT`, tagged as `IOStreams::Errors::NotFound` | `true` |

~~~ruby
# Raises Errno::ENOENT unless the directory exports already exists.
IOStreams.path("exports/daily.csv", create_path: false).write("name,login\n")
~~~

`#create_path` returns it, and the paths that `#join`, `#directory` and `#each_child` return keep it.

### Writing, moving and symbolic links

* Writing writes the file as the block writes it. When the block raises, or the thread that writes it is killed, the
  file is removed, so that it is never left incomplete. When the block returns, or leaves early, such as with `break`,
  the file keeps what was written. A file that cannot be opened, such as a read-only file, is left as it is. See
  [Writing](streams#writing).
* `#move_to` another local path renames the file, or copies it and deletes the original when the target is on another
  file system. A target that is an existing directory raises `ArgumentError`, which names the file within it to supply
  instead, and so does a target that is the same file, whether by the same name, another name, or a symbolic link.
* Reading, writing, `#exist?`, `#size`, `#file?` and `#directory?` follow a symbolic link, as `File` does, while
  `#delete` and `#delete_all` delete the link itself, rather than what it refers to, and `#delete_all` does not follow
  the links within a directory. `#realpath` returns a copy of the path of a file or directory that exists, with `.`,
  `..` and symbolic links resolved, keeping its streams and options. For the links that `#each_child` finds, see
  [Symbolic links](#symbolic-links).
* A name that is not valid UTF-8, such as one that a Windows program wrote in Latin-1, is used as it is, so that the
  file can still be read, listed, moved and deleted. `#display_name` and `#inspect` show each such byte as `\xHH`, such
  as `/data/caf\xE9.csv`.

## AWS S3 {#aws-s3-s3}

An `s3://` url names an object, by its bucket and its key:

~~~ruby
path = IOStreams.path("s3://my-bucket/exports/daily.csv")
~~~

Read it, write it and list it like any other path. The AWS SDK finds the credentials and the region, such as in its
environment variables or credential files, or from the instance profile, unless they are supplied as
[arguments](#optional-arguments-1):

~~~ruby
path.write("name,login\nJack Jones,jjones\n")
path.each(:hash) do |record|
  p record
end

IOStreams.path("s3://my-bucket/exports").each_child("*.csv") do |child|
  puts child
end
~~~

S3 needs the `aws-sdk-s3` gem, which IOStreams loads when it is first needed. So a process without the gem, such as a
web process that only records the path of a file for a job to process, can still create, join, compare and display an
S3 path. Without it, every request of S3 raises `LoadError`, and writing raises it before the block writes any data.

### The url {#required-arguments}

The url is `s3://`, the name of the bucket, `/`, and the key:

* The key is the name of the object as it is, including characters that are not ASCII, spaces and brackets, such as
  `s3://my-bucket/données/café [1].csv`, and a `+`, which is not a space. Only a `%`, `?` or `#` in the key must be
  percent-encoded, as `%25`, `%3F` or `%23`, since they start an escape, the query and a fragment. `#to_s` encodes
  them, so that the path can be created again from its url, and `#path` returns the key. A key must be valid UTF-8, as
  every S3 key is, so a name that is not raises `ArgumentError`.
* `s3://my-bucket` and `s3://my-bucket/` are the bucket itself, see [Keys and directories](#keys-and-directories). A
  key that starts with `/`, which S3 holds as another object, keeps it in its url, such as
  `s3://my-bucket//exports/daily.csv`.
* A query string supplies options of the S3 requests, see [Request options](#request-options), such as
  `s3://my-bucket/exports/daily.csv?acl=bucket-owner-full-control`. They are not part of `#to_s`. Never interpolate an
  untrusted name into the url, since a name such as `file.csv?acl=public-read` would set them: join it onto the path
  instead, see [Untrusted names in urls](security#untrusted-names-in-urls).
* A part of the url that S3 cannot use raises `ArgumentError` when the path is created, with a message that names the
  url without any user name, password or query, and says what to supply instead: a fragment, which is an unencoded
  `#`, such as in `s3://my-bucket/a#b.csv`, a port, a user name or password, or a missing bucket, such as
  `s3:///daily.csv`. A bucket with a space, or with a character that is not ASCII, raises too.

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("s3://my-bucket/100%25.csv").path
# => "100%.csv"

(IOStreams.path("s3://my-bucket/exports") / "a#b.csv").to_s
# => "s3://my-bucket/exports/a%23b.csv"

IOStreams.path("s3://my-bucket:9000/daily.csv")
# ArgumentError: Invalid S3 url "s3://my-bucket:9000/daily.csv": it cannot have a port. Supply the endpoint of
#   another service that implements the S3 API with client: {endpoint: "https://host:port"}
~~~

### Arguments {#optional-arguments-1}

| Argument | Meaning | Default |
|----------|---------|---------|
| `client:` | The `Aws::S3::Client` to use, or a Hash of the options of a new client, such as `{endpoint: "https://s3.example.com"}` for another store that implements the S3 API | A new client, which the AWS SDK configures from its environment |
| `region:` | The AWS region of the bucket | The region that the AWS SDK finds, such as in the `AWS_REGION` environment variable |
| `access_key_id:` | The access key id of the credentials | The credentials that the AWS SDK finds, such as in its environment variables or credential files, or from the instance profile |
| `secret_access_key:` | The secret access key of the credentials | As for `access_key_id:` |
| Any other option | An option of the S3 requests, see [Request options](#request-options) | |

`region:`, `access_key_id:` and `secret_access_key:` are added to the options of a new client, so with an
`Aws::S3::Client` as `client:` they raise `ArgumentError`, since the client already has its own: supply them to
`Aws::S3::Client.new` instead.

~~~ruby
path = IOStreams.path("s3://my-bucket/exports/daily.csv", client: {endpoint: "https://s3.example.com"})
~~~

The client is created when it is first needed, since finding the credentials can be slow, such as from the instance
profile, and is shared by the paths copied from the path, such as by `#join`, `#directory` and `#each_child`. A path
answers `#client`, `#bucket_name`, and `#options`, its request options.

### Request options

Every other option, whether it is supplied as an argument or in the query string of the url, is supplied to each S3
request that accepts it:

| Option | Requests | Meaning |
|--------|----------|---------|
| `acl:` | Writing, and copying within S3 | The canned ACL of the object, such as `"bucket-owner-full-control"` |
| `storage_class:` | Writing, and copying within S3 | The storage class of the object, such as `"STANDARD_IA"` |
| `content_type:`, `cache_control:`, `content_disposition:`, `content_encoding:`, `expires:`, `metadata:`, `tagging:` | Writing, and copying within S3 | The metadata of the object |
| `server_side_encryption:`, `ssekms_key_id:` | Writing, and copying within S3 | Encryption with a key that S3 or AWS KMS holds, such as `server_side_encryption: "aws:kms"` |
| `sse_customer_algorithm:`, `sse_customer_key:`, `sse_customer_key_md5:` | Reading, writing, copying within S3, and checking the object, such as with `#exist?` | Encryption with a key that you supply (SSE-C), which S3 needs to read the object too |
| `request_payer:` | Every request | `"requester"`, for a bucket whose requester pays for each request |
| `expected_bucket_owner:` | Every request | The account that must own the bucket |
| `range:`, `part_number:` | Reading | Read only those bytes of the object, through a temp file, see [Reading an object](#s3-reading) |
| `content_md5:`, `content_length:`, or a checksum, such as `checksum_crc32:` | Writing | Describe the whole object, so the data is written into a temp file first, see [Writing an object](#s3-writing) |

Every option of the AWS SDK's `get_object`, `head_object`, `put_object`, `copy_object`, `delete_object`,
`delete_objects` and `list_objects_v2` requests can be supplied, see
[Aws::S3::Client](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sdk-for-ruby/v3/api/Aws/S3/Client.html).

The options are strict: an option that no S3 request accepts, such as a misspelled `acll:`, raises `ArgumentError`
when the path is created, rather than when a request is made, so that the mistake is reported wherever the code runs.
So does a request parameter that the path sets itself, such as `bucket:`, `key:`, `prefix:` or `delimiter:`, and
`encoding_type:` and `start_after:`, which would change which keys every listing returns, or how. The options are
checked against the AWS SDK, so a process without the `aws-sdk-s3` gem cannot check them, but it cannot
make a request either.

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("s3://my-bucket/daily.csv", acll: "public-read")
# ArgumentError: Unknown S3 option: :acll
~~~

### Reading an object {#s3-reading}

Reading requests the object 8MB at a time, as the block reads it, so that the application starts on the data straight
away, and the object never has to fit on the local disk:

* The first range is requested before the block is called, so a missing object raises `IOStreams::Errors::NotFound`
  before the block runs, and before `#copy_from` changes its target.
* Every later range is read from the same object as the first: in a versioned bucket from the same version, and
  otherwise only while the object has the same ETag. So an object that is replaced while it is read raises
  `Aws::S3::Errors::PreconditionFailed`, rather than returning parts of both.
* A failure part way through the object raises from within the block, once some of the data has been processed.
* The IO that the block reads is not a `File`, so it has no `#rewind` or `#size`, see [Reading](streams#reading).
* S3 returns no checksum for a range of an object, so the AWS SDK checks none, while TLS still protects the data in
  transit.

With the `range:` or `part_number:` option, which choose the bytes to read, the object is downloaded into a temp file
before the block is called, see [When temp files are used](config#when-temp-files-are-used).

### Writing an object {#s3-writing}

Writing uploads the data as the block writes it, so the file never has to fit on the local disk, and the upload
overlaps with writing it. S3 only stores the object once the block completes, so a partial object is never visible:

* Up to 8MB is stored with a single request once the block completes.
* More is uploaded in parts of 8MB, four at a time in other threads, while the block writes the next part, so writing
  holds about 40MB in memory. The size of a part doubles after every 1,000 parts, so that an object can be as large
  as S3 allows, 5TB. An object larger than 8MB has the ETag of a multipart upload, such as `"...-3"`, rather than the
  MD5 digest of its data.
* When the block returns, or leaves early, such as with `break`, the object is stored with what was written. When the
  block raises, its thread is killed, or the upload of a part fails, the upload is aborted, so that S3 discards the
  parts already uploaded, and the exception is raised, such as `Aws::S3::Errors::AccessDenied`.
* A process that is killed while it writes cannot abort its upload, so add a lifecycle rule to the bucket that aborts
  incomplete multipart uploads, such as after a day, so that S3 removes their parts.

With an option that describes the whole object, `content_md5:`, `content_length:`, `write_offset_bytes:`, or a
checksum of its data, such as `checksum_crc32:`, the data is written into a temp file, which is uploaded once the
block completes.

### Copying within S3

A copy as stored from one S3 path to another, with `copy_from(source, convert: false)` or
`copy_to(target, convert: false)`, and `#move_to` from one S3 path to another, ask S3 to copy the object, without
reading its data, for an object smaller than 5GB. A larger object is read and uploaded. The copy returns the number
of bytes copied, like any other copy, and `#move_to` returns the target.

The copy writes the target, so it is requested with the client and options of the target, such as its `acl:` and
`storage_class:`, along with the source's `sse_customer_algorithm:`, `sse_customer_key:` and `sse_customer_key_md5:`,
which S3 needs to read the source, its `request_payer:`, and its `version_id:`, so that the version of the source
that it names is copied. So the client of the target must be able to read the
source, and the new object does not keep the options of the source, such as its `storage_class:`, unless they are set
on the target too:

~~~ruby
source = IOStreams.path("s3://my-bucket/exports/daily.csv")
target = IOStreams.path("s3://partner-bucket/inbound/daily.csv", acl: "bucket-owner-full-control")
source.move_to(target)
~~~

See [Copying and moving](copy_files).

### Keys and directories

S3 has no directories, only keys that contain `/`. A path is a directory when any key is within it, such as
`s3://my-bucket/a` and `s3://my-bucket/a/b` for the key `a/b/c.csv`, or when a folder object exists for it, whose
key ends with `/`, such as the folders that the S3 console creates:

* `#exist?` is true for an object or a directory: when no object has the key, it makes a second request, which lists a
  key within the path. `#file?` checks for an object only, with one request, and `#directory?` lists a key within the
  path.
* `#empty?` is true for an object without any data, and for a directory without any keys within it, apart from its
  folder object.
* The bucket itself, `s3://my-bucket/`, exists, and is a directory, when it exists and can be listed. It is not an
  object, so `#size` and `#mtime` raise `Errno::EISDIR`, tagged as `IOStreams::Errors::NotFound`, and `#size?`
  returns nil.
