A field without a `type` is `any`, as in Frictionless. Empty text is read as `nil`, except for a `string` or `any`
field, which keeps it.

A value that is not one of the type of its field, such as `N/A` for an `integer`, raises
`IOStreams::Errors::InvalidValue`, naming the field and the value, both when reading and when writing. So does a `date`
or `datetime` that does not exist, such as `2026-02-30`, and a `time` that is not on a clock, such as `24:00:00`.

A `time` is written as the time of its own clock, as a Rails app shows it, so a shift that starts at 09:30 in New York
is written as `09:30:00`, whatever time zone the server is in. A `time` read from text with an offset keeps it, such as
`-05:00`, but writes the same `09:30:00`, so give its field a `format` with an offset, such as `"%H:%M:%S%:z"`, to
write the offset too. Use an offset rather than the name of a zone, `%Z`, since a time moved from another day keeps its
offset but not the name of its zone.

JSON writes integers, numbers and booleans as JSON numbers and booleans, with all of the digits of a `number`, and the
digits after the decimal point that its `decimals` give, such as `12.50`, the same as CSV, an `object` or an `array`
as itself, and every other value as text, such as a date, including in an application that uses ActiveSupport, as Rails does, which replaces how Ruby
writes JSON. Reading JSON keeps all of the digits of a `number` too, rather than reading it through a `Float`, while
the numbers of the other fields are a `Float`, as they are without a schema. The `:hash` and `:array` formats keep the
values themselves.

A `number` field needs the `bigdecimal` gem, which is a bundled gem from Ruby 3.4, so add `gem "bigdecimal"` to the
Gemfile, or set `floatNumber: true` to read a `Float` instead.

**A `duration` field needs the `activesupport` gem**, since its values are `ActiveSupport::Duration`s, which keep the
months and days of a duration, such as a PostgreSQL `interval`, apart from its seconds, as neither has a fixed number of
seconds. Rails includes it. Any other application must add `gem "activesupport"` to its Gemfile, otherwise setting a
schema with a `duration` field raises `LoadError`, naming the gem. IOStreams loads `ActiveSupport::Duration` and the
parts of ActiveSupport that it needs, but not ActiveSupport's JSON, so it does not change how the application writes
JSON. A duration is read only from ISO 8601
text, so a number, such as `30600`, raises, since it does not say what it counts.

### Matching columns to fields

Each column of the header row, or key of a JSON record, is matched to the field:

1. Whose name is the column, such as `email` for the column `email`, whether the name is a String or a Symbol.
2. Whose `aliases` include the column, such as `["DOB", "Birth Date"]` for the field `date_of_birth`.
3. Whose name or alias is the same as the column once both are compared without their case, spaces and
   punctuation, and with the forms of a character that Unicode treats as the same made the same. So the field
   `first_name` matches the columns `First Name`, `FIRST.NAME` and `firstname`, the field `email` matches `E-mail`,
   and `id` matches the full width `ＩＤ` that some spreadsheets have.
4. Whose name or alias is the same as the column once both are cleansed as a header row is cleansed without a
   schema, see [Records and rows without a schema](#records-and-rows-without-a-schema), and then compared the same
   way. Cleansing drops the characters that Unicode otherwise makes digits, such as `²`, `½` and `①`, so that a
   field named as the cleansed column, such as `area_m` for `Area (m²)`, matches it, as `area_m2` does.

A column that is the same as several fields in step 3, or as none, is the field whose name or alias is the column
once cleansed, if there is one. So a schema whose fields are named as a header row is cleansed without a schema finds
every column that the cleansing named, such as the fields `e_mail` and `email`, which are the same once compared
loosely, for the columns `E-mail` and `Email`.

The columns are matched once, when the header row is read, or once for each set of keys of the JSON records, which
are usually the same for every record, rather than for each value.

The keys of the records read are the names of their fields as they are given, so a field named with a Symbol, such as
`name: :id`, returns the key `:id`, whatever the column of the file is called, unless `keyType` forms them otherwise,
see [Keys of the records read](#keys-of-the-records-read). For a format with a header row, such as CSV,
`each(:array)` returns a header row of the keys of the fields of its columns, and then the values of those fields of
each row, in the order of the fields. A file without a header row, such as JSON, Parquet or fixed width, or with a
schema whose `header` is false, returns the keys of the fields as its header row, and then the values of every field
of each row, in order, `nil` for a key that a JSON record does not have. A column that the schema does not
list is skipped, or raises, see [fieldsMatch](#fieldsmatch).

A column that could be either of two fields raises `IOStreams::Errors::InvalidHeader`, rather than guess, such as
`amount` for the fields `Amount ($)` and `Amount (€)`, which match their own columns exactly. So do two columns that
are the same field, such as `email` and `Email`, rather than lose the value of one of them.

When writing, the header row is the names of the fields, in order, and the keys of each record written are matched
to the fields in the same way. `writer(:array)` writes that header row itself, before the rows, and takes each row
written as the values of the fields, in order, whatever the format:

~~~ruby
path = IOStreams.path("people.csv").schema(
  fields: [
    {name: "name"},
    {name: "age", type: "integer"}
  ]
)
path.writer(:array) do |io|
  io << ["Jack", 21]
end
path.read
# => "name,age\nJack,21\n"
~~~

A header row written to it, such as the `IOStreams::Row::HeaderRow` that `each(:array)` yields, gives the columns of
the rows after it instead, without a line of its own, and its columns are matched to the fields in the same way, so
that the values of each row after it can be in any order, and the rows read from another file can be written as they
are, by a loop over `each(:array)`, or by `copy_from(source, mode: :array)`. A field that the header row does not have
is written as empty.

So a file can have readable column names, while the code uses its own keys:

~~~ruby
report = IOStreams.path("report.csv").schema(
  fields: [
    {name: "First Name"},
    {name: "Date of Birth", type: "date"}
  ]
)
report.writer(:hash) do |io|
  io << {first_name: "Jack", date_of_birth: Date.new(2001, 2, 3)}
end
report.read
# => "First Name,Date of Birth\nJack,2001-02-03\n"
~~~

### Keys of the records read

`keyType`, which IOStreams adds to the properties of a schema, forms the key of each field in the records read from
its name:

| `keyType` | The key of the field named `First Name` |
|-----------|-----------------------------------------|
| None, the default | `"First Name"`, the name as it is given, a String or a Symbol |
| `string` | `"First Name"`, also for a name that is a Symbol |
| `cleansed` | `"first_name"`, the name once cleansed: lowercase, without leading and trailing spaces, with the spaces and dashes within it made `_`, and the characters other than letters, digits and `_`, in any language, removed |
| `symbol` | `:"First Name"`, also for a name that is a String |
| `cleansedSymbol` | `:first_name` |

So a file can have readable column names, which are the names of the fields, while the code reads the keys that it
needs:

~~~ruby
path = IOStreams.path("people.csv").schema(
  fieldsMatch: "partial",
  keyType:     "cleansedSymbol",
  fields:      [
    {name: "First Name"},
    {name: "Date of Birth", type: "date"}
  ]
)
path.each(:hash) do |person|
  p person
end
# "First Name,Date of Birth\nJack,2001-02-03\n" => {first_name: "Jack", date_of_birth: #<Date: 2001-02-03 ...>}

path.writer(:hash) do |io|
  io << {first_name: "Jill", date_of_birth: Date.new(2002, 3, 4)}
end
# => "First Name,Date of Birth\nJill,2002-03-04\n"
~~~

The header row written is still the names of the fields, and a record written can be keyed by the keys of the
records read, as well as by the names, so that the records read can be written back. A schema held as JSON, or in a
database such as MongoDB, has String names, so `keyType: "symbol"` reads the Symbol keys that a schema in Ruby gives.
Two fields with the same key, such as `First Name` and `first-name` with `cleansed`, raise `ArgumentError`, since a
record could not hold both, and so does a key that is the name or an alias of another field.

### fieldsMatch

`fieldsMatch` says how the columns of the file must match the fields, as Frictionless defines it:

| `fieldsMatch` | The columns of the file | Columns that the schema does not list |
|---------------|-------------------------|---------------------------------------|
| `exact`, the default | are the fields, in the same order | raise |
| `equal` | are the fields, in any order | raise |
| `subset` | include every field | are skipped |
| `superset` | are fields, but a field can be missing | raise |
| `partial` | include at least one field | are skipped |

A file that does not match raises `IOStreams::Errors::InvalidHeader`, which lists each problem, such as the columns
that are not fields, and the fields that are missing. The columns without a name at the end of the header row, such
as the empty column that a spreadsheet exports after the last one, or after a comma at the end of each line, are not
columns, so a value under one is a value after the last column, see below. A column without a name between other
columns is a column that the schema does not list.

`partial` is the easiest to start with, and suits a schema that only gives the type of some of the columns. A schema
for files that are received from elsewhere, such as uploads, is usually stricter: `subset` accepts files with more
columns than the code needs, and `equal` or `exact` accept only the columns that the schema lists.

The keys of each JSON record are checked the same way, in any order. The columns of a file without a header row are
the fields in order, so `header: false` only accepts `exact`, and a fixed width file always has every field.

A row read that has a value after the last column of its header row, or after the last field of a file without one,
such as when a value has a comma that is not quoted, raises `IOStreams::Errors::InvalidHeader` too, unless
`fieldsMatch` skips it, rather than lose the value. A blank value there, such as after a comma at the end of each
line, is not data, so it is ignored.

A file that is written always has every field, so writing only checks the keys of each record, the columns of the
header row of the rows written, and the values of each row after the last field or column: `subset` and `partial`
skip them, and the others raise `IOStreams::Errors::InvalidHeader`. A field that a record does not supply is written
as empty, or as `null` in JSON.

### Keeping the other columns

`extraColumns: "keep"`, which IOStreams adds to the properties of a schema, keeps the columns that `subset` and
`partial` would skip, after the fields, in the order of the columns, each by the key that
[keyType](#keys-of-the-records-read) forms from its column, and with its value as it is. So a file can need some
columns, and the code still read every other column that it has:

~~~ruby
path = IOStreams.path("upload.csv").schema(
  fieldsMatch:  "subset",
  extraColumns: "keep",
  keyType:      "cleansed",
  fields:       [{name: "zip_code", constraints: {required: true}, allowBlank: true}]
)
path.each(:hash) do |record|
  p record
end
# "Zip Code,First Name,Notes\n12345,Jack,hi\n" => {"zip_code" => "12345", "first_name" => "Jack", "notes" => "hi"}
~~~

With `subset`, a schema can then have no fields, to read every column of every file, keyed as `keyType` forms them,
or as the columns are written without it. The keys of each JSON or Parquet record are kept the same way, so their
rows, which have a header row of the keys of the fields, cannot be read with `each(:array)`, which raises
`ArgumentError`, and a Parquet file reads every column, rather than only those of the fields. A fixed
width file has only its fields, so it ignores `extraColumns`. Two columns kept with the same key, such as `Notes` and
`notes` with `keyType: "cleansed"`, raise `IOStreams::Errors::InvalidHeader`, rather than lose one of them, and a
column without a name is not kept. Writing writes only the fields, whichever it is. The default, `"skip"`, leaves them
out, and any other `fieldsMatch` raises `ArgumentError` for `"keep"`, since it does not accept them.

### Required fields

A field whose `constraints` are `required`, as Frictionless defines it, must have a value: a header row, or JSON
record, without the field raises `IOStreams::Errors::InvalidHeader`, whatever `fieldsMatch` is, and a value that is
`nil`, or empty text, raises `IOStreams::Errors::InvalidValue`, both when reading and when writing, including a blank
record or row written, such as `{}`, which is otherwise written as a blank line. A blank row read, whose every value is
`nil` or blank text, is `nil` instead, as a blank line is, see [Blank rows](streams#blank-rows). Text that is only spaces
is a value for a `string` field of a row that has other values, as in Frictionless, but not for a type that reads it
as `nil`, such as an `integer`.

~~~ruby
# An upload, whose columns may be in any order, with names that people typed, and columns that the code ignores.
schema = {
  fieldsMatch: "subset",
  fields:      [
    {name: "first_name",    constraints: {required: true}},
    {name: "email",         aliases: ["E-mail Address"], constraints: {required: true}},
    {name: "date_of_birth", type: "date", aliases: ["DOB", "Birth Date"]}
  ]
}
IOStreams.path("upload.csv").schema(schema).each(:hash) do |contact|
  p contact
end
# "E-mail Address,FIRST NAME,DOB,Notes" =>
# {"first_name" => "Jack", "email" => "j@x.com", "date_of_birth" => #<Date: 2001-02-03 ((2451944j,0s,0n),+0s,2299161j)>}
~~~

A file can need a column whose values can be blank, such as a middle name that must be in every upload, but that
many people do not have. Give its field `allowBlank: true` with `required`: a header row, or JSON record, without
the field still raises, while a value that is `nil`, or empty text, is read and written as it is:

~~~ruby
schema = {
  fieldsMatch: "partial",
  fields:      [
    {name: "first_name",  constraints: {required: true}},
    {name: "middle_name", constraints: {required: true}, allowBlank: true}
  ]
}
IOStreams.path("upload.csv").schema(schema).each(:hash) do |person|
  p person
end
# "First Name,Middle Name\nJack,\n" => {"first_name" => "Jack", "middle_name" => nil}
# "First Name\nJack\n"               => IOStreams::Errors::InvalidHeader, missing the required field "middle_name"
~~~

`allowBlank` is a property of the field that IOStreams adds, rather than a constraint, since Frictionless defines
`required` as `true` or `false`, and a tool reports an error for a constraint that it does not support, while it
accepts other properties of a field. A field that is not `required` raises `ArgumentError` for it, since its values
can be blank anyway.

IOStreams does not support the other constraints of Frictionless yet, such as `maxLength`, so they raise
`ArgumentError`, rather than appear to check values that they do not.

### Schema properties

* `fields` The fields of the file, in the order of its columns, which can be empty with `extraColumns: "keep"`.
  Required.
* `fieldsMatch` How the columns of the file must match the fields, see [fieldsMatch](#fieldsmatch). Default: `exact`
* `header` `false` when the file has no header row, as in a Frictionless Table Dialect. The columns of the file are
  then the fields, in order: reading takes every line as a row, after the names of the fields as the header row that
  `each(:array)` yields, and writing writes no header row, and the fields in order. A format without a header row, such
  as JSON or fixed width, ignores it. Default: `true`
* `width` The length of every line of a fixed width file, see [Fixed width files](#fixed-width-files).
* `keyType` How the keys of the records read are formed from the names of the fields: `string`, `cleansed`, `symbol`
  or `cleansedSymbol`, see [Keys of the records read](#keys-of-the-records-read). IOStreams adds this property.
  Default: the names as they are given.
* `extraColumns` `keep` to keep the columns that the schema does not list, which `subset` and `partial` skip, see
  [Keeping the other columns](#keeping-the-other-columns). IOStreams adds this property. Default: `skip`

`$schema`, `title` and `description` describe the schema to people and have no effect.

~~~ruby
# A CSV file without a header row.
path = IOStreams.path("people.csv").schema(
  header: false,
  fields: [
    {name: "name"},
    {name: "age", type: "integer"}
  ]
)
path.each(:hash) do |person|
  p person
end
# => {"name" => "Jack", "age" => 21}
~~~

A column of a file without a header row that the code does not read still needs a field, which holds its place, so
give it `skip: true`, and the records read leave it out:

~~~ruby
path = IOStreams.path("people.csv").schema(
  header: false,
  fields: [
    {name: "name"},
    {name: "unused", skip: true},
    {name: "age", type: "integer"}
  ]
)
path.each(:hash) do |person|
  p person
end
# "Jack,x,21\n" => {"name" => "Jack", "age" => 21}
~~~

The rows read leave it out too, and writing writes an empty value in its column, from records, and from rows of the
values of the other fields, in order, as the rows read have them.

Since the schema is set on the path, every reader of the path reads the file the same way, including `#copy_from`
and `#copy_to`, whose options only apply to the target.

### Field properties

* `name` The key of the field in each record, and its column in the header row written. Required.
* `type` See [Types](#types). Default: `any`
* `constraints` `{required: true}` for a field that must have a value, see [Required fields](#required-fields).
* `format` For a `date`, a `datetime` or a `time`, the strptime pattern of its text, such as `"%d/%m/%Y"`, `"%Y%m%d"`
  or `"%I:%M %p"` for `9:30 PM`. Default: ISO 8601.
* `trueValues` and `falseValues` For a `boolean`, the text that is true and false.
  Default: `["true", "True", "TRUE", "1"]` and `["false", "False", "FALSE", "0"]`
* `floatNumber` For a `number`, `true` to read a `Float` rather than a `BigDecimal`, as frictionless-py does.
* `aliases` The other names of the column of the field, see [Matching columns to fields](#matching-columns-to-fields).
  IOStreams adds this property.
* `allowBlank` For a field whose `constraints` are `required`, `true` to accept a value that is `nil`, or empty text,
  while the file must still have its column, see [Required fields](#required-fields). IOStreams adds this property.
* `decimals` For a `number`, the number of digits to write after the decimal point, rounding a `BigDecimal` half up,
  and a `Float`, with `floatNumber: true`, as Ruby's `format` does, to the nearest of its binary value, as the layouts
  of fixed width files did before v3.0. IOStreams adds this property.
* `skip` `true` for a field that only holds the place of its column, such as a column of a file without a header row
  that the code does not read: reading leaves it out of the rows and records, and writing writes an empty value in its
  column, or leaves it out of a JSON record, and a Parquet file has no column for it. It takes only the properties
  that place its column, `name`, `aliases`, `width` and `start`. IOStreams adds this property.
* `width`, `start` and `truncate` The position of the field in a fixed width file, see
  [Fixed width files](#fixed-width-files). IOStreams adds these properties. The other formats ignore them, so that
  one schema can describe both a fixed width file and the CSV file that it is converted to.

`title`, `description`, `example` and `rdfType` describe a field to people and have no effect, as do the properties
of other tools, whose names include a `:`, such as `"mytool:owner"`. Any other property raises `ArgumentError`, as do
the parts of Frictionless that IOStreams does not support yet, such as `missingValues`, `primaryKey`, the constraints
other than `required`, and the `year` type, so that a schema never appears to check a value that it does not.

### Values without a field

A value of a file without a schema, or of a field without a type, is written as a field of type `any` writes it:

| Value | Written as |
|-------|------------|
| `BigDecimal` | a plain decimal, such as `12.5`, rather than `0.125e2` |
| `Time` or `DateTime` | ISO 8601, such as `2026-10-13T09:30:00Z`, with as many digits of its fraction of a second as it needs |
| `Date` | ISO 8601, such as `2026-10-13` |
| `Hash` or `Array` | JSON, such as `{"a":1}` or `[1,2]`, as the JSON format writes it |
| any other value | its `to_s`, such as `42` or `true` |

JSON writes a `BigDecimal`, `Date` or `Time` as that text, within an object or an array too, so that a `BigDecimal`
keeps all of its digits, and writes every other value as itself, such as a number or `true`. The `:hash` and `:array`
formats keep the values themselves. To write a value in another form, such as a date as `13/10/2026`, give its field
a type and a `format` in the schema.

### Schemas in IOStreams 2.2 and 3.0

IOStreams 2.2 has the same schema, with the same properties, so an application can move to a schema while it still
runs 2.2. A schema in 2.2 reads and writes as it does here, apart from the changes that 3.0 makes to every file, such
as reading text as UTF-8, see [A schema in v2.2 and v3.0](upgrading#a-schema-in-v22-and-v30). 3.0 also adds the `time`
and `duration` types, which 2.2 raises `ArgumentError` for, as types that it does not support.

## Parquet files

[Apache Parquet](https://parquet.apache.org/) files hold the type of each column, so their records are read with typed
values, such as an `Integer`, `BigDecimal`, `Date` or `Time`, even without a schema. A column of times of day is read
as a `Time` on 2000-01-01, in UTC, as a `time` field reads it. A `.parquet` file name selects the format, and it can also be compressed
or encrypted, such as `data.parquet.pgp`. Install the [parquet](https://github.com/njaremko/parquet-ruby) gem, which is
not available on JRuby.

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("s3://bucket/people.parquet").each(:hash) do |record|
  p record
  # => {"id" => 1, "name" => "Jack", "amount" => 0.1235e2, "born" => #<Date: 2000-02-29 ((2451604j,0s,0n),+0s,2299161j)>}
end
~~~

With a schema, the columns are matched to its fields, and each value is converted to the type of its field, as for any
other format, see [Schema](#schema).

Writing needs a schema, since a Parquet file records the type of each of its columns. Its fields are the columns, and
each type is written as:

| Type | Parquet type |
|------|--------------|
| `string` | `string` |
| `integer` | `int64` |
| `number` | `decimal(38, decimals)`, rounding each value to its `decimals`, or `double` with `floatNumber: true` |
| `boolean` | `boolean` |
| `date` | `date32` |
| `datetime` | `timestamp_micros`, adjusted to UTC, so it is read back in UTC |
| `time` | `time_micros`, not adjusted to UTC, holding the time of its clock, which is read back as a `Time` on 2000-01-01 in UTC |
| `duration` | `string`, holding its ISO 8601 text, such as `P1M2DT3H`, which a schema with the field reads back as an `ActiveSupport::Duration` |
| `object`, `array` | `string`, holding its JSON text, which a schema with the field reads back as a `Hash` or an `Array` |

A `number` field needs `decimals` or `floatNumber: true`, since a Parquet decimal has a fixed number of digits after
its point, and a field of type `any` raises `ArgumentError`, since it has no type. A field whose `constraints` are
`required` is written as a column that cannot be null, unless it has `allowBlank: true`.

~~~ruby
schema = {
  fields: [
    {name: "id", type: "integer", constraints: {required: true}},
    {name: "name", type: "string"},
    {name: "amount", type: "number", decimals: 2},
    {name: "born", type: "date"}
  ]
}

IOStreams.path("people.parquet").schema(schema).writer(:hash) do |writer|
  writer << {"id" => 1, "name" => "Jack", "amount" => BigDecimal("12.35"), "born" => Date.new(2000, 2, 29)}
end

# Convert a CSV file into Parquet
IOStreams.path("people.parquet").schema(schema).copy_from(IOStreams.path("people.csv").schema(schema), mode: :hash)
~~~

Set how its columns are compressed with `option(:parquet, compression: ...)`: `"none"`, `"snappy"`, the default,
`"gzip"`, `"lz4"`, `"zstd"` or `"brotli"`. Reading finds the compression in the file, so it ignores the option, and so
does a file that is not Parquet, as for the options of other streams. `stream(:parquet, ...)` sets it too, and still
applies the streams in the file name, such as `.gz` in `people.parquet.gz`, since Parquet is not one of them.

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("people.parquet").schema(schema).option(:parquet, compression: "zstd").writer(:hash) do |writer|
  writer << {"id" => 1, "name" => "Jack"}
end
~~~

A Parquet file stores each column on its own, so with a schema whose `fieldsMatch` is `"subset"` or `"partial"`, which
skip the columns that it does not list, only the columns of its fields are read and decoded, which is faster for a
wide file. The other values of `fieldsMatch` read every column, so that they can check the others.

A Parquet file records its columns at its end, so it is read from a local file, and a file stored elsewhere, such as
on S3, is first copied into a temp file. Likewise it is written to a temp file, which is then copied to the path. The
records written before the block leaves early, such as with `break`, are kept, as for other formats, and nothing is
written when the block raises, or when the thread writing it is killed. Writing without a schema, with a field that
has no Parquet type, or with a compression that Parquet does not have, raises `ArgumentError` before the file is
opened, so that an existing file is kept.

A value that its column cannot hold raises `IOStreams::Errors::InvalidValue`, naming its field, when the record is
written: an integer outside the range of an `int64`, or a number with more digits before its decimal point than its
`decimal(38, decimals)` holds, that is `38 - decimals`.

A Parquet file has no lines, so the `:line` mode, and the `delimiter:` and `buffer_size:` options, raise
`ArgumentError`, and so does `#encoding`, since its values are not text, which the `parquet` gem reads and writes as
UTF-8. Like JSON, it has no header row, so the first row that `each(:array)` yields is a header row of its columns,
or with a schema of the names of its fields, and each row after it is the values of the fields, in order:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("s3://bucket/people.parquet").each(:array) do |row|
  p row
end
# ["id", "name", "amount", "born"]
# [1, "Jack", 0.1235e2, #<Date: 2000-02-29 ((2451604j,0s,0n),+0s,2299161j)>]
~~~

## Fixed width files

Fixed width files have no delimiters; each field is at the same position in every line. Since the positions cannot be
inferred from the file, the schema gives the `width` of each field, in the order of the line:

~~~ruby
path = IOStreams.path("sample_data").format(:fixed).schema(
  fields: [
    {name: "name",    type: "string",  width: 23},
    {name: "address", type: "string",  width: 40},
    {name: "zip",     type: "integer", width: 5}
  ]
)
path.each(:hash) do |record|
  p record
end
~~~

Writing a fixed width file uses the same schema to render each record:

~~~ruby
path.writer(:hash) do |io|
  io << {"name" => "Jack Jones", "address" => "Somewhere", "zip" => 12345}
end
~~~

A fixed width file has no header row, so `each(:array)` yields the names of the fields as its header row, and then
the values of the fields of each line, in order. `writer(:array)` takes rows of the values of the fields, in order, and
takes the header row that `each(:array)` yields as the header row of the rows after it, so that the rows read from a
file in another format, such as CSV, can be written as they are:

~~~ruby
path.each(:array) do |row|
  p row
end
# ["name", "address", "zip"]
# ["Jack Jones", "Somewhere", 12345]
~~~

The schema can be held in a file, such as this `people.schema.json`:

~~~json
{
  "fields": [
    {"name": "name",    "type": "string",  "width": 23, "truncate": true},
    {"name": "address", "type": "string",  "width": 40},
    {"name": "zip",     "type": "integer", "width": 5,  "start": 66},
    {"name": "weight",  "type": "number",  "width": 10, "decimals": 2},
    {"name": "joined",  "type": "date",    "width": 8,  "format": "%Y%m%d"},
    {"name": "notes",   "type": "string",  "width": "remainder"}
  ]
}
~~~

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("people.txt").format(:fixed).schema("people.schema.json").each(:hash) do |person|
  p person
end
~~~

The properties that place each field:

* `width` The number of characters of the field. The last field may have a width of `"remainder"` to take the rest
  of the line.
* `start` The position of the first character of the field, counting from 1, as the specifications of fixed width
  files do. It skips the characters after the field before it, such as a filler: in the example above, `zip` starts
  at 66, which skips the 2 characters after the 63 characters of `name` and `address`.
  Default: right after the field before it.
* `truncate` For a `string`, `true` to write only the first `width` characters of a longer value. Without it, a value
  that is too long raises `IOStreams::Errors::ValueTooLong`. A number is never truncated, and raises instead.

The `width` at the top level of the schema is the length of every line, when the line ends after the last field, such
as after a filler, for example `{"fields": [...], "width": 94}`. A `width` of `"remainder"` accepts lines of any
length, ignoring what follows the last field. Otherwise every line ends where the last field ends. A line of another
length raises `IOStreams::Errors::InvalidLineLength`.

When reading, each value is the text of its field without its leading and trailing spaces, converted to the type of
its field. The keys of each record are the names of the fields as they are given, so that a field whose name is a
Symbol returns a Symbol key.

When writing, a number is right justified and zero filled, and a missing number is written as zero, as the
specifications of most fixed width files require. A number that is not finite, such as `NaN` or `-INF`, is space
filled instead, so that it can be read back. Any other value is left justified and space filled, with each line
break replaced with a space, so that a value cannot add records. The characters that no field covers, such as a
filler, are spaces. The keys of the records written may be strings or symbols.

### Character encoding

Fixed width files are read and written as ASCII by default. The programs that write them, such as
COBOL programs, and the formats that specify them, such as NACHA ACH and IRS FIRE, count each column's
size in bytes, and their text is ASCII, or a single-byte code page such as ISO-8859-1. So a value read
is a UTF-8 string, like the values of every other format, and any byte that is not ASCII raises
`IOStreams::Errors::InvalidEncoding`, naming the byte and its offset, rather than shifting every
column that follows it.

Each `width` counts the characters of the text as it is read, and when writing, string values are
padded and truncated to `width` characters. In ASCII, and in a single-byte code page, each character
is one byte, so the widths count bytes.

Set the encoding of the file with [`#encoding`](streams#character-encoding) when it is not
ASCII. An encoding that is set always replaces the ASCII default, and `#raw` reads and writes the bytes as
they are stored:

* A single-byte code page, such as ISO-8859-1 or Windows-1252, or EBCDIC from a mainframe: name it
  with the encoding that the values are read as, for example
  `encoding("ISO-8859-1:UTF-8")`, `"Windows-1252:UTF-8"`, or `"IBM037:UTF-8"` for
  EBCDIC. The widths count bytes, and the values are UTF-8 strings.
* To load a file anyway, replacing each byte that is not ASCII with a space, so that the columns stay
  aligned: `encoding(replace: " ")`.
* UTF-8 written by a program that counts characters: `encoding("UTF-8")`.
* UTF-8 written by a program that counts bytes, which is rare: read it as binary, with
  `encoding("BINARY")`, whose values are binary strings, or with `replace: " "`.

An EBCDIC file is split into lines after it is converted, so its lines must end with the EBCDIC line
feed (`0x25`), which converts to `\n`. The EBCDIC new line (`0x15`) converts to U+0085, so supply
`delimiter: "\u0085"` to `#each` or `#reader` for a file whose lines end with it.

The `:line` mode reads ASCII too when the format of the path is `:fixed`, set with `#format` or
detected from a file name such as `data.fixed`.

When writing, a value that is not ASCII raises `Encoding::UndefinedConversionError`, rather than
writing a line that is longer than the schema in bytes. Set the encoding of the file, such as
`encoding("ISO-8859-1")`, whose lines are then the length of the schema in bytes, or
`replace: " "` to write a space for each character that is not ASCII:

~~~ruby
path = IOStreams.path("people.txt").encoding("ISO-8859-1")
path.format(:fixed).schema(
  fields: [
    {name: "name", width: 10},
    {name: "zip", width: 5}
  ]
)
path.writer(:hash) do |io|
  io << {"name" => "José", "zip" => "12345"}
end
~~~

### Cleaning fixed width files

To remove non-printable characters, such as NUL padding, from a fixed width file, replace them with a
space, so that every column after them stays in place:

~~~ruby
path.encoding(cleaner: :replace_non_printable, replace: " ")
~~~

Since `replace:` also replaces invalid characters, each byte that is not ASCII is replaced with a space
too, unless the encoding of the file is set.

The `:printable` cleaner removes non-printable characters rather than replacing them, even with
`replace:`, which only replaces invalid characters. So each one it removes moves every column that
follows it, and a line with one raises `IOStreams::Errors::InvalidLineLength`.

## Rows and records in memory

Two more formats, `:array` and `:hash`, are for rows and records that are already Ruby objects rather than text,
such as those that another library passes, so they are not used for files.

---

# Compression and Encryption

The extensions at the end of a file name say how the file is compressed or encrypted, and IOStreams reads and writes
the file through the stream of each one, a block at a time. `example.csv.gz.pgp` is compressed with gzip and then
encrypted with PGP, so reading it decrypts it, and then decompresses it. How a file name becomes a pipeline of streams,
and how to set the streams of a file whose name has none, is explained in
[Streams from the file name](streams#streams-from-the-file-name).

| Extension | Stream | Needs | Options when reading | Options when writing |
|-----------|--------|-------|----------------------|----------------------|
| `.gz`, `.gzip` | [gzip](#gzip) | Nothing: `zlib` is part of Ruby | None | `level` |
| `.bz2` | [bzip2](#bzip2) | The `bzip2-ffi` gem | `small`, `first_only`, `autoclose` | `block_size`, `work_factor`, `autoclose` |
| `.zip` | [Zip](#zip) | The `rubyzip` gem to read, and `zip_kit` to write | `entry_file_name` | `entry_file_name` |
| `.zst` | [Zstandard](#zstandard) | The `zstd-ruby` gem, 2.0.0 or later, or on JRuby the zstd-jni jar | None | `level` |
| `.enc` | [Symmetric Encryption](#symmetric-encryption) | The `symmetric-encryption` gem, with its ciphers configured | `version`, `buffer_size` | `compress`, `version`, `cipher_name`, `header`, `random_key`, `random_iv` |
| `.pgp`, `.gpg` | [PGP](#pgp) | The `gpg` program of GnuPG | `passphrase`, `signer` and more, see [Reader options](pgp#reader-options) | `recipient`, `signer` and more, see [Writer options](pgp#writer-options) |
| `.xlsx`, `.xlsm` | [Excel spreadsheets](#excel-spreadsheets) | The `creek` gem to read, and `xlsxtream` to write | None | `sheet_name`, `auto_format`, `use_shared_strings` |

Only the registered extensions at the end of the name count, after its first `.`, whatever their case, so
`DATA.CSV.GZ` is compressed with gzip, while `data.gz.csv` and `report.csv.bak` have no streams. `IOStreams.extensions`
returns the format registered for each extension:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.extensions.keys
# => [:bz2, :enc, :gz, :gzip, :zip, :pgp, :gpg, :xlsx, :xlsm, :zst]
~~~

IOStreams does not depend on any of these gems, so add to the Gemfile those of the streams that your application uses.
Each one is loaded when its stream is first used, and a gem that is not installed raises `LoadError`, naming it:

~~~
LoadError: Please install the gem 'bzip2-ffi' to support Bzip2. cannot load such file -- bzip2/ffi
~~~

## Setting options

Set the options of a stream on the path with `#option`, and they apply when the file name includes that stream:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("example.csv.gz").option(:gz, level: 9).write("name,login\nJack Jones,jjones\n")
~~~

* An option for a stream that the file name does not include has no effect, so the same code can set the options of
  every stream that a path held in configuration might use.
* An option for a stream applies to each of its extensions: `option(:gz, ...)` to a `.gzip` file, `option(:pgp, ...)`
  to a `.gpg` file, and `option(:xlsx, ...)` to a `.xlsm` file.
* For a file whose name does not name its streams, set them with `#stream`, which takes the same options, such as
  `IOStreams.path("tempfile2527").stream(:gz, level: 9)`, see [Stream](streams#stream).

The name of each option is checked when it is set. An option that neither the reader nor the writer of the stream
takes raises `ArgumentError`, which lists the valid options, even when the file name does not include that stream, so
a misspelled option is reported wherever the code runs:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("example.csv").option(:gz, levle: 9)
# ArgumentError: Unknown option :levle for a :gz stream. Valid options: :level.
~~~

The value of each option is checked when the file is written, before it is opened. So a value that a stream cannot
write with, such as a gzip `level` that is out of range, or a stream whose gem is not installed, raises before an
existing file is replaced:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("example.csv.gz").option(:gz, level: 10).write("name,login\nJack Jones,jjones\n")
# ArgumentError: Invalid gzip level 10: supply an Integer from 0, no compression, to 9, the best compression, or -1 for the default
~~~

What only the stream itself can find out, such as whether gpg has the key of a PGP recipient, raises once the file has
been opened, and the write fails like any other, see [Writing](streams#writing).

### Options for reading and writing

One set of options is shared by the reader and the writer of a stream, so that a path can be written and then read.
Each direction ignores the options of the other, such as the gzip `level` when reading, or the PGP `passphrase` when
writing, and the table above lists the options that each direction uses:

~~~ruby
path = IOStreams.path("example.csv.bz2").option(:bz2, block_size: 1, small: true)
path.write("name,login\nJack Jones,jjones\n")
path.read
# => "name,login\nJack Jones,jjones\n"
~~~

An option of the writer that a reader could seem to use, but does not, raises when reading, rather than being ignored:
the `sheet_name` of a spreadsheet, since reading always reads the first worksheet. See
[Options for reading and writing](streams#options-for-reading-and-writing).

## Compression {#compression-options}

Each compression stream compresses the data as it is written, and decompresses it as it is read, so that a file of any
size is processed a block at a time. Zip is the exception when reading: a zip file lists its contents at its end, so
reading one needs the whole file on local disk.

### gzip

gzip uses `zlib`, which is part of Ruby.

| Option | When | Default | Description |
|--------|------|---------|-------------|
| `level` | Writing | -1, zlib's default, which is 6 | The compression level, from 0, no compression, to 9, the best compression. |

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("example.csv.gz").option(:gz, level: 9).writer(:hash) do |io|
  io << {"name" => "Jack Jones", "login" => "jjones"}
end
~~~

Reading returns the data of every member of a gzip file, as `gunzip` does, so gzip files that were joined, such as with
`cat a.gz b.gz > ab.gz`, are read as one file. Zero bytes after the last member, which some programs add, are ignored,
while any other data after it raises `Zlib::GzipFile::Error`, with the message `not in gzip format`.

### bzip2

bzip2 uses the `bzip2-ffi` gem, which calls the bzip2 library, libbz2, of the system.

| Option | When | Default | Description |
|--------|------|---------|-------------|
| `block_size` | Writing | 9 | The size of the blocks that are compressed, from 1, 100KB, to 9, 900KB. A larger block compresses better, and uses more memory. |
| `work_factor` | Writing | 0, libbz2's default, which is 30 | How hard to try with data that repeats a lot before using a slower algorithm, from 0 to 250. |
| `small` | Reading | `false` | Decompress with an algorithm that uses less memory, about 2,300KB less, at about half the speed. |
| `first_only` | Reading | `false` | Read only the first bzip2 stream of a file that holds several, such as bzip2 files that were joined. By default every one is read. |
| `autoclose` | Both | `false` | Close the IO beneath the bzip2 stream when the stream ends, such as an IO supplied to `IOStreams.stream`, which IOStreams otherwise leaves open, see [When writing fails](#when-writing-fails). |

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("example.csv.bz2").option(:bz2, block_size: 1).write("name,login\nJack Jones,jjones\n")
~~~

bzip2 data always starts with its header, even when it holds no data, so an empty file is not bzip2 data, and reading
one raises `IOStreams::Errors::Corrupt`, as `bzip2 -d` does.

### Zip

Reading a `.zip` file reads one file within it: the first file, skipping any folders, or the file that
`entry_file_name` names, including its folders:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("offices.zip").option(:zip, entry_file_name: "data/offices.csv").each(:hash) do |office|
  p office
end
~~~

Reading uses the `rubyzip` gem. JRuby reads zip files with Java's own support instead, so it does not need `rubyzip`.

A zip file lists its contents at its end, so it is read from a local file. A local path, and the temp file that an
SFTP path downloads into, are read where they are, while a zip file on S3 or HTTP, or within another stream, such as
`example.csv.zip.pgp`, is first copied into a temp file, see [When temp files are used](config#when-temp-files-are-used).

Reading raises `IOStreams::Errors::StreamFailure`, naming the zip file by the name of the file that is read, such as
its path, the key of an S3 object or the path of a url, tagged with the kind of failure, which is the same on every
platform, see [Errors](errors#what-each-stream-raises):

* `IOStreams::Errors::MissingEntry` when the zip file does not contain the file to read: one of only folders, or one
  without the file that `entry_file_name` names, or where it names a folder:

  ~~~
  IOStreams::Errors::StreamFailure: The zip file /data/offices.zip does not contain the file "data/missing.csv"
  ~~~

* `IOStreams::Errors::Corrupt` when the file within it is corrupt: once all of it has been read, its size, or its
  CRC32 checksum, is not the one that the zip file records. So the block has already read the corrupt data, as with
  any check that needs the whole file:

  ~~~
  IOStreams::Errors::StreamFailure: The file "data.csv" within the zip file /data/a.zip is corrupt: invalid entry CRC (expected 0x9d0b854a but got 0x1e367632)
  ~~~

A file that is not a zip file, or data that cannot be decompressed, also raises an exception tagged as
`IOStreams::Errors::Corrupt`, naming the zip file too.

Writing uses the `zip_kit` gem, which streams the zip file as it is written, without a temp file, even to S3, or into
another stream, such as `example.csv.zip.pgp`. The zip file holds one file, which is named after the path, without the
`.zip` extension and any that follow it, so `example.csv.zip` and `example.csv.zip.pgp` both hold `example.csv`.
`entry_file_name` names it instead, and a stream without a file name, such as one supplied to `IOStreams.stream`, names
it `file`.

| Option | When | Default | Description |
|--------|------|---------|-------------|
| `entry_file_name` | Both | Reading: the first file. Writing: the name of the path without `.zip`, or `file` | The name of the file within the zip file, including its folders, such as `data/offices.csv`. |

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("export.zip").option(:zip, entry_file_name: "people.csv").writer(:hash) do |io|
  io << {"name" => "Jack Jones", "login" => "jjones"}
end
~~~

### Zstandard

Zstandard uses the `zstd-ruby` gem, 2.0.0 or later, which decompresses one zstd block, 128KB, at a time, however well
the data compresses.

JRuby cannot load `zstd-ruby`, which is a C extension, so on JRuby IOStreams uses the
[zstd-jni](https://github.com/luben/zstd-jni) jar instead, which the application adds to the classpath, for example
with jar-dependencies, which is part of JRuby:

~~~ruby
require_jar "com.github.luben", "zstd-jni", "1.5.7-3"
~~~

| Option | When | Default | Description |
|--------|------|---------|-------------|
| `level` | Writing | 3, zstd's default | The compression level, from 1, the fastest, to 22, the best compression, or a negative level, down to -131072, for faster compression still. 0 selects the default. |

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("example.csv.zst").option(:zst, level: 19).writer(:hash) do |io|
  io << {"name" => "Jack Jones", "login" => "jjones"}
end
~~~

* Reading returns the data of every frame of a zstd file, as `zstd -d` does, so zstd files that were joined are read
  as one file.
* Reading checks the checksum of each frame that has one, such as a frame that the `zstd` command wrote, and raises
  `RuntimeError` when the data does not match it. On JRuby each frame that IOStreams writes has a checksum, as the
  `zstd` command writes it. On MRI it does not, since `zstd-ruby` cannot write one.
* Empty data is not zstd, so reading it raises `RuntimeError: zstd decompress error: the data is empty`, as
  `zstd -d` does.
* A file that was cut short, such as by an interrupted download, raises
  `RuntimeError: zstd decompress error: Truncated source`, as `zstd -d` does. IOStreams follows the frames of the data
  itself to find it, since `zstd-ruby` does not report it, and zstd-jni does not report a frame cut off before its
  checksum.

## Encryption

### Symmetric Encryption

`.enc` encrypts with the [Symmetric Encryption](https://encryption.reidmorrison.com/) gem, `symmetric-encryption`,
using the ciphers that the application configures for it, such as in `config/symmetric-encryption.yml` in a Rails
application. When no cipher is configured, reading raises `SymmetricEncryption::ConfigError`, and so does writing,
before the file is opened.

By default each file is compressed with gzip, and then encrypted with a random key and IV of its own. The header at
the start of the file holds them, the key encrypted with the configured cipher, and records whether the data is
compressed, so reading needs no options:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("example.csv.enc").writer(:hash) do |io|
  io << {"name" => "Jack Jones", "ssn" => "123-45-6789"}
end

IOStreams.path("example.csv.enc").each(:hash) do |record|
  p record
end
# => {"name" => "Jack Jones", "ssn" => "123-45-6789"}
~~~

| Option | When | Default | Description |
|--------|------|---------|-------------|
| `compress` | Writing | `true` | Compress the data with gzip before encrypting it. Set `false` for data that is already compressed. |
| `version` | Both | The primary cipher | When writing, the version of the configured cipher to encrypt with. When reading a file without a header, the version of the cipher to decrypt it with, since the header otherwise names it. |
| `cipher_name` | Writing | The cipher of `version` | The OpenSSL cipher to encrypt the data with, such as `"aes-256-cbc"`, with a random key and IV. |
| `random_key` | Writing | `true` | Encrypt with a random key, which the header holds encrypted. Needs `random_iv: true`. |
| `random_iv` | Writing | `true` | Encrypt with a random IV, which the header holds. |
| `header` | Writing | `true` | Write the header. A file is only written without one with `compress: false`, `random_key: false` and `random_iv: false`. |
| `buffer_size` | Reading | 16384 | The number of bytes to read from the file at a time. |

A `version` that is not configured raises `SymmetricEncryption::CipherError` before the file is opened.

Reading a file whose header names a version of the cipher that is not configured raises
`SymmetricEncryption::CipherError`, tagged as `IOStreams::Errors::MissingKey`. Data that the cipher cannot decrypt,
such as data that is damaged, cut short, or encrypted with another key, raises `OpenSSL::Cipher::CipherError`, tagged
as `IOStreams::Errors::Corrupt`, and so does an empty file, which the writer never writes, since encrypting no data
still writes the header, or a block of padding. See [Errors](errors#what-each-stream-raises).

### PGP

`.pgp` and `.gpg` files are encrypted, decrypted, signed and verified with the `gpg` program of GnuPG, which must be
installed wherever they are read or written. Writing needs the recipient to encrypt the file for, and reading the
passphrase of the recipient's private key:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("example.csv.pgp").option(:pgp, recipient: "receiver@example.org").write("name,login\nJack Jones,jjones\n")

IOStreams.path("example.csv.pgp").option(:pgp, passphrase: "receiver_passphrase").read
# => "name,login\nJack Jones,jjones\n"
~~~

See [PGP Encryption](pgp) for creating and importing keys, signing and verifying files, and every option.

## Excel spreadsheets

A spreadsheet, `.xlsx` or `.xlsm`, is read as CSV, one line for each row of its first worksheet, and written from CSV
into a workbook with one worksheet. So the `:line`, `:array` and `:hash` modes apply, and the format of its rows is
always CSV. See [Excel spreadsheets](formats#excel-spreadsheets) for the values that each cell is read as.

### Reading an Excel spreadsheet

Reading uses the `creek` gem, which reads a local file and returns its rows to a block, so the rows are converted into
CSV in a temp file for your code to read. A spreadsheet on S3 or HTTP, or within another stream, is first copied into a
temp file of its own, see [When temp files are used](config#when-temp-files-are-used). Reading takes no options, and
raises `ArgumentError` for `sheet_name`, since it always reads the first worksheet.

A spreadsheet is a zip file of parts, such as its worksheets. Before creek reads it, IOStreams checks the size and the
CRC32 of each part, which creek does not, so that a damaged spreadsheet raises `IOStreams::Errors::Corrupt`, rather than
reading wrong values, see [Errors](errors#what-each-stream-raises).

### Writing an Excel spreadsheet

Writing uses the `xlsxtream` gem, which streams the workbook without a temp file. Its options, `sheet_name`,
`auto_format` and `use_shared_strings`, are described in [Excel spreadsheets](formats#excel-spreadsheets).

## The stream that a block reads or writes

`#reader` and `#writer`, in the `:stream` mode, which is their default, supply the block with the stream closest to your
code. Whichever compression or encryption the file uses, the stream behaves like an IO, so code that reads or writes
it, and a library that takes an IO, such as `CSV`, keeps working when the file name changes, such as from `.gz` to
`.bz2`.

When reading, the stream responds to `#read(length = nil, outbuf = nil)`, `#readpartial`, `#gets`, `#readline`,
`#readlines`, `#each_line` and `#eof?`:

~~~ruby
require "csv"

IOStreams.path("people.csv.bz2").reader do |io|
  CSV.new(io, headers: true).map(&:to_h)
end
# => [{"name" => "Jack", "zip" => "12345"}, {"name" => "Jill", "zip" => "98101"}]
~~~

When writing, it responds to `#write`, with one or more arguments, `#<<`, which returns the stream so that writes can
be chained, `#print`, `#puts` and `#printf`:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("example.txt.gz").writer do |io|
  io << "name," << "login\n"
  io.puts("Jack Jones,jjones")
  io.printf("%s,%s\n", "Jill Smith", "jsmith")
end
~~~

The stream is not the reader or writer of the gem, such as a `Zlib::GzipReader`, so their other methods, such as
`#rewind`, `#pos`, `#lineno`, `#getc` and `#size`, raise `NoMethodError`. To read lines, use `each(:line)`, and where a
library needs a `File`, copy the file into a local file first, see [Copying and moving](copy_files).

An encoding set with `#encoding` is converted by a stream of its own, closest to your code, which reads like an IO that
converts text, such as `File.open(name, "r:Windows-1252:UTF-8")`: what it reads is in the encoding that your code
reads, and its `read(length)` and `#readpartial` return whole characters, up to `length` bytes of them, rather than
bytes. See [Character encoding](streams#character-encoding).

### When writing fails

How a write ends decides whether the stream ends its data, such as the trailer of a gzip file, the last block of a
cipher, or the central directory of a zip file:

* When the block returns, or leaves early, such as with `break` or `return`, each stream ends its data, so what was
  written is a complete file.
* When the block raises, or its thread is killed, the streams do not end their data, so that what was written cannot
  be taken for a complete file. A path then discards it: a local file is removed, an S3 upload is aborted, and an SFTP or
  HTTP file is not uploaded, see [Writing](streams#writing).

An IO that you supply with `IOStreams.stream(io)` keeps what was written to it before the failure, without the end of
the data, so reading it raises, or returns less data than was written:

~~~ruby
io = StringIO.new
IOStreams.stream(io).stream(:gz).writer do |stream|
  stream << "name,login\nJack Jones,jjones\n"
  raise "The source failed"
end
# RuntimeError: The source failed

IOStreams.stream(StringIO.new(io.string)).stream(:gz).read
# Zlib::GzipFile::Error: unexpected end of file
~~~

Discard what the IO holds after a failure. A stream never closes the IO supplied to it, so close it yourself, unless
you set the bzip2 option `autoclose: true`, which closes it.

## Character encoding

The encoding of the text that your code reads and writes is not a stream of the file name: set it on the path with
`#encoding`. It is converted closest to your code, after the file is decompressed or decrypted, so
`IOStreams.path("export.csv.gz").encoding("Windows-1252:UTF-8")` reads a compressed Windows-1252 file as UTF-8 strings.
See [Character encoding](streams#character-encoding).

## Registering a custom extension

To read and write another extension, such as `.xz`, register a format for it with `IOStreams.register_extension`, see
[Registering a format](extending#registering-a-format). To read and write a built-in format under another extension,
see [Another extension for a built-in format](extending#another-extension-for-a-built-in-format).

---

# Copying and Moving Files

`#copy_from` copies a file into the path, and `#copy_to` copies the path into another file. Both read the source a
block at a time while they write the target, so a file of any size can be copied, and both apply the streams of each
file name, so a copy can also convert the file:

* from one storage location to another, such as from SFTP to S3;
* from one compression or encryption to another, such as from `.gz` to `.pgp`;
* from one tabular format to another, such as from CSV to JSON or Parquet.

## Copying a file

Decompress `example.csv.gz` into `example.csv`:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("example.csv").copy_from("example.csv.gz")
~~~

The source can be a file name, a path, or an IO. Encrypt a file with PGP so that only `receiver@example.org` can
read it:

~~~ruby
target = IOStreams.path("example.csv.pgp").option(:pgp, recipient: "receiver@example.org")
target.copy_from(IOStreams.path("example.csv"))
~~~

Copy a file from SFTP to S3, decrypting it on the way:

~~~ruby
source = IOStreams.path("sftp://sftp.example.org/outbound/orders.csv.pgp").option(:pgp, passphrase: ENV.fetch("PGP_PASSPHRASE"))
source.copy_to("s3://my-bucket/imports/orders.csv")
~~~

When a file name has no extensions to say how it is stored, set its streams with `#stream`. Here `CUSTOMER_DATA` was
encrypted with Symmetric Encryption, and is encrypted for `receiver@example.org` with PGP instead:

~~~ruby
input = IOStreams.path("CUSTOMER_DATA").stream(:enc)
IOStreams.path("xyz.csv.pgp").option(:pgp, recipient: "receiver@example.org").copy_from(input)
~~~

A copy without a mode returns the number of bytes copied, as written to the target before its streams.

The source of a copy in the `:array` or `:hash` mode can also be an Active Record relation, whose rows are read with
one query, and written by the types of its columns, see [Exporting queries](queries):

~~~ruby
orders = Order.where(paid: true).select(:id, :amount, :created_at)
IOStreams.path("s3://my-bucket/exports/orders.parquet").copy_from(orders, mode: :hash)
~~~

## Copying as stored

`convert: false` copies the data as it is stored, without applying the streams of either file name, such as to
download a zip file without unzipping it:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("downloads/sample.json.zip").copy_from("https://example.com/files/sample.json.zip", convert: false)
~~~

A copy as stored takes no other options, so any other option raises `ArgumentError`. A copy between two S3 paths with
`convert: false` asks S3 to copy the object itself, without reading it, for an object smaller than 5GB.

## Converting rows and records

With a mode, a copy reads the source, and writes the target, a line, a row or a record at a time, so that it converts
the tabular format too. Copy a CSV file into JSON, parsing and rendering each record:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("target_file.json").copy_from("source_file.csv", mode: :hash)
~~~

The mode is one of:

* `:line`, which copies each line;
* `:array`, which copies each row, after the header row of the source, which gives the target the columns of its
  rows: the header row of a file with one, such as CSV, the keys of the first record of a JSON or Parquet file without
  a schema, or the names of the fields of a file without a header row, such as fixed width;
* `:hash`, which copies each record, so that the target writes the value of each key in its column.

Both copy between any of the formats, such as JSON into CSV:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("people.csv").copy_from("people.json", mode: :array)
~~~

Use `:hash` for JSON whose records do not all have the same keys, since a row has no column for a key that the first
record does not have, so the `:array` mode raises `IOStreams::Errors::InvalidHeader` for it. A blank row of the
source, such as an empty line or a line of only commas, is skipped, see [Blank rows](streams#blank-rows).

## Choosing the columns

The other options of a copy are used to write the target, and the source is read with the settings of its own path,
so describe each file on its own path: its format, encoding and [schema](formats#schema). To choose the columns that
are written, and their order, set a schema on the target, whose fields are the columns written:

~~~ruby
target = IOStreams.path("people.json").schema(
  fieldsMatch: "subset",
  fields:      [
    {name: "name"},
    {name: "age"}
  ]
)
target.copy_from("people.csv", mode: :hash)
~~~

`fieldsMatch: "subset"` skips the other columns of the source. A CSV file without a header row is described by a
schema with `header: false` on its path, whose fields are its columns, in order:

~~~ruby
source = IOStreams.path("people.csv").schema(
  header: false,
  fields: [
    {name: "name"},
    {name: "age", type: "integer"}
  ]
)
IOStreams.path("people.json").copy_from(source, mode: :hash)
~~~

An option that only applies when reading, such as `buffer_size:`, raises `ArgumentError` for a copy, rather than being
ignored, see [Settings on the path, options for each call](streams#settings-on-the-path-options-for-each-call).

## Moving a file

`#move_to` copies the file as it is stored, see `convert: false` above, and then deletes it, so the file keeps its
name's format, compression and encryption, and returns the target path:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("uploads/orders.csv.pgp").move_to("s3://my-bucket/archive/orders.csv.pgp")
~~~

It creates the directories of the target first, and moving onto the same file, by any name, raises `ArgumentError`,
rather than deleting it. So does moving a local file onto an existing directory, rather than into it, as `mv` would:
join the name of the file to the directory, such as `path.move_to(IOStreams.path("archive").join(path.basename))`.
A move within S3 copies the object within S3, with the client and options of the target, such as its `acl:`, and a
move between local files renames the file.

## When a copy fails

* The source is opened before the target, so a source that does not exist, or cannot be read, raises before the target
  is changed. A missing source raises `IOStreams::Errors::NotFound`, wherever it is stored, see [Errors](errors).
* When the copy fails part way, the target is not left with part of the file: a local file is removed, an S3 upload
  is aborted, and an SFTP or HTTP file is not uploaded. An existing target is only replaced once the copy completes on
  S3 and HTTP.
* A move only deletes the source once the copy completed.

## Copying a directory

`#each_child` lists the files of a directory, and `#relative_path_from` names each one relative to the directory, to
copy them into another store:

~~~ruby
source = IOStreams.path("/var/exports")
target = IOStreams.path("s3://my-bucket/exports")

source.each_child("**/*") do |file|
  target.join(file.relative_path_from(source)).copy_from(file, convert: false)
end
~~~

---

# Exporting Queries

IOStreams reads the rows of an Active Record query the way it reads the rows of a file, so one line exports a query to
any format and store that a path names:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("s3://my-bucket/exports/orders.csv.gz").copy_from(Order.where(paid: true), mode: :hash)
~~~

The path decides the format, compression, encryption and storage, so the same code writes CSV in development and
encrypted Parquet on S3 in production, when the path comes from configuration:

~~~ruby
orders = Order.where(paid: true).select(:id, :customer_id, :amount, :status, :created_at)

IOStreams.path(ENV.fetch("ORDERS_EXPORT_PATH")).copy_from(orders, mode: :hash)
~~~

Every format holds the values of these columns, while a column of JSON or binary data needs more care, see
[Columns that need a type](#columns-that-need-a-type).

The query runs once, and its rows are read from the database in small parts while they are written, so the memory
that an export takes does not grow with the number of its rows. Active Record 7.2 or later is needed. PostgreSQL,
MySQL with the `mysql2` gem, and SQLite stream the rows of a query, also on JRuby with the adapters of AR-JDBC, and any
database can read them in batches, see [Each database](#each-database).

## Exporting a query

Copy a relation into a path with `#copy_from`, in the `:hash` mode, which copies each row as a record, or the
`:array` mode, which copies each row as its values, after a header row of the names of the columns:

~~~ruby
paid_orders = Order.where(paid: true).order(:created_at).select(:id, :customer_id, :amount, :status, :created_at)

IOStreams.path("orders.csv").copy_from(paid_orders, mode: :hash)
IOStreams.path("orders.json").copy_from(paid_orders, mode: :hash)
IOStreams.path("orders.parquet").copy_from(paid_orders, mode: :hash)
IOStreams.path("orders.xlsx").option(:xlsx, auto_format: true).copy_from(paid_orders, mode: :array)
~~~

A spreadsheet is written with each value as text, unless `auto_format: true` writes those that look like numbers,
dates, times or booleans as the values of Excel, so that Excel can add up the amounts, and sort by date. It applies to
every column, so text that looks like a number, such as the zip code `01234`, is written as a number too, see
[Excel spreadsheets](formats#excel-spreadsheets).

Select the columns to export with `select`, which can join other tables and compute columns, as any query can:

~~~ruby
report = Order.
  joins(:customer).
  where(paid: true).
  group("customers.name").
  order("customers.name").
  select("customers.name AS customer, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(orders.amount) AS total")

IOStreams.path("totals.csv").copy_from(report, mode: :hash)
~~~

The columns of the file are the columns of the query, in order. Give each column a name of its own with `AS`, since a
record has one value for each name: two columns of the same name raise `ArgumentError`. A column named with `AS` has
the type that the database gives it, rather than that of an attribute, see
[Keeping the types of the columns](#keeping-the-types-of-the-columns).

A copy needs a mode, since a query holds rows rather than bytes, so `copy_from(relation)` without one raises
`ArgumentError`. It returns the number of rows read, header row included, as the copy of a file returns the number of
its lines.

A relation that is read as one query is opened, and its first rows are read, before the copy opens its target, so that
a query that cannot run, such as on a database that cannot stream it, keeps an existing file as it was. A failure after
that, such as of a value that the schema does not accept, fails the copy part way, see
[When a copy fails](copy_files#when-a-copy-fails).

### Into a writer that is already open

A copy into a row or record writer that is already open, such as the one that `writer(:hash)` yields, handed to
`IOStreams.stream`, writes the rows with the settings of that writer, rather than by the types of the columns of the
query, see [Streams of an IO](streams#streams-of-an-io). For example, to write the rows of two queries into one file:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("orders.csv").writer(:hash) do |writer|
  IOStreams.stream(writer).copy_from(Order.where(paid: true).select(:id, :amount), mode: :hash)
  IOStreams.stream(writer).copy_from(ArchivedOrder.where(paid: true).select(:id, :amount), mode: :hash)
end
~~~

So a number is written with the digits that it has, such as `12.5`, rather than with the decimals of its column, unless
the path has a schema.

## Reading the rows of a query

`IOStreams.stream(relation)` returns a stream of the rows of the query, which reads them as the rows of a file are
read, with `#each` or `#reader`:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.stream(Order.where(paid: true)).each(:hash) do |order|
  puts "#{order['id']}: #{order['amount']}"
end
~~~

The keys of each record are the names of the columns, as Strings. `each(:array)` yields a header row of the names of
the columns, and then the values of each row:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.stream(Order.select(:id, :amount)).each(:array) do |row|
  p row
end
# ["id", "amount"]
# [1, 0.125e2]
# [2, 0.3e1]
~~~

`#each` returns the number of rows that it read, header row included, as it returns the number of lines of a file. A
second traversal of the reader that `#reader` yields continues where the first stopped, as for a file.

Each value is cast as `pluck` casts it, which is how the attributes of a model hold it, but without building a model,
so that its methods, such as a reader that it overrides, do not run: an enum attribute is the name of its value, such
as `"shipped"`, an encrypted attribute is its plain text, a JSON column is the value of its JSON, such as a Hash, and a
datetime is an `ActiveSupport::TimeWithZone` in the time zone of the application. The columns of a joined table are
cast by the attributes of its model, such as the enum `tier` of `select("orders.id", "customers.tier")`.

The query runs the SQL, with its binds, that Active Record runs for the relation, so it reads the rows that
`relation.to_a` would read. Before it reads them, a query of no rows, with `LIMIT 0`, describes its columns, once for
each stream. The log of Rails, and the subscribers of Active Record, such as for APM, see these queries as those of
Active Record, with the tags of `ActiveRecord::QueryLogs`: the query that describes the columns as `IOStreams Columns`,
and the query that reads the rows as `IOStreams Query`.

Every row of a query is a record, so a row whose every value is null or empty is read and copied, unlike a
[blank row](streams#blank-rows) of a file, which `skip_blanks: true` would skip.

### Slices of a query

`each(:slice)` yields the rows of a query in slices, as for a file, such as to hand them to other threads or jobs, see
[Background jobs](background_jobs). A slice of a query holds the values of its rows as the query cast them, such as an
`ActiveSupport::TimeWithZone` or a `BigDecimal`, rather than text, in the `:array` format. Each of its rows is a
record, also where the slice is parsed, so a row of nulls is not read as a blank row. Read its rows with the schema of
the query, so that each value is read as its type:

~~~ruby
relation = Order.where(paid: true).select(:id, :amount, :created_at)
schema   = IOStreams.stream(relation).schema

IOStreams.stream(relation).each(:slice, size: 1_000) do |slice|
  queue << slice
end

# Elsewhere, such as in another thread:
IOStreams.stream(queue.pop).schema(schema).each(:hash) do |order|
  p order
end
~~~

Since `slice.to_h` holds the values themselves, a store of slices must keep them. JSON holds a time as text: the
`to_json` of ActiveSupport writes it to the millisecond, while `JSON.generate` writes the text of `Time#to_s`, without
its fraction of a second, which a `datetime` field does not read. BSON keeps a time to the millisecond. So the times of
a stored slice are read back to the millisecond at best, rather than to the microsecond that a database can hold.
A slice of a query holds `"typed" => true`, unless the stream has a schema of its own, so that a value that a store
keeps in another form is read back as its type: a duration, which BSON keeps as its number of seconds, is a duration
again.

## One query or batches

A relation is read as one query, which the database streams to IOStreams, so a sorted, grouped or joined query runs
once, in the order that it asks for. To read a query in the batches of Rails instead, supply what
`relation.in_batches` returns, with its own settings:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("orders.csv").copy_from(Order.where(paid: true).in_batches(of: 5_000), mode: :hash)
~~~

Rails runs two queries for each batch, one that finds the keys of its rows, or where it ends, and then the one that
reads its rows, so the database filters and sorts the rows again for every batch. For a sorted query, that grows with
the size of the table. Exporting 832,995 of 1,000,000 orders to a CSV file on local disk, sorted by an amount without
an index, on PostgreSQL 17 in Docker on a laptop:

| How the rows are read | Export | Queries | Rows that PostgreSQL read |
|-----------------------|--------|---------|---------------------------|
| One query, `order(:amount, :id)` | 12.9 s | 1.7 s | 1,000,000 |
| `in_batches(of: 10_000, cursor: [:amount, :id], use_ranges: true)` | 20.8 s | 9.1 s | 169,000,000 |
| `in_batches(cursor: [:amount, :id])`, 1,000 rows at a time | 61.8 s | 41.6 s | about 834,000,000 |

The time of the export includes casting the values and writing the file, and the time of the queries is the time that
PostgreSQL took to answer them, as Active Record reports it.

Batches still suit a scan of a large table in the order of its primary key, which costs little: `in_batches(of: 10_000)`
exported the same orders, by their ids, in 14.6 seconds. Each batch is a query of its own, so that the database holds
no query, and no snapshot, open from one batch to the next, see
[Connections and transactions](#connections-and-transactions). Each batch is read whole, so its size, `of:`, decides
the memory that it takes.

Rails gives each batch no order of its own, so IOStreams reads the rows of each batch in the order of the primary key,
which is the order of the batches by default. With another `cursor:`, or `order: :desc`, the batches are in that order,
while the rows within each batch are in the ascending order of the primary key, so the rows are in neither order. The
rows of each batch of a model without a primary key are in the order that the database returns them. `cursor:` needs
Active Record 8.0 or later.

Some queries return other rows in batches than as one query, or cannot be read in batches:

* A grouped query, with `group` or `having`, raises `ArgumentError`, since each batch would aggregate only its own rows,
  and so do a distinct query, since each batch would be distinct only within its own rows, and a query with an
  `offset`, which Rails applies to each batch. Read them as one query.
* A relation that was already loaded, such as by `to_a`, `present?` or a preloaded association, is read by the primary
  keys of its records, each row once, as it is now in the database. When its records have no primary key, since the
  model has none, or the query does not select it, it raises `ArgumentError`. To find whether there is anything to
  export, ask `exists?`, which loads no records, rather than `present?`, which loads them all.

A relation that is read as one query is opened before a copy opens its target, see
[Exporting a query](#exporting-a-query), while the batches of a relation are read as the target is written, so a
failure of the first batch fails the copy part way. Rails starts its batches again each time that they are read, so a
second traversal of the reader that `#reader` yields reads no row once the first read them all, and raises
`ArgumentError` when the first stopped early.

The `Enumerator` that `find_each` or `find_in_batches` return without a block raises `ArgumentError`, since it cannot
say how it reads its rows: supply the relation, or `relation.in_batches(...)`.

## Keeping the types of the columns

The types of the columns of the query describe the rows that it reads, as a [schema](formats#schema) does for a file.
`#schema` returns them, such as on PostgreSQL:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.stream(Order.select(:id, :amount, :status, :created_at)).schema
# {fields: [{name: "id", type: "integer", constraints: {required: true}},
#           {name: "amount", type: "number", decimals: 2, constraints: {required: true}},
#           {name: "status", type: "string"},
#           {name: "created_at", type: "datetime", constraints: {required: true}}]}
~~~

A copy gives this schema to a target that has none, so that a Parquet file has a column of the type of each column of
the query, and CSV and JSON write each number with the decimals of its column, such as `12.50`, and each date and time
in ISO 8601. The type of each column is the one that `pluck` casts it by: the attribute of that name of the model, or of
a model that the query joins, otherwise the type that the database gives the column of the result:

| Active Record type | Schema field | Parquet column |
|--------------------|--------------|----------------|
| integer, bigint, or a decimal of scale 0 of up to 18 digits, such as `decimal(10, 0)` | `integer` | int64 |
| a decimal of scale 0 of more digits, such as `decimal(20, 0)`, or MySQL's `bigint unsigned`, as a `BigDecimal` | `number`, with `decimals: 0` | decimal |
| decimal with a scale, such as `decimal(10, 2)` | `number`, with `decimals` of the scale | decimal |
| decimal without a scale, such as a PostgreSQL `numeric`, or a sum that PostgreSQL computes | `number` | needs `decimals` |
| float | `number`, with `floatNumber: true` | double |
| string, text, uuid, an enum | `string` | string |
| a PostgreSQL `inet` or `cidr` address, as the text that PostgreSQL returns, such as `10.0.0.0/8` | `string` | string |
| boolean | `boolean` | boolean |
| date | `date` | date32 |
| datetime | `datetime` | timestamp in UTC |
| time, as the time of its clock in the time zone of the application, see [Times of day](#times-of-day) | `time` | time of day, not adjusted to UTC |
| a PostgreSQL `interval`, as an `ActiveSupport::Duration` | `duration` | the ISO 8601 text of the duration, such as `P1M2DT3H` |
| a PostgreSQL type that Active Record does not know, such as `timetz`, as the text that PostgreSQL returns, such as `17:00:00+02` | `string` | string |
| a PostgreSQL array, such as `text[]`, with an array of addresses as their text | `array` | the JSON text of the array |
| json, binary, a serialized attribute, or a type of the application | `any` | needs a type |

* An attribute that Active Record decorates, such as one that `encrypts` or `normalizes`, has the type of the
  attribute within, so an encrypted string is a `string`. A serialized attribute, also one that is encrypted, and an
  attribute of a type of the application, such as `attribute :price, MoneyType.new`, are `any`, since their values can
  be objects of any class, which a format of text writes as it writes a
  [value without a field](formats#values-without-a-field).
* A column that the query computes, or names with `AS`, has the type that the database gives the column of its
  result, unless it has the name of an attribute of the model. PostgreSQL gives a type to every column, without the
  scale of a decimal, so that a sum is a `number` without decimals. SQLite gives a type only to a column of a table,
  and MySQL to none, so a computed column is `any` there, and on MySQL so is every column named with `AS`. As for
  `pluck`, a column named with `AS` is not cast by the attribute of its column, so an enum is then the number that the
  table holds.
* A column is required, so that its Parquet column is not nullable, when it is `NOT NULL`, the query selects only
  columns of the table of the model, by their names, without joins, and groups by nothing else, and the database
  always gives such a column a value of its type once Active Record casts it: on PostgreSQL an integer, number,
  boolean, date, datetime, time, interval or array, and on MySQL with `mysql2` an integer, number or boolean, since
  `mysql2` reads a zero date, such as `0000-00-00`, which MySQL can hold in a `NOT NULL` column, as nil. On SQLite no
  column is required, since its columns hold values of any type, such as empty text in an integer column, which Active
  Record casts to nil, nor on a database that IOStreams cannot stream a query from, such as MySQL with `trilogy`. A
  string is never required, since it can be empty, and a query that joins another table, computes any column, or
  groups by anything else, such as with `ROLLUP`, requires none of its columns.

### Columns that need a type

A Parquet file needs the type of every column, so a column of `any`, or a number without decimals, raises
`ArgumentError` before the file is written. The other formats write such a column, apart from binary data:

* A JSON column is `any`, since its values can be objects, arrays, or any other JSON value. CSV writes each value as
  its JSON text, and JSON as itself. For Parquet, give it the type `object` when each of its values is an object, or
  `array` when each is an array, which Parquet holds as their JSON text. Otherwise, leave it out, or select its JSON
