  text as a column of another name, such as `details::text AS details_json` on PostgreSQL, which is a `string`. On
  MySQL and SQLite, whose computed columns are `any`, give such a column the type `string` in the schema, see below.
* A binary column is `any` too, and its bytes are not text: CSV writes them as they are, which is not valid UTF-8, so
  reading the file raises `IOStreams::Errors::InvalidEncoding`, and JSON raises it as it writes them. Leave it out,
  or select it as text, such as `encode(image, 'base64') AS image_base64` on PostgreSQL, or
  `TO_BASE64(image) AS image_base64` on MySQL.
* A number without decimals, such as a sum on PostgreSQL, needs its `decimals`.

To give a column a type, set the schema of the query. It replaces the schema of every column, so start from the one
that `#schema` returns, and change the fields that need it:

~~~ruby
report = Order.select(:id, :amount, "SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS running_total")
stream = IOStreams.stream(report)
fields = stream.schema[:fields].map do |field|
  field[:name] == "running_total" ? field.merge(type: "number", decimals: 2) : field
end

IOStreams.path("orders.parquet").copy_from(stream.schema(fields: fields), mode: :hash)
~~~

The rows are then read by that schema, so a value that is not of the type of its field raises
`IOStreams::Errors::InvalidValue`, such as a JSON array for an `object`.

A schema with `header: false` matches its fields to the columns of the query by their position, rather than their
names, so its fields can give them other names. A copy gives that schema to a target without one, `header: false`
included, so a CSV file is then written without a header row, unless the target has a schema of its own.

### A schema of the target

A target with a schema of its own writes by that schema instead, for example to write only some of the columns, or to
give them other names with `aliases`. Its fields are then all that the target knows of the columns, so give each one
its type, such as the decimals of a number, which Parquet needs, and `fieldsMatch: "subset"`, which skips the other
columns of the query, since the default, `"exact"`, raises `IOStreams::Errors::InvalidHeader` for them:

~~~ruby
target = IOStreams.path("orders.csv").schema(
  fieldsMatch: "subset",
  fields:      [
    {name: "order_id", aliases: ["id"], type: "integer"},
    {name: "total", aliases: ["amount"], type: "number", decimals: 2}
  ]
)
target.copy_from(Order.where(paid: true), mode: :hash)
~~~

This also names the columns of the file otherwise without losing the types of the attributes, which naming them with
`AS` in the query would.

### Dates and times

A datetime is read as an `ActiveSupport::TimeWithZone` in the time zone of the application, which CSV and JSON write in
ISO 8601 with its offset, such as `2026-10-01T05:30:15.123456-04:00`, and Parquet as a timestamp in UTC.

A date or time that the query computes, such as `MAX(created_at) AS last_ordered_at`, is not an attribute of the model,
so it is not in the time zone of the application: on PostgreSQL it is a `Time` in UTC, on MySQL a `Time` in UTC of the
type `any`, and on SQLite the text that SQLite holds, such as `2026-10-03 11:00:00`, also of the type `any`. Name the
column after an attribute of the model, such as `MAX(created_at) AS created_at`, or declare an attribute of its name in
the model, such as `attribute :last_ordered_at, :datetime`, so that it is cast as a datetime in the time zone of the
application. On JRuby, the results of AR-JDBC have no types, so a column that the query computes is of the type `any` on
PostgreSQL too, whose value its driver casts, see [JRuby](#jruby).

On PostgreSQL, Active Record casts a date or time of `'infinity'` or `'-infinity'` to `Float::INFINITY`, which a `date`
or `datetime` field does not accept, so the read raises `IOStreams::Errors::InvalidValue` at the first of them. Select
such a column as null when it is not finite, which keeps its type:

~~~ruby
plans = Plan.select(:id, :name, "CASE WHEN isfinite(valid_until) THEN valid_until END AS valid_until")

IOStreams.path("plans.parquet").copy_from(plans, mode: :hash)
~~~

Or select it as its text, such as `valid_until::text AS valid_until_text`, which is `infinity` for an infinite one.

### Times of day

Rails stores a `time` column in UTC, on the date 2000-01-01, and Active Record reads it in the time zone of the
application, so a shift that starts at 09:30 in New York is stored as `14:30:00`, and the application shows `09:30`. A
query reads it as a `time` field, which writes the time that the application shows, its clock, without an offset:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path("shifts.csv").copy_from(Shift.select(:name, :starts_at), mode: :hash)
# name,starts_at
# Morning,09:30:00
~~~

Its value is a `Time` on 2000-01-01, as Active Record holds it, so a time late in the evening of a time zone west of
UTC, which Active Record reads on 1999-12-31, is moved to 2000-01-01, keeping the time of its clock. Parquet holds it as
a time of day, not adjusted to UTC. Active Record reads every `time` column this way, as `pluck` does, also one that
another program filled with local times rather than UTC, whose times then move by the offset of the time zone, so select
such a column as text to export it as stored, such as `starts_at::text AS starts_at_text` on PostgreSQL.

A time outside a day raises `IOStreams::Errors::InvalidValue`, naming the column and the value, rather than export a
wrong one: PostgreSQL's `24:00:00`, the end of a day, which Active Record reads as the start of the next day, or a
MySQL `TIME`, which also holds lengths of time, such as `25:30:00` or `-01:00:00`, which `mysql2` reads as nil, or
raises for. Select such a column as text, or as a number of seconds, such as with `TIME_TO_SEC(duration)` on MySQL. So
that it can check them, IOStreams reads the values of a query with a `time` column on MySQL as the text that MySQL
returns, which it casts as `pluck` does, when Active Record knows the type of every column. A query that also has a
column that only `mysql2` gives a type to, such as one that the query computes, or of a type of the application, is
read as `mysql2` casts it, as are Rails' batches, and a connection with a transaction open, such as in transactional
tests, so there `mysql2` reads a negative `TIME`, or one such as `838:59:59`, as nil, and raises `ArgumentError` for one
such as `25:30:00`, while `24:00:00` raises `IOStreams::Errors::InvalidValue`. `trilogy`, whose queries are read in
batches, also reads a negative `TIME`, or one such as `838:59:59`, as nil.

A PostgreSQL `interval` is read as an `ActiveSupport::Duration`, as a `duration` field, which keeps its months and days
apart from its seconds, and writes it in ISO 8601, such as `P1M2DT3H`. An infinite interval, `infinity` or `-infinity`,
which PostgreSQL 17 holds, raises `IOStreams::Errors::InvalidValue`, since Active Record reads it as nil, which would
export an empty value. Select it as null when it is not finite, such as with
`CASE WHEN isfinite(wait) THEN wait END AS wait`, or as text, such as `wait::text AS wait_text`. A `timetz`, which
Active Record does not know, is read as the text that PostgreSQL returns, such as `17:00:00+02`, as a `string`.

On JRuby, the drivers of AR-JDBC read a time of day themselves, as `pluck` does there:

* Connector/J raises for a MySQL `TIME` outside a day, apart from a negative one of less than an hour, such as
  `-00:00:01`, which it reads without its sign, as `00:00:01`, which IOStreams cannot tell apart from a time of day,
  see [AR-JDBC #1233](https://github.com/jruby/activerecord-jdbc-adapter/issues/1233).
* AR-JDBC raises for PostgreSQL's `24:00:00`, with an exception of Joda-Time that is not a `StandardError`, see
  [AR-JDBC #1232](https://github.com/jruby/activerecord-jdbc-adapter/issues/1232).
* AR-JDBC returns a PostgreSQL `interval` that is zero, infinite, or has less than a millisecond of seconds as text that
  Active Record reads as nil, so an interval column is never required there, see
  [AR-JDBC #1230](https://github.com/jruby/activerecord-jdbc-adapter/issues/1230).
* AR-JDBC returns a `timetz` as a `Time` in UTC, without its offset, of the type `any`, see
  [AR-JDBC #1231](https://github.com/jruby/activerecord-jdbc-adapter/issues/1231).

Select such columns as text, as above, to export them as stored.

## Connections and transactions

A relation that is read as one query is read on a connection of its own, which the query checks out of the pool of
its model, and checks back in when the export ends, or the block is left with `break` or an exception. The block that
the rows are yielded to runs its own queries on the connection of the caller, independently of the read, on every
database:

* The block can read and write the database, such as to update each row that it exports. What it writes is part of
  the transaction of the caller, when the caller has one open, and is otherwise committed at once, whatever happens to
  the export.
* An `ActiveRecord::Rollback` that the block raises reaches the caller, as it would from any other block: it rolls
  back the transaction of the caller, or is raised by `#each` when there is none.
* The read sees what was committed, rather than what the open transaction of the caller has written, which it has not
  committed yet.
* The queries that read the rows skip the query cache, which would keep every row in memory, while the queries of the
  block use the query cache as the caller left it.

So the pool needs a connection free besides the one of the caller. Otherwise the read waits for one, for the
`checkout_timeout` of the pool, 5 seconds by default, and raises `ActiveRecord::ConnectionTimeoutError`, tagged as
`IOStreams::Errors::Unavailable`. A pool needs one connection more than the threads that use it, for each thread that
can export at the same time.

The batches of a relation are read on the connection of the caller instead, as Rails reads them, each batch whole
before its rows are yielded, so they see what the open transaction of the caller has written. The block runs its
queries as it does for one query, and keeps the query cache as the caller left it, while each batch is read without
it.

In the transactional tests of Rails, which share one connection between the test and the application, the pool checks
out that connection for the read too, so the read sees the fixtures, and what the test wrote. An in-memory SQLite
database, and a SQLite database that is not in WAL mode, are read on the connection of the caller instead, see
[SQLite](#sqlite).

One query reads one snapshot of the database for the whole export, so that it reads each row once, as it was when the
export started, however the block, or anything else, changes the table meanwhile, apart from where SQLite reads on the
connection of the caller. Holding that snapshot keeps PostgreSQL from vacuuming, and InnoDB from purging, the old
versions of the rows that change while the export runs, and keeps SQLite from starting its WAL file again. The batches
of a relation each read a snapshot of their own.

To spare a busy primary, export from a replica:

~~~ruby
ActiveRecord::Base.connected_to(role: :reading) do
  IOStreams.path("orders.csv").copy_from(Order.where(paid: true), mode: :hash)
end
~~~

On PostgreSQL, a hot standby that replays the vacuum of rows that the snapshot of an export still needs cancels the
export, once it has waited for `max_standby_streaming_delay`, 30 seconds by default, with an exception tagged as
`Unavailable`, which a retry can meet again. With `hot_standby_feedback` on, the standby does not cancel it, but holds
back vacuum on the primary for as long as the export runs, as an export on the primary does. Raise
`max_standby_streaming_delay` on a standby that exports, which delays its replay instead, or read the query in batches,
whose snapshots each last for one batch. On MySQL, an export on a replica holds back the purge of that replica only.

## Each database

| Database | How a query is read |
|----------|---------------------|
| PostgreSQL, also through PostGIS, with `pg`, or with AR-JDBC on JRuby | A cursor, which fetches 100 rows, then as many as hold about 8 MB of their values, at most 10,000 at a time |
| MySQL, with `mysql2` | The `stream: true` mode of `mysql2`, which reads one row at a time |
| MySQL, with AR-JDBC on JRuby | A streamed result of Connector/J, which reads one row at a time |
| SQLite, with `sqlite3` | A statement of the `sqlite3` gem, which steps through the rows |
| SQLite, with AR-JDBC on JRuby | A statement of sqlite-jdbc, which steps through the rows |
| MySQL with `trilogy`, and any other database | Raises `ArgumentError`: read it in batches |

A query that cannot be streamed raises, before a copy opens its target, rather than read the query in batches without
being asked, so that a query only runs once for each batch when that is the choice. Its message says how:
`IOStreams.stream(relation.in_batches(of: 10_000))`.

### PostgreSQL

A cursor needs a transaction, which the read opens on its own connection, so that the statements of the block are not
part of it. In the transactional tests of Rails, whose connection the read shares, it is a savepoint of the
transaction of the test, which a read that fails rolls back, rather than the transaction of the test.

The `statement_timeout` of the connection that reads the query applies to each fetch, rather than to the whole export,
while the first fetch of a sorted query still waits for the sort. A `SET` on the connection of the caller, such as a
`SET LOCAL statement_timeout` within its transaction, does not reach that connection. So set the timeout of an export
for every connection of the pool that it reads, with the `variables` of its database configuration, such as for the
replica that `connected_to(role: :reading)` reads, see [Connections and transactions](#connections-and-transactions):

~~~yaml
# config/database.yml
production:
  primary_replica:
    <<: *default
    replica: true
    variables:
      statement_timeout: 10min
~~~

Or set it for the role of PostgreSQL that the export connects as, with
`ALTER ROLE exporter SET statement_timeout = '10min'`.

Within the transaction, IOStreams sets `cursor_tuple_fraction` to 1.0, so that PostgreSQL plans the query for every
row, rather than for its first 10%, `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout` to 0, from PostgreSQL 9.6, so that a target
that is slow to write, such as an upload, does not leave the transaction idle for long enough that PostgreSQL closes the
connection, and `transaction_timeout` to 0, from PostgreSQL 17, so that the transaction of a long export is not ended.
They end with the transaction, or are set back in a transaction that was already open, as in transactional tests.

A cursor never runs its query in parallel, so a query that PostgreSQL runs with parallel workers otherwise, such as an
aggregate of a large table, can take longer to export than it takes in `psql`.

When the block raises, or the export is interrupted, such as by `Timeout`, Active Record rolls back the transaction of
the cursor, which cancels a fetch that is still running. On JRuby, PgJDBC waits for a fetch in Java, which a `Timeout`
interrupts only once the fetch returns, see [JRuby](#jruby). A failure to close the cursor, after the block finishes or
leaves with `break`, is raised, so that the export does not return as if it had ended where the block left it.

### MySQL

`mysql2` streams the rows of a query on a connection of its own, which cannot run another query until every row is
read, so that the block queries the database on the connection of the caller, as on the other databases.

MySQL ends a query whose client does not take a row within `net_write_timeout` seconds, 60 by default, so that a slow
target could lose the connection, and `max_execution_time` ends a `SELECT` that runs for longer than it allows, which
counts the time that the client takes to read its rows. While the rows are read, IOStreams raises the
`net_write_timeout` of the session to an hour, unless it is higher, and lifts its `max_execution_time`, and sets them
back afterwards. A limit of the query itself still applies, such as
`Order.optimizer_hints("MAX_EXECUTION_TIME(600000)")`.

Leaving the block early, with `break` or an exception, ends the connection of the read, which ends the query on the
server at once, rather than read the rest of its rows, and the pool connects it again when it is next checked out.

A connection that the read shares with the caller, such as the one of the transactional tests of Rails, is read whole
before the first row is yielded, so that the block can query it.

Leave `prepared_statements` false, the default of `mysql2`, for a connection that IOStreams reads: `mysql2` cannot
stream a prepared statement, and with `prepared_statements: true`, `mysql2` 0.5.7 raises `NoMemoryError` for a query
without rows, such as the one that describes the columns of a query.

`trilogy` reads every row of a query at once, so a query on a connection of `trilogy` raises `ArgumentError`: read it
in batches, whose failures are tagged as they are for `mysql2`, see [Errors](#errors).

On JRuby, the MySQL adapter of AR-JDBC reads a query with Connector/J, which streams the rows of a statement whose fetch
size is `Integer.MIN_VALUE`, which IOStreams sets as the `defaultFetchSize` of the connection of the read, one of its
own, while the statement starts. AR-JDBC gives every statement the `jdbc_fetch_size` of the configuration of the
database instead, when it is set, so a connection whose configuration sets it raises `ArgumentError`: read it in
batches. The statement runs in a transaction of its own, since AR-JDBC runs a statement again after a failure that
Connector/J deems transient, such as a lock wait timeout or a deadlock, unless a transaction is open, which would read
its rows again. Connector/J also sets `net_write_timeout` while it streams, to its `netTimeoutForStreamingResults` of
600 seconds, and afterwards to the value that the session had when it connected, rather than the one that `variables`
set, so IOStreams turns that off while it reads, and raises the limits of the session itself, as above. Leaving the
block early aborts the connection, since Connector/J would read the rest of the rows to close it. The adapter prepares
statements by default, which Connector/J streams too. IOStreams streams only with Connector/J, so a connection of the
adapter with MariaDB Connector/J raises `ArgumentError`: read it in batches.

### SQLite

A statement of the `sqlite3` gem steps through the rows, on a connection of its own when the database is in WAL mode,
the default of Rails, whose readers each read a snapshot that the writes of other connections, such as those of the
block, neither change nor wait for. While a read is open, SQLite cannot start its WAL file again, so the WAL file grows
with every write to the database until the export ends.

An in-memory database, which is a database of its own on each connection, and a database in another journal mode, are
read on the connection of the caller instead, and in the transactional tests of Rails the read shares their connection.
There, a block that changes the rows that the query reads, such as by updating the column that the query is sorted by,
can read them again, without end: change them once the export ends, or read the query in batches of its primary key. In
the other journal modes, a read also keeps the writes of other connections waiting until it ends.

On JRuby, the SQLite adapter of AR-JDBC steps through the rows with sqlite-jdbc, on a connection of its own in WAL
mode, as above.

### JRuby

JRuby cannot load `pg`, `mysql2` or `sqlite3`, which are C extensions, so it reads a query with the adapters of
[AR-JDBC](https://github.com/jruby/activerecord-jdbc-adapter), `activerecord-jdbcpostgresql-adapter`,
`activerecord-jdbcmysql-adapter` and `activerecord-jdbcsqlite3-adapter`, whose drivers are jars. IOStreams is tested
with their pre-release 80.0.pre1, for Active Record 8.0. AR-JDBC yields the rows of MySQL and SQLite to a block as its
driver reads them, so IOStreams reads them on a thread of its own, which hands them over a batch at a time: the first
row as the statement starts, then batches twice the size of the one before, up to 1,000 rows, so that the first rows of
a slow query are read as soon as they arrive. It reads each batch only once the block has taken the rows of the one
before, so that the driver never uses the connection while the block does, and the rows can be read on any thread, as
on MRI.

A `Timeout`, or another interrupt, of an export on JRuby is raised once the driver stops waiting for the database, such
as for the first rows of a slow query, since the drivers wait in Java: PgJDBC once its fetch returns, Connector/J once
the server sends its next packet, which the connection that IOStreams aborted then fails to read, and sqlite-jdbc once
it steps to the next row.

AR-JDBC reads some values differently, as `pluck` does on JRuby:

* Its results have no types, so a column that the query computes on PostgreSQL is of the type `any`, see
  [Dates and times](#dates-and-times).
* It reads some times of day and intervals otherwise, see [Times of day](#times-of-day).
* Connector/J reads a MySQL `YEAR` as a date, which the integer type of Active Record raises for, so set
  `yearIsDateType: false` in the `properties` of the configuration of the database, which reads it as an integer, see
  [AR-JDBC #1234](https://github.com/jruby/activerecord-jdbc-adapter/issues/1234).
* Its drivers raise `ActiveRecord::JDBCError` for every failure, also for a connection that could not be made, see
  [What a query raises](errors#what-a-query-raises).

AR-JDBC applies no query transformers, such as the tags of `ActiveRecord::QueryLogs`, to the statements that it runs,
including the cursor of PostgreSQL, see [AR-JDBC #1227](https://github.com/jruby/activerecord-jdbc-adapter/issues/1227), while IOStreams applies them to the query
that it runs with the driver on MySQL and SQLite, as Active Record does.

## Errors

A failure of the database is tagged, as a failure of storage is, so that an export can be retried on
`IOStreams::Errors::Unavailable`, whether it reads a query or a file: such as when the database refuses the connection,
or loses it, the query is canceled or times out, a lock wait times out, or the pool has no connection free. A failure
that a retry does not change, such as a password that the database rejects, or a table that the user may not read, is
`IOStreams::Errors::PermissionDenied`. No failure of a query is `NotFound`, since a mistake, such as a table that does
not exist, a host that does not resolve, or an error in the SQL, is not tagged, nor is an exception that the block
raises. See [What a query raises](errors#what-a-query-raises) for each database:

~~~ruby
begin
  IOStreams.path(ENV.fetch("ORDERS_EXPORT_PATH")).copy_from(orders, mode: :hash)
rescue IOStreams::Errors::Unavailable => e
  # The database, or the storage of the target, could not be reached: the same export can succeed later.
  puts "Export failed, try again later: #{e.message}"
end
~~~

The message of a failure of the query starts with the name of the query, such as `Order query`, which the exception
answers as its `#display_name`.

A stream of a query is only read, so writing, `#read`, the `:stream` and `:line` modes, `#stream`, `#option`,
`#encoding`, `#raw`, a format other than `:array`, and the options of lines, such as `delimiter:`, raise
`ArgumentError`, as for a slice: copy its rows to a path instead, such as with `copy_to("orders.csv", mode: :hash)`.
So does a file name, which would have no effect on rows that are always in the `:array` format: name the file that the
rows are copied to instead. So do `includes`, `preload` and `eager_load`, which load the associations of models rather
than rows: join their tables with `joins`, and select their columns, instead.

---

# Background Jobs

A large file, such as an upload of a million rows, takes too long to process in a web request, and often too long for
one background job. IOStreams reads the file, wherever it is stored and however it is compressed or encrypted, and hands
your jobs the work in pieces that a job queue can schedule:

* **Slices, for jobs that run in parallel.** Read the file once, cut it into slices of a few hundred rows, and enqueue a
  job for each slice. The workers parse and process the slices at the same time, and a last job writes their results
  to one file.
* **A cursor, for a job that resumes.** One job processes the file in order and keeps the number of the last record
  that it processed, so that when it is stopped, such as by a deploy, it carries on after that record rather than
  starting the file again.

IOStreams only reads the file, cuts the slices and counts the records, while the job queue runs the jobs, so the same
code works with Active Job, whichever backend it uses, such as Solid Queue, Sidekiq or GoodJob, with Sidekiq's own
jobs, and with any other job queue.

## Choosing an approach

| | One job per slice | One job that resumes |
|-|-------------------|----------------------|
| Speed | As fast as the workers that you run | One worker at a time |
| Order of the rows | Any order, which the results are put back in | The order of the file |
| When a worker stops | The queue retries the job of the slice | The job resumes after its cursor |
| Suits | Large imports and exports | Work that must happen in order, or at a limited rate |

Both read the file the same way, so a job can start as one, and change to the other as the files grow.

## Slices

A slice holds up to `size` rows of the file as they are in the file, before they are parsed, such as the lines of a
CSV file, and describes them, so that any worker can parse them on its own:

* **The reader does not parse.** Reading a file in slices only splits it into rows, so the one process that reads the
  file stays fast, and the workers, which run in parallel, do the parsing.
* **A slice describes itself.** It carries the header row of its file and the format of its rows, such as CSV, so a
  worker reads its rows correctly without knowing how, or where, the file was read.
* **A slice is plain data.** It turns into a Hash of Strings, Arrays and Integers, which JSON, a job queue or a database
  stores as it is, and back into a slice where the worker runs.
* **A file is checked before any work starts.** Its header row is matched to the [schema](formats#schema) before the
  first slice is handed on, so a file with the wrong columns raises before any job is enqueued.
* **Each row keeps its place in the file.** A slice holds the line and record number of each of its rows, so a job can
  report the line of a row that fails, and a job that resumes knows where it stopped.

### The parts

| Step | Method | What it does |
|------|--------|--------------|
| Read a file or query in slices | `each(:slice, size: 500)` | Yields slices of the rows, as they are, after checking the header row |
| Write rows into slices | `IOStreams.stream(store)` | Writes the lines, rows or records that your code writes, or copies, to your store, in slices |
| Send a slice elsewhere | `slice.to_h`, `IOStreams.slice(hash)` | Turns a slice into plain data and back |
| Parse a slice | `IOStreams.stream(slice)` | Reads the rows of a slice as the rows of its file, by a schema |
| Resume at a record | `each(:slice, size: 500, resume_at: cursor)` | Reads the slices from the record of the cursor on, see [One job that resumes](#one-job-that-resumes) |
| Write slices to a file | `writer(:slice)` | Writes slices to one file, after their header row, without parsing them when it can |

## One job per slice {#background-jobs}

A job reads the file in slices, and enqueues a job for each one. Job arguments must be plain data, so it sends the Hash
that `slice.to_h` returns, which the job of the slice turns back into a slice with `IOStreams.slice`:

~~~ruby
class ImportPeopleJob < ApplicationJob
  def perform(url)
    IOStreams.path(url).schema(People::SCHEMA).each(:slice, size: 500) do |slice|
      ImportPeopleSliceJob.perform_later(slice.to_h)
    end
  end
end

class ImportPeopleSliceJob < ApplicationJob
  def perform(rows)
    slice = IOStreams.slice(rows)
    IOStreams.stream(slice).schema(People::SCHEMA).each(:hash) do |person|
      Person.upsert(person) if person
    end
  end
end
~~~

where `People::SCHEMA` is the [schema](formats#schema) of the file, a Hash that each process reads once:

~~~ruby
module People
  SCHEMA = JSON.parse(File.read(Rails.root.join("config/schemas/people.json"))).freeze
end
~~~

* The url is configuration, so the same jobs read a local file in development and an S3 object, compressed or
  encrypted, in production, see [Paths](path).
* `each(:slice)` checks the header row of the file against the schema before it yields the first slice, so a file
  whose columns do not match raises `IOStreams::Errors::InvalidHeader` before any job is enqueued.
* Each record is a Hash of its fields, with each value read as its type, such as an Integer or a Date, as `each(:hash)`
  reads the file itself. A blank row is read as `nil`, which is why the job skips it.
* `ActiveJob.perform_all_later` enqueues many jobs at once, such as the jobs of 100 slices, for a backend that enqueues
  them together.

`slice.to_h` holds the rows as they are in the file, the header row, the format, and the numbers of the rows, see
[Find a row in the file](#find-a-row-in-the-file):

~~~ruby
slice.to_h
# => {"rows" => ["Jack,21", "Jill,22"], "header" => ["Name", "AGE"], "format" => "csv", "line_number" => 2,
#     "record_number" => 1}
~~~

* The rows of a file are Strings, and the header row is an Array of Strings, so JSON keeps the Hash as it is. That
  suits every job queue, including Sidekiq's own jobs, whose arguments must be JSON.
* `IOStreams.slice` takes the keys, and the format, as Strings or Symbols, since a queue may change them, and raises
  `ArgumentError` for a Hash that does not describe a slice.
* The header row travels with every slice, so each job reads its rows by the columns of their own file, even when the
  files that feed the same job have their columns in different orders.
* The rows and records that a program writes to a [store of slices](#a-store-of-slices) in the `:array` or `:hash`
  mode are each a record, also when every value is blank, so their slice holds `"blank_rows" => false`. With a schema,
  in the `:array` or `:hash` format, they are the values of its fields themselves, such as Integers and Dates, so
  their slice also holds `"typed" => true`. `IOStreams.stream(slice)` then matches their keys to the schema and hands
  the job each value in the type of its field, also when the queue changed its form: a duration that BSON keeps as its
  seconds is a duration again, and a Date that BSON returns as a Time is a Date. To replace the rows of a slice with
  others in the same form, `slice.with_rows(rows)` returns a new slice that keeps everything else that the slice says.

### Choosing the size of a slice

The size is a trade-off between overhead and memory:

* **Larger slices** mean fewer jobs to enqueue and less overhead per row, but each job holds more rows in memory, and a
  failed job has more rows to retry.
* **Smaller slices** spread the work more evenly across workers, and retry less, but add more jobs and more header rows
  to store.

A few hundred to a few thousand rows is a good place to start. The size is a number of rows, so a file with wide rows
needs smaller slices to keep the arguments of each job small.

### Where to keep the slices

Sending each slice as the argument of its job is the simplest, but a job queue limits the size of a job: Solid Queue
keeps each job in a `text` column, which holds 64 KB on MySQL, Amazon SQS holds 1 MB in a message, and Sidekiq advises
small arguments. A slice of 500 rows of 200 bytes is about 100 KB, so for slices of that size, keep each one in a table
of your own, and enqueue its id. A [store of slices](#a-store-of-slices) receives each slice as it is read:

~~~ruby
class ImportSlices
  include IOStreams::Slice::Target

  def initialize(import)
    @import = import
  end

  def slice_size
    500
  end

  # import_slices has a JSON column, rows.
  def write_slice(slice)
    @import.import_slices.create!(number: slice.record_number, rows: slice.to_h)
  end
end
~~~

~~~ruby
import = Import.create!(url: url)
IOStreams.stream(ImportSlices.new(import)).schema(People::SCHEMA).copy_from(url, mode: :line)

import.import_slices.ids.each do |id|
  ImportPeopleSliceJob.perform_later(id)
end
~~~

The job of each slice then reads it from the table:

~~~ruby
class ImportPeopleSliceJob < ApplicationJob
  def perform(id)
    slice = IOStreams.slice(ImportSlice.find(id).rows)
    IOStreams.stream(slice).schema(People::SCHEMA).each(:hash) do |person|
      Person.upsert(person) if person
    end
  end
end
~~~

* The jobs are enqueued once the whole file has been read, so a file that fails part way through, such as one that is
  cut short, leaves slices to delete rather than half an import, see
  [Hand on the slices only once the file is read](#hand-on-the-slices-only-once-the-file-is-read).
* The number of a slice is the record number of its first row, which orders the slices of an import, and names them in
  a report.
* The table keeps the rows of a failed slice to look at, or to run again.

A slice of text compresses well, so compress it where you keep it, such as in a binary column, with the streams of
IOStreams, which can also encrypt it, see [Compression and encryption](extensions):

~~~ruby
# Compresses the 19 KB of JSON of a slice of 500 short rows to under 3 KB.
def compressed(slice)
  io = StringIO.new
  IOStreams.stream(io).stream(:gz).write(slice.to_json)
  io.string
end

def from_compressed(data)
  json = IOStreams.stream(StringIO.new(data)).stream(:gz).read
  IOStreams.slice(JSON.parse(json))
end
~~~

### Knowing when every slice is done

To act once every slice has been processed, such as to write the results, or to email whoever uploaded the file, use
the batches of your job queue, which call a job of yours once every job of the batch has finished:

~~~ruby
SolidQueue::Batch.enqueue(on_success: ImportFinishedJob.new(import.id)) do
  import.import_slices.ids.each do |id|
    ImportPeopleSliceJob.perform_later(id)
  end
end
~~~

* [Solid Queue](https://github.com/rails/solid_queue#batch-jobs), above, and
  [GoodJob](https://github.com/bensheldon/good_job#batches) batch Active Job jobs, and
  [Sidekiq Pro](https://github.com/sidekiq/sidekiq/wiki/Batches) batches Sidekiq's own jobs. Active Job itself has no
  batches, so the job queue decides how.
* Without batches, let each job of a slice mark its slice as done, and let the job that finds no slice left start the
  final step, within a transaction, so that two jobs that finish together do not both start it.

### Writing the results

When the jobs produce output, such as a status for each person imported, write it to one file at the end. Each job
writes its results as a slice too, to a store that keeps them with the number of its input slice, since jobs finish in
any order:

~~~ruby
class ResultSlices
  include IOStreams::Slice::Target

  def initialize(import_slice)
    @import_slice = import_slice
  end

  def slice_size
    1_000
  end

  # Keeps the results with the number of their input slice, which orders them.
  def write_slice(slice)
    ResultSlice.create!(import_id: @import_slice.import_id, number: @import_slice.number, rows: slice.to_h)
  end
end

class ImportPeopleSliceJob < ApplicationJob
  REPORT_SCHEMA = {
    "fields" => [
      {"name" => "name"},
      {"name" => "status"}
    ]
  }.freeze

  def perform(id)
    import_slice = ImportSlice.find(id)
    slice        = IOStreams.slice(import_slice.rows)
    results      = IOStreams.stream(ResultSlices.new(import_slice)).schema(REPORT_SCHEMA)

    results.writer(:hash) do |io|
      IOStreams.stream(slice).schema(People::SCHEMA).each(:hash) do |person|
        io << {"name" => person["name"], "status" => import(person)} if person
      end
    end
  end
end
~~~

Once every job has finished, such as in the job that the batch calls, write the result slices to the output file, in
the order of the input:

~~~ruby
class ImportFinishedJob < ApplicationJob
  def perform(import_id)
    import = Import.find(import_id)
    report = IOStreams.path(import.report_url).schema(ImportPeopleSliceJob::REPORT_SCHEMA)
    report.writer(:slice) do |io|
      ResultSlice.where(import_id: import.id).order(:number, :id).each do |result|
        io << IOStreams.slice(result.rows)
      end
    end
  end
end
~~~

* The header row is written once, before the rows of the first slice.
* A slice in the format of the file is written as it is, line for line, without parsing its rows. A slice in another
  format, such as CSV results written to a JSON file, is read by its header row and written in the format of the file.
* Every slice must come from the same file, or the same kind of results: a slice with another header row or format
  raises `ArgumentError`.
* `validate: true` parses each row before it is written, to catch a value that is not valid before it reaches the file.
* As for any writer, the file is kept when the block returns, and not when it raises.
* A job whose input slice holds more rows than the `slice_size` of its store of results, 100 unless the store says
  otherwise, writes more than one result slice, each with the number of its input slice, so they are still in the
  order of the input.

## One job that resumes

A job that processes a whole file on its own, in order, can be stopped part way through, such as when its worker is
restarted by a deploy. `resume_at:` reads the file from the record of the number supplied, so the job keeps the number
of the next record to process as its cursor, and supplies it when it starts again:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path(url).each(:slice, size: 100, resume_at: cursor) do |slice|
  process(slice)
  cursor = slice.record_number_at(-1) + 1
end
~~~

* Records are numbered from 1, without the header row, as the slices number their rows, so once a slice is processed,
  the job resumes at the record after its last row, `slice.record_number_at(-1) + 1`.
* `nil` reads the whole file, so the cursor of a job that has not started yet, which is usually `nil`, can be supplied
  as it is.
* The file is read again up to the cursor, since a file cannot be read from the middle, such as when it is compressed,
  but those rows are not parsed, so it is quick. The header row is still read, and matched to the schema.
* `each(:hash, resume_at: cursor)` works too, for a job that keeps a cursor for each record, see
  [Resuming at a record](streams#resuming-at-a-record).
* A query is read again from its start too, so give the relation an order, such as `order(:id)`, so that its rows come
  back in the same order each time, and the rows skipped are those that were processed.
* The job of one slice resumes the same way, with `IOStreams.stream(slice).each(:hash, resume_at: cursor)`, where the
  cursor is one of the record numbers that the slice holds, as `slice.each` gives them, or the one after its last. A
  record before its first row or after the one after its last raises `ArgumentError`, so that a cursor from another
  slice cannot skip its rows. A slice holds only the numbers of its rows, so once a job removes its first or last rows,
  it resumes at a record that the slice still holds.

The job queue decides when to save the cursor, and when to stop the job, so each one is written a little differently.

### Active Job continuations

[Active Job continuations](https://guides.rubyonrails.org/active_job_basics.html), in Rails 8.1 and later, run a job in
steps, and save the cursor of a step with `step.set!`, or with `step.advance!`, which saves the value after the one that
it is given. When its worker is stopping, the job stops at that point, and is enqueued again, to run from the cursor
that it saved:

~~~ruby
class ImportPeopleJob < ApplicationJob
  include ActiveJob::Continuable

  def perform(url)
    step :import do |step|
      IOStreams.path(url).schema(People::SCHEMA).each(:slice, size: 100, resume_at: step.cursor) do |slice|
        Person.transaction do
          IOStreams.stream(slice).schema(People::SCHEMA).each(:hash) do |person|
            Person.upsert(person) if person
          end
        end
        step.advance!(from: slice.record_number_at(-1))
      end
    end
  end
end
~~~

* `step.cursor` is `nil` the first time the job runs, and `step.advance!(from:)` saves the number of the record after
  the last row of the slice, where the job resumes, as the Rails guide does with `find_each(start: step.cursor)` and
  the id of each record.
* Save the cursor once the slice is committed, outside its transaction, since Rails raises
  `ActiveJob::Continuation::CheckpointError` for a cursor saved within one.
* The queue adapter tells the job when its worker is stopping, which those of Solid Queue, Sidekiq and GoodJob do.

### Sidekiq iterable jobs

[Sidekiq's iterable jobs](https://github.com/sidekiq/sidekiq/wiki/Iteration), in Sidekiq 7.3 and later, ask the job
for an Enumerator of each item with its cursor, and call `each_iteration` with each item. Sidekiq saves the cursor of an
item before it processes it, and starts again with that item, so the cursor of a slice is the number of its first
record:

~~~ruby
class ImportPeopleJob
  include Sidekiq::IterableJob

  def build_enumerator(url, cursor:)
    Enumerator.new do |yielder|
      IOStreams.path(url).schema(People::SCHEMA).each(:slice, size: 100, resume_at: cursor) do |slice|
        yielder << [slice, slice.record_number]
      end
    end
  end

  def each_iteration(slice, _url)
    IOStreams.stream(slice).schema(People::SCHEMA).each(:hash) do |person|
      Person.upsert(person) if person
    end
  end
end
~~~

Sidekiq iterates the Enumerator with `each`, so the file is read as the job runs, and closed when the job stops.

### job-iteration

Shopify's [job-iteration](https://github.com/Shopify/job-iteration) runs Active Job jobs that iterate in the same way,
but saves the cursor of an item once it has processed it, so the cursor of a slice is the number of the record after
it, where the job resumes. It expects the Enumerator to be wrapped with `enumerator_builder.wrap`:

~~~ruby
class ImportPeopleJob < ApplicationJob
  include JobIteration::Iteration

  def build_enumerator(url, cursor:)
    slices = Enumerator.new do |yielder|
      IOStreams.path(url).schema(People::SCHEMA).each(:slice, size: 100, resume_at: cursor) do |slice|
        yielder << [slice, slice.record_number_at(-1) + 1]
      end
    end
    enumerator_builder.wrap(enumerator_builder, slices)
  end

  def each_iteration(slice, _url)
    IOStreams.stream(slice).schema(People::SCHEMA).each(:hash) do |person|
      Person.upsert(person) if person
    end
  end
end
~~~

## A file of lines

A file of email addresses, ids or urls, one on each line, has no header row, and its lines are not CSV, which would
take its first line as the header row. Read it in the `:text` format, whose rows are the text of each row as it is, see
[Text](formats#text):

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path(url).format(:text).each(:slice, size: 1_000) do |slice|
  SendInvitationsJob.perform_later(slice.to_h)
end
~~~

~~~ruby
class SendInvitationsJob < ApplicationJob
  def perform(rows)
    IOStreams.slice(rows).each do |email, line_number|
      Invitation.deliver(email, line: line_number) unless email.blank?
    end
  end
end
~~~

`slice.each` yields each row as it is, with its line and record number, so a job of a file of lines needs no schema.

A spreadsheet has no lines: read as `:text`, each row is the CSV text of a row of the sheet, without a line number, its
header row too, and a value that holds a comma or a quote is quoted, see [Text](formats#text), so this job would send an
invitation to the header row, and to quoted addresses. Read the email addresses of a spreadsheet as its records
instead, by a schema that names their column, see [One job per slice](#background-jobs).

## Failures

Decide what should happen when the file, or a job, fails part way through.

### Check the file before handing it on

A file whose header row does not match the schema raises before the first slice. A value that is not valid, such as
`abc` in an integer field, is normally found by the job that parses its row, after the slices before it have been
handed on. To find such rows before any slice is handed on, parse each row while the file is read, with
`validate: true`:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.path(url).schema(People::SCHEMA).each(:slice, size: 500, validate: true) do |slice|
  ImportPeopleSliceJob.perform_later(slice.to_h)
end
~~~

The slices still hold the rows as they are in the file. Validating parses every row twice, once here and once in the
job, so it is worth it when starting work on a file that is only partly valid is worse than reading it slower.

### Hand on the slices only once the file is read

`each(:slice)` yields each slice as soon as it is read, so when reading fails part way through, such as for a value
that is not valid, or a file that is cut short, the slices before the failure have already been handed on. When a job
must process all of a file or none of it, store the slices first, and start the work only once the whole file has been
read, as in [Where to keep the slices](#where-to-keep-the-slices): write each slice to a table under the id of the
upload, then enqueue the jobs once the copy returns, or delete the slices of that id when it raises.

### Find a row in the file

When a row fails, support staff need to find it in the file. A slice holds the numbers of each of its rows:

* **Its line number**, the line of the file that it starts on, as a text editor numbers it. The header row and blank
  lines count, and so does each line of a quoted value that holds line breaks, so the first row of a CSV file whose
  header row is on line 1 is on line 2.
* **Its record number**, the number of the row in the file, counting from 1, without the header row. A blank row counts
  too. IOStreams counts it as it reads the rows into slices.

`slice.line_number_at(index)` and `slice.record_number_at(index)` return them for the row at an index of the slice.
Name them in what the job reports:

~~~ruby
def perform(rows)
  slice = IOStreams.slice(rows)
  index = 0
  IOStreams.stream(slice).schema(People::SCHEMA).each(:hash) do |person|
    Person.upsert(person) if person
    index += 1
  end
rescue StandardError => e
  raise unless slice && index < slice.size

  record = slice.record_number_at(index)
  line   = slice.line_number_at(index)
  raise(e.exception("Record #{record}, on line #{line} of the file: #{e.message}"))
end
~~~

* A row that cannot be parsed raises before it is yielded, so `index` is the index of that row. A blank row is yielded
  as `nil`, so it counts too, which is why this job does not skip blank rows with `skip_blanks: true`.
* `slice.each { |row, line_number, record_number| }` yields each row as it is in the file, with its numbers, such as
  to list the rows of a slice that failed. `slice.line_number` and `slice.record_number` are those of its first row.
* Rows that are not lines of a file have no line number, `nil`, only their record number: the rows of a Parquet file,
  of a query, and rows or records written to a store of slices with `writer(:array)` or `writer(:hash)`, or copied to
  it in those modes.
* The rows of an Excel spreadsheet, `.xlsx`, have no line number either, also once copied to a store of slices in the
  `:line` mode. Its rows are read as CSV text, whose lines are not the rows of the sheet, since a cell that holds line
  breaks takes a line for each. Their record numbers count the rows that are read, and the empty rows of the sheet are
  left out, so a record number is not always the row in Excel either.
* The slices read from a slice, such as with `IOStreams.stream(slice).each(:slice, size: 10)`, keep the line and record
  numbers of its rows.
* A row added to a slice by your code without numbers, see [A slice](#a-slice), has none, `nil`, as do the rows of a
  Hash stored before IOStreams held them.

### Retry a slice

A slice holds everything a job needs, so a job that fails can be retried with the same arguments. Make the processing
of a row safe to repeat, such as with an upsert by a key of the record, since a retried job processes the rows again
that it processed before it failed. The same applies to a job that resumes, which processes again the rows that it
processed after it last saved its cursor.

To process again only the rows from the one that failed, such as once its data is corrected, resume the slice at the
record number of that row, which the job reported, see [Find a row in the file](#find-a-row-in-the-file):

~~~ruby
IOStreams.stream(slice).schema(People::SCHEMA).each(:hash, resume_at: failed_record_number) do |person|
  Person.upsert(person) if person
end
~~~

## A store of slices

Sometimes the rows do not come from a file that you read with `each(:slice)`: your code writes them, such as rows it
builds, or a query, or you want each slice to go straight into a durable store, as in
[Where to keep the slices](#where-to-keep-the-slices). Write them to a store of slices, an object of your own that
receives each slice. Include `IOStreams::Slice::Target` in its class, and implement `#write_slice(slice)`:

~~~ruby
class PeopleSlices
  include IOStreams::Slice::Target

  def initialize(upload_id)
    @upload_id = upload_id
  end

  # Optional: the number of rows of each slice, 100 by default.
  def slice_size
    500
  end

  def write_slice(slice)
    UploadSlice.create!(upload_id: @upload_id, rows: slice.to_h)
  end
end
~~~

`IOStreams.stream(store)` returns a stream that writes to the store in slices, in its format and by its schema, as it
would write a file. Copy a file to it:

~~~ruby
store = PeopleSlices.new(upload.id)
IOStreams.stream(store).schema(schema).copy_from("people.csv.gz", mode: :line)
~~~

Or write records to it:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.stream(store).schema(schema).writer(:hash) do |io|
  io << {"name" => "Jack", "age" => 21}
  io << {"name" => "Jill", "age" => 22}
end
~~~

* **What arrives at the store.** The records are written as lines of the format, CSV unless another is set with
  `#format`, so the slices hold text that any job queue or database stores as it is. The header row is matched to the
  schema before the first slice is written, and each slice carries it, exactly as `each(:slice)` gives them.
* **Lines that are not CSV.** A copy of the lines of a file keeps the format of the file, so read a file of lines in the
  `:text` format, see [A file of lines](#a-file-of-lines), to store its lines as they are:
  `IOStreams.stream(store).copy_from(IOStreams.path(url).format(:text), mode: :line)`. A copy stores each row as its
  source read it, so the CSV text of a row of a spreadsheet read as `:text` stays one row when a cell holds a line
  break, whereas the lines written with `writer(:line)` are split as reading a file of the store's format would split
  them, see [Writing to a store of slices](#writing-to-a-store-of-slices).
* **When the last slice is written.** The last slice is written when the block returns, or leaves early, such as with
  `break`, but not when it raises. So a failed write never hands on a part of its last slice. The slices before it
  were already written, so remove them by the id of the upload, as above.
* **Seeing the header row first.** Implement `#write_header(header)` as well to receive the header row once, as soon
  as it has been read, before the first slice, and also for a file that has a header row and no rows. Use it, for
  example, to record the columns of the upload. It is not called for a file without a header row, such as JSON.
* **Validating as you write.** `validate: true` parses each row before the slice that holds it is written, as for
  `each(:slice)`: `writer(:hash, validate: true)` or `copy_from(path, mode: :line, validate: true)`.

The store decides the size of its slices, rather than each call, since it knows how it keeps them.

### Slices of a query

An Active Record query can be cut into slices the same way, see [Exporting queries](queries). Copy its records to a
store, and they are written as lines of CSV, by the types of its columns:

~~~ruby
relation = Order.where(paid: true).select(:id, :amount, :created_at)
schema   = IOStreams.stream(relation).schema

IOStreams.stream(store).copy_from(relation, mode: :hash)
~~~

The jobs read each slice with the schema of the query, so that each value is read back as its type:

~~~ruby
IOStreams.stream(slice).schema(schema).each(:hash) do |order|
  p order
end
~~~

Rows whose values are all null are records of the query, rather than blank lines of a file, and each slice says so,
so the jobs read them as records.

The query can also be read in slices directly, with `IOStreams.stream(relation).each(:slice, size: 500)`. Those slices
hold the values themselves, such as a `BigDecimal` or a time, rather than text. Active Job can serialize such values,
but a queue whose arguments must be JSON cannot, and JSON keeps a time only to the precision of its text. Copying the
query to a store, as above, gives slices of text that every queue keeps as they are.

## Threads

Slices also share the work of one process between threads. The producer reads the file in slices and puts each one on
a queue, and the workers take slices off the queue and read their records:

~~~ruby
schema = JSON.parse(IOStreams.path("people.json").read)
queue  = Thread::Queue.new

workers = 4.times.map do
  Thread.new do
    while (slice = queue.pop)
      IOStreams.stream(slice).schema(schema).each(:hash) do |person|
        Person.create!(person) if person
      end
    end
  end
end

IOStreams.path("people.csv.gz").schema(schema).each(:slice, size: 500) do |slice|
  queue << slice
end
queue.close
workers.each(&:join)
~~~

* The schema is read once, and its Hash is given to the stream of each slice. A path to the schema file would work
  too, but each slice would read the file again.
* A blank row is read as `nil`, which the worker skips.
* `Thread::Queue#pop` returns nil once the queue is closed and empty, which ends each worker's loop.

## Details

### Reading a file in slices

* Blank lines before the header row are skipped. A blank line after it is a row of its slice, as it is in the file.
  Read the slice with `IOStreams.stream(slice).each(:hash, skip_blanks: true)` to skip it there, see
  [Blank rows](streams#blank-rows).
* A file without a header row, such as fixed width, JSON, a file of lines, or a schema with `"header": false`, gives its
  slices no header row, `nil`.
* A format whose rows are not lines, such as Parquet, gives slices of the records that it reads, which have record
  numbers but no line numbers, see [Find a row in the file](#find-a-row-in-the-file).
* `resume_at:` starts the slices at the record of the number supplied, see
  [One job that resumes](#one-job-that-resumes) and [Resuming at a record](streams#resuming-at-a-record).
* The header row of every slice of a file is the same frozen Array, so change a copy of it.
* `#reader(:slice, size: 500)` yields the reader, whose `#header` is the header row once it has been read, also for a
  file without any rows.

### A slice

A slice holds its rows, and is responsible for them and their numbers, so it is not an Array:

* `slice.each { |row, line_number, record_number| }` yields each row as it is in the file, with its numbers, see
  [Find a row in the file](#find-a-row-in-the-file). A block, lambda or method that takes one argument receives the
  row alone, such as `slice.each(&method(:process))`.
* `slice.rows` returns the rows in an Array of their own, to read them with the methods of an Array, such as `map`.
  Changing that Array does not change the slice.
* `slice.size`, `slice.empty?` and `slice[index]` read the rows as an Array does.
* `slice.header` is the header row of its file, as it was read, and `slice.header?` says whether the slice carries
  one: a slice of a file without one, such as fixed width or JSON, has none. A header row is never blank, so
  `IOStreams.slice` raises `ArgumentError` for one that is, such as `[]`, rather than read the first row as the header
  row.
* `slice.add(row, line_number: 12, record_number: 10)` adds a row after the others, with its numbers, and
  `slice << row` adds one without them, such as a row that is not from a file. A line number or record number is a
  positive Integer, and belongs to a row, so an empty slice has none: give the first row its numbers as it is added.
* `slice[index] = row` replaces a row, such as to correct one that could not be processed, and it keeps the numbers of
  the row that it replaces.
* `slice.delete_at(index)` and `slice.delete_if { |row, line_number, record_number| ... }` remove rows, and the rows
  that are left keep their numbers.
* `slice.drop(count)` returns a new slice of the rows after the first `count`, with their numbers, such as the rows
  still to be processed once the first ones were, and leaves the slice as it is. `slice.from_record(record_number)`
  returns the rows from a record that the slice holds, or from the row after a record between its first and last that
  it no longer holds, or none from the record after its last, or of a slice without rows, and raises `ArgumentError`
  for a record before its first row or after the one after its last.
* Slices are equal when they hold the same rows, with the same numbers, header row and format.
* `slice.to_json` writes the Hash that `slice.to_h` returns, which `IOStreams.slice(JSON.parse(json))` turns back into
  the slice.

When a row does not follow the row before it, such as the row after a quoted value that holds line breaks, the Hash of
the slice lists it under `"jumps"`, as `[index, line_number, record_number]`, and numbers the rows after it from it:

~~~ruby
slice.to_h
# => {"rows" => ["Jack,21", "Jill,\"line one\nline two\"", "Joe,23"], "header" => ["Name", "NOTE"],
#     "format" => "csv", "line_number" => 2, "record_number" => 1, "jumps" => [[2, 5, 3]]}
~~~

### The stream of a slice

`IOStreams.stream(slice)` reads a slice like any other stream, apart from what needs the bytes of a file, which a slice
does not have:

* Its rows start with the header row that the slice carries, so `each(:array)` yields it first, as for a file, and the
  header row is matched to the schema, raising `IOStreams::Errors::InvalidHeader` when they do not match. The rows of
  a slice that carries a header row are read by it even when the schema says `"header": false`.
* The rows of a slice without a header row, such as a slice of a file without one, have none, whatever the schema
  says, so its first row is a record. A schema reads them as its fields in order, as for a file whose schema has
  `"header": false`, so its `fieldsMatch` must be `"exact"`. Without a schema, nothing names their columns:
  `each(:array)` reads them, while `each(:hash)` raises `ArgumentError`, as does a copy of them in the `:array` mode to
  a target that would take its columns from the first row, such as CSV without a schema.
* `#format` is the format of the slice. A slice without a format, such as one turned back from a Hash without one, is
  read as CSV unless its format is set.
* `resume_at:` is one of the record numbers that the slice holds, see [One job that resumes](#one-job-that-resumes),
  and the slices read from a slice keep the line and record number of each of its rows.
* The `:stream` and `:line` modes, `#read`, `#stream`, `#option`, `#encoding` and `#raw` raise `ArgumentError`, since
  the rows of a slice are already split and decoded. Read them from the slice itself, with `slice.each` or
  `slice.rows`, for its rows as they are in the file.
* A slice is only read, so `#writer`, `#write` and `#copy_from` raise `ArgumentError`. Copy its records to a file with
  `copy_to(path, mode: :hash)`.

### Writing to a store of slices

* In the `:line` mode, each line written is a row of the file, after its header row, without a newline after it. A
  line that holds newlines is split into rows the way reading the file back would split it, so a newline inside a
  quoted CSV value stays in its row, while a line of the `:text` format, which has no quotes, is split at each newline.
  A quoted value that is not closed raises `IOStreams::Errors::MalformedDataError` with the number of the line that it
  starts on, as reading the file would, once the text written after it reaches 640KB, or when the block returns, rather
  than keeping the lines written after it in memory. A copy in the `:line` mode stores each row as its source read it
  instead, such as the CSV text of a row of a spreadsheet read as `:text` whose cell holds a newline.
* Each row holds its record number, and in the `:line` mode the line that it starts on, see
  [Find a row in the file](#find-a-row-in-the-file), counting every line written, as reading the file would. The rows
  and records written in the `:array` and `:hash` modes have no line, as for a query.
* The rows of a slice are UTF-8 text, as reading a file gives them. A line in another encoding, such as ISO-8859-1, is
  converted to UTF-8, and the bytes of a binary line are read as UTF-8. A character in a line that is not valid, or
  that UTF-8 does not have, raises `IOStreams::Errors::InvalidEncoding`, with the byte offset and line that reading
  the UTF-8 file would name, counting the header row and blank lines, for example
  `"\xFF" is not valid UTF-8 at byte offset 43 on line 7`. To replace each one instead, set `replace:` on the store's
  stream:

  ```ruby
  IOStreams.stream(store).format(:csv).encoding(replace: "").writer(:line) do |io|
    io << line
  end
  ```
* To clean each line before it is stored, set `cleaner:` on the store's stream, as for a path, see
  [Character encoding](streams#character-encoding): `:printable` removes the characters that are not printable,
  apart from line endings, `:replace_non_printable` replaces them with `replace:`, and a Proc is called with a copy of
  each line written and the `replace:` value, and returns the cleaned text as a String, or raises `ArgumentError`. A
  line is cleaned before it is split into rows, as reading a file cleans its text first, and the header row is cleaned
  too, before it is matched to the schema. Reading a file calls a Proc with each block of text that it reads, rather
  than each line, so a Proc gives the rows that reading the file gives when it cleans each character on its own, as
  the built-in rules do:

  ```ruby
  IOStreams.stream(store).format(:csv).encoding(cleaner: :printable, replace: "").writer(:line) do |io|
    io << "name,note"
    io << "Jack,a\tb"  # stored as the row "Jack,ab"
  end

  # Spaces keep the columns of a fixed width file in place.
  spaces = ->(text, _replace) { text.gsub(/[^[:print:]\r\n]/, " ") }
  IOStreams.stream(store).format(:fixed).schema(schema).encoding(cleaner: spaces).writer(:line) do |io|
    io << "Ja\x01ck     12345"  # stored as the row "Ja ck     12345"
  end
  ```
* `replace:` and `cleaner:` are the only options of `#encoding` that a store takes. For now they apply only to the
  `:line` mode, so the `:array` and `:hash` modes, whose rows and records are usually built by code, raise
  `ArgumentError` when either one is set.
* A copy in the `:line` mode keeps the lines in their format, so the slices are in the format of the source. Setting
  another format on the store's stream raises `ArgumentError`; copy in the `:array` or `:hash` mode to convert the
  rows instead.
* A store holds slices of rows rather than bytes, so the `:stream` mode, `#write`, `#stream`, `#option`, an encoding
  set with `#encoding`, `#raw`, `#file_name`, and a format whose rows are not lines, such as Parquet, raise `ArgumentError`. Compress or
  encrypt the slices where the store keeps them, see [Where to keep the slices](#where-to-keep-the-slices). It is only
  written, so `#each`, `#reader` and `#read` raise `ArgumentError` too.
* A store whose class inherits methods named `slice_size`, `write_header` or `write_slice` keeps them:
  `IOStreams::Slice::Target` calls them rather than its defaults.

---

# Errors

When a path's storage fails, for example because the file does not exist, the path raises the exception that its
storage raised, such as `Errno::ENOENT` for a local file or `Aws::S3::Errors::NoSuchKey` for S3. It tags that
exception with the kind of failure: `IOStreams::Errors::NotFound`, `PermissionDenied` or `Unavailable`.

Likewise, when a stream cannot read the data of a file, for example because a file named `.gz` is not gzip data, or a
zip file does not contain the file to read, the stream raises the exception of its gem, such as
`Zlib::GzipFile::Error`, tagged with the kind of failure: `IOStreams::Errors::Corrupt`, `MissingEntry` or
`MissingKey`.

Rescue the kind of failure, rather than the exception from one storage or one gem, so that the same code keeps working
when the path changes, for example from a local file in development to S3 in production, or from `.gz` to `.zip`. See
[Paths are configuration](config#paths-are-configuration). It also keeps working when IOStreams replaces the gem that
reads a stream with a newer or better one, or reads it with another library on another platform, as JRuby reads zip
files with Java.

## Rescue the kind of failure

~~~ruby
path = IOStreams.path(ENV.fetch("IMPORT_PATH"))

begin
  path.each(:hash) do |record|
    Order.import(record)
  end
rescue IOStreams::Errors::NotFound => e
  logger.info("Nothing to import yet: #{e.display_name}")
end
~~~

The same rescue handles the missing file whether `IMPORT_PATH` is `~/imports/orders.csv`,
`sftp://sftp.example.org/~/orders.csv`, `s3://my-bucket/imports/orders.csv` or
`https://example.org/orders.csv`.

Rescuing the exception of one storage only works for that storage:

~~~ruby
# Avoid: misses a file that does not exist on S3, SFTP or HTTP.
rescue Errno::ENOENT

# Avoid: has to know every storage, and also rescues SFTP and HTTP failures that are not a missing file.
rescue Errno::ENOENT, Aws::S3::Errors::NoSuchKey, IOStreams::Errors::CommunicationsFailure
~~~

## Rescue a file that cannot be read, whatever its streams

~~~ruby
path = IOStreams.path(ENV.fetch("IMPORT_PATH"))

begin
  path.each(:hash) do |record|
    Order.import(record)
  end
rescue IOStreams::Errors::Corrupt => e
  logger.error("#{path.display_name} cannot be read, ask for it to be sent again", e)
end
~~~

The same rescue handles a file that is damaged, cut short, or not what its file name says at all, whether `IMPORT_PATH` is
`orders.csv.gz`, `orders.csv.bz2`, `orders.csv.zst`, `orders.zip`, `orders.csv.enc`, `orders.csv.pgp` or `orders.xlsx`.

Rescuing the exception of one gem only works for that stream:

~~~ruby
# Avoid: misses a corrupt file once the file name changes to .bz2 or .zip.
rescue Zlib::GzipFile::Error
~~~

A key that is missing, or a passphrase that is wrong, is a problem of the configuration rather than of the file, so it
raises `IOStreams::Errors::MissingKey` instead, which sending the file again will not fix:

~~~ruby
begin
  path.each(:hash) do |record|
    Order.import(record)
  end
rescue IOStreams::Errors::MissingKey => e
  raise(ConfigurationError, "Check the PGP keys and passphrase for #{e.display_name || path.display_name}")
end
~~~

## The exception tree

The kinds of failure are modules that tag the exception that the storage, or the gem of a stream, raised:

* `IOStreams::Errors::StorageError`: the storage of a path, or the database of a query, failed, see
  [What a query raises](#what-a-query-raises). Every kind of failure of the storage includes it.
  * `IOStreams::Errors::NotFound`: the file, a directory that it is in, or its S3 bucket, does not exist.
  * `IOStreams::Errors::PermissionDenied`: the storage does not permit the access, or the credentials for it are
    missing or not valid.
  * `IOStreams::Errors::Unavailable`: the storage could not be reached, or could not handle the request at the time,
    so that the same request can succeed when it is made again later.
* `IOStreams::Errors::StreamError`: a stream, such as gzip or zip, cannot read the data of the file. Every kind of
  failure of a stream includes it.
  * `IOStreams::Errors::Corrupt`: the data is not valid in the format of its stream: it is damaged, cut short, or
    not in that format at all, such as a text file named `.gz`, or it uses a part of the format that the stream does
    not support, such as a zip file encrypted with a password.
  * `IOStreams::Errors::MissingEntry`: the file does not contain the entry to read, such as a zip file without the
    file named by `entry_file_name`, or without any file at all.
  * `IOStreams::Errors::MissingKey`: a key that reading the data needs is missing, or cannot be used: the secret key
    that decrypts a PGP file is not in the keyring, or its passphrase is missing or wrong, the public key that checks
    its signature is not in the keyring, or the cipher of the version that encrypted an `.enc` file is not configured.

A failure of the storage is never a failure of a stream, so rescuing `NotFound` does not rescue a zip file without
the file to read, which reading again will not fix.

IOStreams raises these classes itself:

* `IOStreams::Errors::Error`, a `StandardError`:
  * `IOStreams::Errors::AccessDenied`: the path is not within the allowed paths, see
    [Allowed paths](security#allowed-paths). It is not a `PermissionDenied`, see below.
  * `IOStreams::Errors::CommunicationsFailure`: an SFTP or HTTP request failed. It is also tagged with the kind
    of failure when the failure is known, such as a `404 Not Found` response.
  * `IOStreams::Errors::StreamFailure`: a stream found that it cannot read the data, such as a zip file that does not
    contain the file to read, or a file within a zip file whose CRC32 is not the one that the zip file records. It is
    tagged with the kind of failure, `Corrupt` or `MissingEntry`.
  * `IOStreams::Errors::MissingHeader`: the columns are needed, but are not known: to write a header row when they
    are not set, or, with a schema, to read a row of a file with a header row before the header row is read.
  * `IOStreams::Errors::InvalidHeader`: the columns of a file do not match its [schema](formats#fieldsmatch): when
    reading, a header row, or the keys of a JSON record, has columns that `fieldsMatch` does not allow, or is missing
    a required field, or a row has values after its last column that the schema does not skip, and when writing, the
    keys of a record, or the columns or values of a row, that the schema does not skip.
  * `IOStreams::Errors::TypeMismatch`: a row or record cannot be converted to the format, such as, with a schema, a
    row written that is neither a Hash nor an Array, or a JSON line that is not an object.
  * `IOStreams::Errors::DelimiterNotFound`: no line delimiter was found within the maximum line length.
  * `IOStreams::Errors::InvalidValue`: a value is not of the type of its field in the schema, or a field that is
    required has no value, see [Schema](formats#schema), or a time of day that a query reads is outside a day, or an
    interval that it reads is infinite, see [Times of day](queries#times-of-day).
  * `IOStreams::Errors::InvalidLineLength`: a fixed width line does not have the length of its schema.
  * `IOStreams::Errors::ValueTooLong`: a value does not fit within its fixed width field.
  * `IOStreams::Errors::InvalidLayout`: nothing raises it since v3.0 removed the layout of a fixed width file, which a
    schema replaces, see [Upgrading](upgrading#format_options-is-replaced-by-schema). It is kept so that code that
    rescues it still works.
* `IOStreams::Errors::MalformedDataError`, a `RuntimeError`: a quoted value is not closed, by the end of the data
  or within 10 blocks of lines, 640KB by default, see [Lines](streams#lines). Its `#line_number` is the line that the
  value starts on.
* `IOStreams::Errors::InvalidEncoding`, an `Encoding::UndefinedConversionError`: the data is not valid in the
  encoding that it is read or written in, such as UTF-8. Its `#byte_offset` is the offset of the first invalid byte
  within the data after any decompression or decryption, and its `#line_number` is the line that it is on, when it
  is read a line at a time, such as with `each(:line)` or `each(:hash)`, where the lines before it are read first.
  Lines written to a store of slices with `writer(:line)` raise it at the byte offset and on the line that reading
  them from a file would, also for a character that UTF-8 does not have, see [Slices](background_jobs#writing-to-a-store-of-slices).
  The JSON format checks the text of each key and value that it writes, before its line is written, so it raises it
  at the byte offset within that key or value, without a line, such as
  `In a key or value written to JSON, "\xE9" is not valid UTF-8 at byte offset 3`.
  For example `"\xE9" is not valid UTF-8 at byte offset 1043 on line 12`. As an `Encoding::UndefinedConversionError`,
  its `#error_char` is the invalid bytes, and its `#source_encoding` and `#destination_encoding` the encodings that
  they were read and checked as.
* `IOStreams::Pgp::Failure`, a `StandardError`: gpg failed, for example to decrypt a file or to check its signature,
  or could not be run. When gpg reports why it could not read a file, it is tagged with the kind of failure, see
  [What each stream raises](#what-each-stream-raises).

## What each storage raises

The exception that each storage raises, which is tagged with the kind of failure:

| Kind of failure | Local file | S3 | SFTP | HTTP |
|-----------------|------------|----|------|------|
| `NotFound` | `Errno::ENOENT`, or `Errno::ENOTDIR` below a file | `Aws::S3::Errors::NoSuchKey`, `NoSuchBucket`, `NoSuchVersion`, or `NotFound` from a HEAD request | `IOStreams::Errors::CommunicationsFailure` when reading or writing, or `Net::SFTP::StatusException` | `IOStreams::Errors::CommunicationsFailure` for `404 Not Found` or `410 Gone` |
| `PermissionDenied` | `Errno::EACCES` or `Errno::EPERM` | `Aws::S3::Errors::AccessDenied`, `InvalidAccessKeyId`, `SignatureDoesNotMatch`, `ExpiredToken` and the like, `Forbidden` from a HEAD request, or `Aws::Errors::MissingCredentialsError` | `IOStreams::Errors::CommunicationsFailure` when reading or writing, `Net::SFTP::StatusException`, or `Net::SSH::AuthenticationFailed` | `IOStreams::Errors::CommunicationsFailure` for `401 Unauthorized`, `403 Forbidden` or `407 Proxy Authentication Required` |
| `Unavailable` | Never | `Seahorse::Client::NetworkingError` when S3 cannot be reached, or `Aws::S3::Errors::SlowDown`, `InternalError`, `ServiceUnavailable`, `RequestTimeout`, or a `429`, `500`, `502`, `503` or `504` response, once the AWS SDK has retried the request | `IOStreams::Errors::CommunicationsFailure` when reading or writing, a connection error such as `Errno::ECONNREFUSED` or `SocketError`, or `Net::SSH::Disconnect` | A connection error such as `Errno::ECONNREFUSED`, `SocketError` or `Net::ReadTimeout`, or `IOStreams::Errors::CommunicationsFailure` for `408`, `429`, `500`, `502`, `503` or `504` |

A Google Cloud Storage path makes its requests with the AWS SDK, so it raises the exceptions of the S3 column, and
also tags `Aws::S3::Errors::AuthenticationRequired`, `InvalidAuthentication` and `InvalidSecurity`, which Cloud Storage
raises for credentials that are missing or not valid, as `PermissionDenied`.

A host name that does not resolve, such as a mistyped host, is not `Unavailable`, see [Notes](#notes).

SFTP reads and writes files with the `sftp` program, and uses the `net-sftp` gem for everything else, such as
`#each_child`, `#exist?` and `#delete`.

A failure that is none of these kinds raises its exception without a tag, such as an SFTP host key that does not
match, or an HTTPS certificate that is not trusted.

## What a query raises

Reading the rows of an Active Record query, such as with `IOStreams.stream(relation)` or
`path.copy_from(relation, mode: :hash)`, tags the exception that its database raised in the same way, so that an export
can be retried on `Unavailable`, whether it reads a query or a file:

| Kind of failure | Any database, through Active Record | PostgreSQL | MySQL | SQLite |
|-----------------|-------------------------------------|------------|-------|--------|
| `NotFound` | Never | Never | Never | Never |
| `PermissionDenied` | `ActiveRecord::DatabaseConnectionError` for a user name or password that the database rejects, when its driver does not say otherwise | `PG::InsufficientPrivilege`, for a table or column that the user may not read, or `PG::ConnectionBad` for credentials that the server does not accept, by any method of authentication, such as a password, a client certificate, peer, PAM or LDAP, a role that may not log in, or connect to the database, or a host that `pg_hba.conf` rejects | `Mysql2::Error` of mysql2, or `Trilogy::Error` of trilogy, for an access that MySQL denies, such as error 1045 for a password that it rejects, 1044 for a database that the user may not use, 1142 for a table that the user may not read, or 1370 for a function that the user may not run, or for an account that it does not let connect, such as 3118 for one that is locked, 1862 for one whose password has expired, or 1130 for a client host that no account allows | `SQLite3::PermissionException` or `SQLite3::AuthorizationException` |
| `Unavailable` | `ActiveRecord::ConnectionNotEstablished`, such as `ConnectionTimeoutError` when no connection is free in the pool, when its driver does not say otherwise, `ActiveRecord::QueryAborted`, such as `QueryCanceled`, `StatementTimeout`, `AdapterTimeout` or `ConnectionFailed`, `ActiveRecord::LockWaitTimeout`, or `ActiveRecord::TransactionRollbackError`, such as `Deadlocked` | `PG::ConnectionBad` for a server that refused the connection, could not be reached, timed out, is starting up or shutting down, or has no connection free, or a temporary failure to resolve its host, `PG::AdminShutdown` or `PG::CrashShutdown` for a server that ended the query, `PG::IdleInTransactionSessionTimeout` for a session that it ended, and `PG::UnableToSend` for a query that could not be sent, since the connection was lost | `Mysql2::Error` of mysql2, or `Trilogy::Error` of trilogy, for a connection that was refused or lost, a temporary failure to resolve its host, too many connections, a server that is shutting down, a lock wait timeout, a deadlock, or a query that `KILL QUERY` or `max_execution_time` interrupted, also while mysql2 streams the rows of the query, `Mysql2::Error::TimeoutError` or `Trilogy::TimeoutError` for the `read_timeout` of the driver, and `Trilogy::EOFError` for a connection that the server closed | `SQLite3::BusyException` or `SQLite3::LockedException`, for a database that another connection has locked |

On JRuby, the adapters of AR-JDBC raise `ActiveRecord::JDBCError` for every failure of their driver, also for a
connection that could not be made, rather than `ActiveRecord::ConnectionNotEstablished`, apart from a database that does
not exist, or that the user may not use, which is `ActiveRecord::NoDatabaseError`, and a query that PostgreSQL cancels,
which is `ActiveRecord::QueryCanceled`. It is tagged by the `java.sql.SQLException` of the driver that it wraps:
